answer_a:
Title: Structurally-Grounded Automated Literature Review Generation via
Citation-Graph-Guided Section PlanningProblem: Generating a coherent,
comprehensive, and correctly cited literature survey from a corpus of papers is
an open challenge. Existing approaches (e.g., extractive summarization, naive
retrieval-augmented generation) produce reviews that either (a) list papers
sequentially without organizing them into a narrative structure, (b) hallucinate
citations or misattribute claims, or (c) fail to cover the breadth of a field
because they lack explicit awareness of how papers relate to one another
(support, contradict, extend, apply). A literature review is fundamentally a
structured argument about the state of a field, not a compressed document.
Current methods treat structure as a post-hoc decoration rather than a
first-class planning objective.

Hypothesis: If a system first constructs a citation graph over the input paper
set, extracts structural roles (seminal work, baseline, improvement,
application, rebuttal) and relationship types (extends, contradicts, reproduces,
benchmarks) from citation contexts, and uses these to plan
hierarchically-organized sections before generating prose, then the resulting
literature review will achieve higher citation-fidelity, better topical
coverage, and more coherent narrative flow than systems that generate sections
either sequentially or from flat retrieval.

Method: We propose a three-stage pipeline:

 1 Citation-Graph Construction & Role Assignment. Given a query topic and a seed
   set of papers (from the initial corpus), construct a directed citation graph.
   For each edge, extract the citing sentence and classify the relationship into
   one of five categories using a fine-tuned sentence encoder: extends,
   contradicts, reproduces, benchmarks-against, or unrelated. Simultaneously,
   assign each paper a structural role (seminal, baseline, state-of-the-art,
   survey, application, tool/dataset) based on its citation profile (in-degree,
   recency, h-index of venue) and abstract content.
 2 Hierarchical Section Planning. Use a planner (e.g., an LLM prompted with
   graph statistics or a lightweight learned policy over section templates) to
   produce a two-level outline. At level1, sections correspond to topic clusters
   extracted from the citation graph via community detection (e.g., Louvain on
   co-citation edges). At level2, within each section, papers are ordered by a
   combination of role priority (seminal → baseline → SotA → extension) and
   chronological flow. Each section's plan specifies: (a) which papers to cite,
   (b) what relationship narrative to use (e.g., "X extended Y by..."), and (c)
   a one-sentence section thesis summarizing the contribution of that group of
   papers to the field.
 3 Controlled Generation with Citation-Grounded Decoding. Generate section text
   section-by-section using an LLM prompted with (i) the section thesis, (ii)
   the ordered paper list with extracted relationship sentences, and (iii) the
   full abstract of each paper. To reduce hallucination, we apply a
   citation-grounded decoding constraint: after each generated sentence, the
   model must select at least one citation from the paper list for that section;
   generation stops per section when all planned citations for that section have
   been used or the section thesis has been fully addressed. No cross-section
   citations are permitted unless a paper appears in two planned sections (which
   is allowed with a cross-reference marker).

Dataset / Benchmark: We use the SciReviewGen corpus (introduced by Luu et
al.,2024), which pairs query topics with full gold-standard survey papers and
their reference lists. We filter for topics where at least15–25 papers in the
gold survey are available as full text (via S2ORC or unpaywall). This yields
approximately80–120 evaluation topics across computer science subfields. Each
gold review is split into sections at the level-2 heading depth.

Evaluation Metrics:

 • ROUGE-1/2/L and BLEU for n-gram overlap with gold reviews (standard measure,
   known limitations).
 • Citation-F1 (proposed): the F1 score over the set of cited papers per
   section, compared against the gold review's reference list per section.
   Penalizes hallucinated citations and missing required citations.
 • Narrative Coherence (proposed): human evaluation (5-point Likert) of logical
   flow, section-to-section transitions, and thesis clarity, rated by at least3
   annotators per example on30 randomly sampled topics.
 • Factual Consistency: measured via DeBERTa-based NLI (entailment rate between
   generated claims and source abstracts), averaged across all sections.
 • Coverage: fraction of gold-reference papers that appear in the generated
   review at least once.

Baselines:

 1 Naive RAG: retrieve top-10 papers per query, generate a flat list-style
   summary via GPT-4o (no structure planning).
 2 Sequential Section Generation: section-level retrieval (K=5 papers per
   section) with GPT-4o, sections generated in order with no cross-section
   planning (Gidiotis & Tsoumakas,2023).
 3 Topic-Model-Guided: LDA on all paper abstracts → topic clusters → generate
   one paragraph per topic → concatenate (standard text mining baseline).
 4 Our Method (Full): the full pipeline described above.
 5 Ablation: No Graph Roles: same pipeline but skip role assignment — use
   community detection only, no relationship-edge labels.

Ablations (Table-3 style):


 Variant  Component Removed                  Expected Impact
 -GR      Citation-graph role assignment     Reduced citation-F1 (model cannot
                                             distinguish seminal from
                                             peripheral papers)
 -HD      Hierarchical section planning;     Reduced narrative coherence
          replace with flat                  (sections become independent
          topic-to-section mapping           blocks)
 -CGD     Citation-grounded decoding         Increased hallucination rate;
          constraint; allow free generation  reduced citation-F1
 -IDE     Idea-direction evolution from      Isolated effect of not leveraging
          memory                             previously-proven research
                                             directions from prior idea
                                             generations


Expected failure modes and how they are handled:

 • Fragmentary output. If community detection produces too many small clusters
   (e.g.,20+ for25 papers), sections become too narrow. Mitigation: merge
   clusters smaller than3 papers into the nearest large cluster.
 • Citation assignment errors. Classifying "extends" vs "benchmarks-against" is
   ambiguous in dense subfields (e.g., LLM evaluation). Mitigation: use a
   confidence threshold (p ≥0.65); below threshold, default to "unrelated" and
   omit the edge from planning.
 • Thesis drift during generation. The LLM may generate text that wanders from
   the section thesis. Mitigation: include the section thesis as a fixed prefix
   prompt term; after the draft, run an entailment classifier between generated
   sentences and the thesis; flag and regenerate sentences that fall below a0.5
   entailment threshold.

Limitations:

 • The method depends on the availability of a reasonably complete citation
   graph. Fields with sparse citation practices or small paper counts (<10) may
   yield poor results.
 • Citation roles are assigned heuristically; a paper's actual contribution may
   not match its citation-profile-based role (e.g., a highly-cited paper that is
   primarily a method survey may be misclassified as "seminal").
 • The generation step uses a closed-source LLM (GPT-4o), introducing
   reproducibility concerns and potential API-level drift over time. All
   experiments will log exact model, temperature (0.3 for all), and seed
   parameters.
 • Human evaluation for narrative coherence is expensive and covers only a
   subset of topics. We will report inter-annotator agreement (Krippendorff's α)
   and release annotation guidelines.
 • The citation-grounded decoding constraint is a soft heuristic (prompt-level
   instruction + post-hoc filtering), not a trained decoding objective, and may
   occasionally be ignored by the model despite the prompt.

Title: Structured Critical Literature Review Generation via Hierarchical
Contradiction-Aware Synthesis---

Problem
Current automated literature review systems (LLM-based or
retrieval-augmented) produce fluent but shallow summaries — they list findings
paper-by-paper, avoid conflicting results, and fail to organize knowledge into
the canonical sub-topics, debates, and open questions a human reviewer would
surface. No existing system explicitly models contradictions across papers or
generates a structured review with sections like "consensus findings,"
"conflicting evidence," and "methodological gaps."

Hypothesis
A hierarchical, contradiction-aware pipeline that (1) retrieves and
clusters papers by sub-topic, (2) extracts claim-level triples (method, finding,
direction of effect), and (3) explicitly identifies and resolves or flags
contradictions, will produce literature reviews that are rated by domain experts
as more organized, more critical, and more useful than retrieval-augmented
baselines that only summarize per-paper or per-topic.

Method
Stage1 — Hierarchical topic structuring. Given a query (e.g.
"chain-of-thought reasoning"), query a paper corpus (e.g. S2ORC / Semantic
Scholar) and cluster retrieved abstracts using a hierarchical embedding +
LLM-labeling pipeline (HDBSCAN on SBERT embeddings, then GPT-4o-mini assigns
canonical section headings).

Stage2 — Claim extraction and contradiction detection. For each paper, extract
structured claim triples (entity, predicate, direction/sign) via a fine-tuned
DeBERTa-v3 or prompted LLM. Within each sub-topic cluster, compare claim triples
for directional mismatches (e.g. "CoT improves accuracy on GSM8K" vs "CoT does
not improve accuracy on GSM8K"). Flag contradictions with supporting citations
on both sides.

Stage3 — Contradiction-aware synthesis. Generate the review section-by-section
using a controlled generation loop: (a) draft a section from the consensus
claims, (b) conditionally append a "conflicting evidence" sub-section if
contradictions were detected, (c) append an "open questions" sub-section
identifying gaps where evidence is absent or contradictory.

Stage4 — Citation grounding and fact verification. Each generated claim is
back-linked to the original source passage. A lightweight fact-verification step
(NLI-based, e.g. TrueTeacher) verifies whether the generated claim is entailed
by the cited passage. Unverifiable claims are removed or softened.

Dataset / Benchmark- Corpus: Semantic Scholar Open Research Corpus (S2ORC) — ~8M
papers, with full text when available. Restrict to4-5 well-surveyed domains
(e.g., LLM reasoning, protein folding, adversarial robustness, representation
learning, NLP for low-resource languages).

• Gold-standard reviews: For each domain, collect2-3 human-written survey
papers (e.g. from arXiv, JMLR, ACL anthology). Segment into sections as
ground-truth structure.
• Review quality evaluation set: Construct50 query-review pairs per domain,
each with3 expert ratings along organization, coverage, critical depth, and
usefulness (1–5 Likert).

Evaluation Metrics| Dimension | Metric | How measured |

|---|---|---| | Structure | Section overlap (ROUGE-L / Jaccard on section
headings) | Against human survey TOC | | Coverage | Recall of cited papers from
human survey reference list | Macro-averaged per section | | Critical depth |
Contradiction recall — fraction of known conflicting findings surfaced |
Hand-labeled conflict set | | Faithfulness | % of claims entailed by cited
passages | NLI-based verification + human spot-check | | Overall quality |
Expert rating (1–5) on organization, usefulness | Blind rating by3 domain
experts |

Baselines1. Naive RAG — Retrieve top-20 papers, concatenate abstracts, prompt
GPT-4o to write a review.

2 Per-paper summarization — Summarize each paper individually, then concatenate
under LLM-generated headings (Liu et al.,2024-style).
3 Topic-cluster summarization — Cluster papers by topic, summarize cluster,
then synthesize (similar to Scim,2024).
4 Ours w/o contradiction detection — Same pipeline but skip Stage2
contradiction flagging (ablate the core mechanism).

Ablations- A1: Remove hierarchical clustering → flat topic list (tests whether
hierarchy improves organization).

• A2: Remove fact-verification filter (tests whether filtering reduces
hallucination at the cost of coverage).
• A3: Replace GPT-4o claim extraction with fine-tuned DeBERTa-v3 (tests whether
a smaller model suffices).
• A4: Remove contradiction-aware sub-section generation → always write
consensus-only text (tests the value of explicit contradiction flagging vs.
implicit handling).

Expected Failure Modes1. Contradictions are rare or subtle. Most papers in a
well-matured field may agree on fundamentals, leaving little for the
contradiction module to surface. Mitigation: evaluate on at least one rapidly
evolving domain (e.g., LLM reasoning post-2023) where disagreements are common.

2 Claim extraction noise propagates. A false-positive contradiction (two claims
that appear contradictory but differ in experimental setup) degrades the
review. Mitigation: require supporting citations on both sides; add a
confidence threshold for contradiction flagging.
3 Expert raters prefer concise over critical. Human readers may rate a fluent,
uncontroversial summary higher than one that honestly reports messy
disagreements. Mitigation: structure expert evaluation to score critical
depth and usefulness separately from fluency and organization.
4 Structure diversity across human surveys. Two human surveys on the same topic
often use different section taxonomies, making section-overlap metrics noisy.
Mitigation: use macro-averaged ROUGE-L and report variance; also report
expert agreement (Fleiss' κ) on organization.
5 Domain shift. A pipeline tuned on NLP papers may fail for biomedical or
physics literature where citation practices and claim phrasing differ.
Mitigation: hold out one domain for final evaluation only, to measure
generalization.

answer_a:
Ablation variant -IDE: idea-direction evolution disabled. No prior memory or
distilled research directions are used. The proposal below is generated from the

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

TitlePhoneme-Bootstrapped Self-Supervised Learning for Low-Resource Speech
Recognition

ProblemAutomatic speech recognition (ASR) for low-resource languages remains a
fundamental bottleneck in speech technology. While self-supervised learning
(SSL) models (wav2vec2.0, HuBERT, WavLM) achieve strong results when fine-tuned
on hundreds of hours of labeled data, most of the world's ~7,000 languages have
fewer than10 hours of transcribed speech. In this setting, standard SSL
fine-tuning collapses: the model overfits to the small labeled set and fails to
generalize to unseen acoustic conditions, speakers, and lexical variation. The
core problem is that the SSL pre-trained representations encode rich acoustic
structure but lack an explicit inductive bias toward phonemic invariance, which
is precisely what a low-resource learner most needs.

HypothesisH1 (primary): Introducing a phoneme-discovery bottleneck between the
SSL encoder and the downstream transcription head will improve low-resource ASR
word error rate (WER) by at least15% relative over standard SSL fine-tuning when
labeled data ≤10 hours.

H2 (auxiliary): The benefit of the phoneme bottleneck is largest when the
bottleneck is learned jointly (not frozen) and constrained via a
minimum-edit-distance loss at the phoneme-sequence level, rather than
frame-level cross-entropy alone.

Rationale. A discrete phoneme bottleneck forces the model to map continuous SSL
representations into a small inventory of language-agnostic sound categories.
This acts as a strong regularizer — it throws away irrelevant acoustic detail
(speaker identity, noise type) and retains only phonemically salient structure.
Because the bottleneck is shared across fine-tuning and inference, it decouples
the transcription decoder from the full variability of the SSL representation
space.

MethodWe propose Phone-Bootstrapped SSL (PB-SSL), a three-stage pipeline:

Stage1 — Phoneme tokenizer (unsupervised). Given the target language's unlabeled
audio (any amount, including the same untranscribed data), train a small
(2-layer) HuBERT-style discrete tokenizer with a K-means codebook of size K
=128. This produces a frame-level phoneme-like token sequence for every
utterance. No transcriptions are used.

Stage2 — SSL encoder + bottleneck. Load a pre-trained SSL backbone (wav2vec2.0
Base,95M params). Insert a phoneme bottleneck module between the encoder output
and the downstream head:

 • A linear projection to256 dims → a Gumbel-Softmax discrete bottleneck with128
   codes → a learned embedding lookup.
 • Two decoding paths:
 • Phoneme-path: Predicts the frame-level phoneme token sequence from Stage1
   (cross-entropy + minimum edit distance (MED) loss between predicted and
   target token sequences, computed via differentiable approximations of
   Levenshtein distance).
 • Transcription-path: The discrete bottleneck output is fed into a lightweight
   transformer (2 layers,4 heads) that produces character-level logits.
 • A shared weight term α balances phoneme-path loss vs. transcription-path
   loss: L_total = L_ctc + α * (L_ce_phone + λ * L_med).

Stage3 — Joint fine-tuning. Fine-tune both paths jointly on the labeled
low-resource data. The phoneme-path is not frozen — it receives gradient from
both losses, allowing the bottleneck to adapt to the target language's phonology
during fine-tuning.

Discrete bottleneck. Use straight-through Gumbel-Softmax with temperature
annealing (τ:2.0 →0.5 over training). This is close to a hard categorical
selection during inference, producing a transparent phoneme-like representation
that can be inspected.

Dataset / BenchmarkPrimary: Common Voice11.0 — select three languages with <10
hours validated transcribed speech:

 • Language A (Tamashek / taq): ~6 hours — typologically distant from English,
   tests generalization- Language B (Dholuo / luo): ~8 hours — Niger-Congo,
   tonal (tests tone encoding)
 • Language C (Erzya / myv): ~4 hours — Uralic, agglutinative (tests
   morphological complexity)

**Development sets:**30 minutes per language (official dev splits). **Test
sets:**1 hour per language (official test splits).

Secondary: FLEURS (Federated Learning for Extended-Resource Speech) — use
the2-hour low-resource splits for Fongbe and Limburgish to test cross-benchmark
transfer.

**Unlabeled data per language:**50–200 hours of in-domain unlabeled audio from
Common Voice raw recordings and YouTube audio — used only for the Stage1 phoneme
tokenizer.

Evaluation Metrics1. Word Error Rate (WER) — primary metric, case-insensitive,
evaluated on the official test set.

 2 Phoneme Error Rate (PER) — on the phoneme-path output, to measure bottleneck
   quality.
 3 Normalized Mutual Information (NMI) between bottleneck code assignments and
   ground-truth phoneme categories (where available via external phonological
   lexicons) — measures how well the bottleneck aligns with linguistic phonemes.
 4 Effective codebook utilization — proportion of the128 codes activated on
   held-out data. Low utilization (<20%) indicates codebook collapse.
 5 WER confidence intervals — bootstrap resampling (1,000 samples) over the test
   set, reported as95% CIs.

Baselines1. Tight lower bound: Fine-tune the SSL encoder directly with a linear
projection + CTC head on the same data (no bottleneck).

 2 Standard SSL fine-tuning (upper bound reference): Same as (1) but with the
   full10-hour labeled set (no ablation on data size).
 3 Wav2vec2.0 + K-means pseudo-labeling: The standard pseudo-labeling baseline
   where the speech is discretized and the model is trained on pseudo-labels
   before fine-tuning (Xu et al.,2021).

Research Proposal: Confidence-Gated Iterative Pseudo-Labeling with
Phoneme-Constrained Augmentation for Low-Resource ASRTitle: Semi-Supervised
Self-Training with Audited Pseudo-Labels and Phoneme-Preserving Augmentation for
Under-10-Hour Speech Recognition---

Problem
State-of-the-art ASR systems (e.g., Whisper, wav2vec2.0) degrade
catastrophically when fine-tuned on fewer than10 hours of transcribed speech.
Two failure modes dominate: (1) overfitting to the small labeled set, and (2)
confirmation bias in self-training, where the model reinforces its own errors
through noisy pseudo-labels on unlabeled data. No existing method jointly
addresses label quality and data diversity in the under-10-hour regime on a
single pipeline.

Hypothesis
A self-training loop that audits pseudo-labels through a separate
confidence calibrator (rather than the ASR model's own softmax) and couples them
with phoneme-preserving augmentations (time-stretch, pitch-shift, and speed
perturbation clipped to per-phoneme duration bounds) will outperform standard
pseudo-labeling and unsupervised pre-training when labeled data ≤10 hours. The
key claim: auditing prevents confirmation bias, and phoneme-constrained
augmentation prevents the augmentations from destroying linguistic content that
the small labeled set cannot recover.

Method1. Seed model — Fine-tune a small SSL encoder (wav2vec2.0 Base, ~95M
params) on the labeled set (≤10 h). Use a single linear projection head.

2 Pseudo-labeling loop (3 rounds):

• Decode the unlabeled pool with the current model (CTC greedy decoding).
• Audit each pseudo-label: pass the logits to a separate lightweight confidence
estimator (a2-layer MLP over mean-pooled encoder features, trained on the
seed set's held-out fold) and retain only utterances where estimated
confidence ≥0.9 threshold.
• Combine audited pseudo-labeled utterances with the original labeled set.

3 Phoneme-constrained augmentation — Before each training epoch, apply:

• Time stretching (0.85x–1.15x) with per-phoneme duration floor.
• Pitch shift (±2 semitones).
• Speed perturbation (0.9x–1.1x).
• Constraint: a forced-alignment phoneme recognizer (pretrained multilingual)
verifies that the augmented audio's phoneme sequence matches the original;
discard any augmentation where >20% of phonemes shift.

4 Re-train the SSL encoder + projection head from the seed checkpoint on the
combined (labeled + audited pseudo-labeled + augmented) data. Repeat for3
rounds.

Dataset / Benchmark- Primary: Common Voice (Tamil, Sinhala, Catalan, Kyrgyz —4
languages with2–8 h of validated train data each). Evaluate on each language's
official dev/test splits.

• Secondary (sanity check): FLEURS10-hour subset for2 additional languages
(Swahili, Bengali).

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Purpose |

|---|---| | Character Error Rate (CER) | Primary metric; report mean ± std over3
seeds. | | Word Error Rate (WER) | Secondary, for languages with space-delimited
orthography. | | Pseudo-label acceptance rate | Diagnostic: % unlabeled
utterances retained per round. | | Oracle accuracy of accepted pseudo-labels |
Diagnostic: if a held-out reference exists for the unlabeled pool, measure what
fraction of accepted labels are correct. |

Report effect sizes with95% bootstrap confidence intervals across seeds.

Baselines| Baseline | Why |

|---|---| | Seed-only (fine-tune on labeled data only, no self-training) | Lower
bound — isolates the value of unlabeled data. | | Standard pseudo-labeling (no
auditing, no augmentation) | Ablates the audit mechanism. | | No-augmentation
self-training (audit + pseudo-label, no phoneme constraint) | Ablates the
augmentation contribution. | | SpecAugment self-training (SpecAugment instead of
phoneme-constrained augmentation) | Compares against a widely-used augmentation
baseline. | | wav2vec2.0 Base fine-tuned on full Common Voice (where available,
e.g., Catalan ~80 h) | Upper bound — what performance looks like with abundant
data. | | Whisper Small zero-shot | Compares against a strong multitask model
that has never seen the target language during adaptation. |

Ablations1. Audit threshold sweep — Vary the confidence threshold
(0.7,0.8,0.9,0.95) on one language to measure the precision-recall trade-off in
pseudo-label acceptance.

2 Augmentation constraint strength — Compare the phoneme-preserving constraint
against an unconstrained version (same augmentations, no phoneme-validity
check).
3 Number of self-training rounds — Compare1,2,3, and5 rounds on one language to
measure when performance plateaus or degrades.
4 Size of labeled seed — Sub-sample to1 h,2 h,5 h on a language with8 h
available, and measure whether the method's advantage grows as labeled data
shrinks.

Expected Failure Modes1. Phoneme-constraint too aggressive — The multilingual
forced-aligner may have poor accuracy on a target language it was not trained
on, causing most augmentations to be discarded. Mitigation: Relax the threshold
to40% phoneme shift tolerance; also measure the discard rate and report it.

2 Confidence estimator is poorly calibrated — On languages far from the seed
set, the auditor may either accept noisy labels (false positive) or reject
correct ones (false negative). Mitigation: Use temperature scaling (Platt
scaling) on the confidence estimator; report calibration curves (ECE) per
round.
3 Diminishing returns by round3 — The model may saturate because the unlabeled
pool's acoustic diversity is exhausted. Mitigation: If WER improvement from
round2→3 is <0.5% relative, stop early and report the saturating round as a
finding.
4 CTC beam search decoding with a weak language model — Without a
target-language n-gram or neural LM, decoding may be brittle. Mitigation: Do
not use an external LM for the main experiment (to keep the ablation clean),
but add a shallow fusion with a3-gram LM as a secondary ablation to measure
the orthogonal gain.
5 Hardware constraints — Self-training with augmentation on the full unlabeled
pool (typically50–200 h per language) may be slow. Mitigation: Downsample the
unlabeled pool to20 h per language via random sampling, stratified by speaker
if speaker metadata is available.

Research Proposal: Breaking the Performance Ceiling of Small Language Models via
Targeted Capacity Allocation## Title
Beyond Scaling Alone: Targeted Capacity
Allocation for Breaking the Performance Ceiling of Sub-1B Language Models

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Small language models (<1B parameters) exhibit a well-documented but
poorly understood phenomenon: diminishing returns past a critical data scale,
where additional tokens yield negligible or even negative performance gains on
held-out benchmarks. This "performance ceiling" is typically attributed to
insufficient model capacity, but recent evidence suggests that capacity is not
uniformly the bottleneck — certain capabilities (e.g., factual recall,
long-range reasoning) saturate earlier than others (e.g., syntactic fluency,
in-context pattern matching). The research problem is: Can we identify the
precise structural causes of saturation in small models and design targeted
interventions that reallocate limited capacity to the binding constraints?

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Primary hypothesis: The performance ceiling in small models is driven
by capacity-competition between world-knowledge memorization and compositional
reasoning pathways, not by a global lack of parameters. When a small model
saturates, additional training data primarily overfits its already-congested
feedforward memory (FFN layers) while the attention-based compositional routing
remains underutilized.

Secondary hypothesis: A structured intervention that decouples these two
functions — compressing factual knowledge into a fixed, non-parametric memory
(retrieval augmentation with a small bottleneck) and freeing FFN parameters for
compositional reasoning — will raise the ceiling by10–20% on reasoning-heavy
benchmarks while matching or exceeding baselines on factual recall.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
The proposal has three stages:

Stage1: Ceiling CharacterizationTrain a350M-parameter decoder-only transformer
on increasing data scales (50M,100M,250M,500M,1B,2B,5B,10B tokens). At each
checkpoint, measure per-capability saturation curves across five categories:
factual recall, syntactic well-formedness, short-range reasoning (2 hops),
long-range reasoning (5+ hops), and in-context learning. Use influence functions
and representation similarity (CKA between hidden states at different data
scales) to identify which layers/modules saturate first and correlate with which
capability.

Stage2: Bottleneck DiagnosisInsert capacity probes — lightweight linear
classifiers at each layer that predict whether a given capability fires — to
identify the specific (layer, module) pairs where representation collision
occurs. The hypothesis is that mid-to-late FFN layers become the bottleneck for
factual recall while lower attention layers saturate for compositional
reasoning.

Stage3: Targeted Capacity AllocationIf the diagnosis confirms the hypothesis,
intervene by:

• Retrieval-Augmented Distillation (RAD): Compress the factual knowledge stored
in FFN layers into a small external memory (a frozen key-value store with ~4K
slots). Shrink the model's FFN hidden dimension by25–40% and retrain from
scratch, relying on retrieval for factual queries and freeing FFN capacity
for reasoning.
• Optional control arm: Compare against a naive "bigger FFN" baseline (same
total parameters, no retrieval) to confirm that how capacity is allocated
matters more than how much.

If the diagnosis contradicts the hypothesis (e.g., attention is the bottleneck),
pivot to attention head pruning + reallocation — removing redundant heads to
increase per-head dimensionality.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark- Training: A deduplicated, controlled-quality mix of C4
(natural language), MathPile (math/reasoning), and a synthetic factual QA
dataset (Wiki-QA, ~2M question-answer pairs with provenance). All tokenized with
the same tokenizer to avoid confounds.

• Evaluation (4 benchmarks):
• Factual recall: NaturalQuestions, TriviaQA (exact match)
• Short reasoning: BigBench-Hard subset (boolean expressions, causal judgment)
• Long reasoning: GSM8K (grade-school math, multi-step), HotpotQA (multi-hop
retrieval)
• In-context learning: MMLU (5-shot)
• Saturation diagnosis: Custom probe tasks —500 hand-written examples per
capability with controlled difficulty levels.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Rationale |

|--------|-----------| | Accuracy (per benchmark) | Primary capability-level
metric | | Saturation threshold (η) | The data scale (in tokens) at which
performance plateaus within1% of final value | | Representation Collapse Score
(RCS) | Average pairwise CKA similarity >0.95 between adjacent data-scale
checkpoints in bottleneck layers — a proxy for when representations stop
differentiating | | Parameter-Utilization Efficiency (PUE) | Per-point
improvement per million train tokens normalized by model size; captures
diminishing returns | | Retrieval Hit Rate (RAD variant only) | Fraction of
queries where the external memory returns the correct factual document |

Primary success signal: RAD variant achieves >10% relative improvement on GSM8K
and HotpotQA over the350M baseline at the same total parameter budget, without
regressing more than2% on NaturalQuestions.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines1. Standard350M decoder (no intervention) — the ceiling-establishing
baseline2. 350M with increased FFN dimension (+25% FFN, -25% attention heads,
same total params) — tests whether naive capacity reallocation achieves similar
gains3. 350M with vanilla RAG (retrieval + standard model, no capacity
reduction) — tests whether retrieval helps regardless of capacity rebalancing4.
Distilled350M from a7B teacher (knowledge distillation alone) — tests whether
the ceiling is a training limitation vs. architectural5. 550M standard decoder
(more parameters entirely) — the "just scale up" ceiling comparison---

Ablations1. RAD without FFN shrinkage — does retrieval help when FFN capacity is
not freed?

2 RAD with different memory sizes (2K,4K,8K slots) — sensitivity to memory
bottleneck3. RAD applied at different layers (early vs. mid vs. late FFN) —
where is compressed storage most effective?
3 Retrieval-free control — train the shrunken-FFN model without retrieval;
isolates whether the gain comes from the architecture change or the
retrieval5. Ceiling characterization on a different architecture (e.g., a350M
MoE with same total params) — is the ceiling mechanism architecture-specific?

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes| Failure Mode | Mitigation / Response |

|---|---| | No clear bottleneck emerges (all modules saturate simultaneously) |
The pluralistic-ceiling hypothesis fails. Fallback: test if training recipe (LR
schedule, weight decay) is the real ceiling — ablate optimizer settings. | | RAD
improves reasoning but kills factual recall >2% | Memory size was too small.
Re-run with16K slots or use a learned gating mechanism to route queries. | |
Naive FFN-increase baseline matches or beats RAD | Capacity allocation is not
the bottleneck; the ceiling is truly total-parameter-limited. Concede and report
the negative result as a contribution (important for the community). | | No
ceiling observed (performance continues scaling linearly at10B tokens) | The350M
model was too large for the data scales tested. Scale up to50B tokens or test
a100M model to find the ceiling. | | RAD improves only on seen-document queries
(memorization, not generalization) | Evaluate on held-out timestamps and topics.
If gains vanish, the retrieval store is overfitting to the training set.
Introduce a stricter train/test split on documents. | | CKA-based diagnosis is
inconclusive | Supplement with probing classifiers and leave-one-out accuracy
drops to cross-validate which layers matter for each capability. |

Compositional Constraint Propagation: A Modular Reasoning Framework for
Multi-Step Agentic Tasks### ProblemCurrent LLM-based agents exhibit brittle
performance on tasks requiring sustained multi-step reasoning. When a chain of
deductions spans more than3–5 steps, error rates compound: a single incorrect
intermediate inference propagates forward, and the final answer degrades
non-linearly with chain length. Existing mitigations — chain-of-thought
prompting, self-consistency sampling, and verification loops — treat reasoning
as a left-to-right autoregressive process and do not structurally isolate
sub-problems. As a result, agents cannot reliably backtrack, re-derive a
corrupted intermediate value, or verify a partial solution before consuming it
as input to the next step. This places a hard ceiling on tasks like multi-hop QA
over conflicting documents, nested tool-use planning, and
constraint-satisfaction problems with interdependent variables.

HypothesisWe hypothesize that decomposing multi-step reasoning into a
constraint-propagation graph — where each node is a self-contained sub-reasoning
module that communicates only through typed, verifiable intermediate assertions
— reduces end-to-end error rates compared to monolithic autoregressive
generation. Specifically:

▌ H1 (Primary). A structured constraint-propagation framework that
▌ materializes intermediate assertions as typed variables with explicit
▌ pre-conditions and post-conditions will improve accuracy on multi-step
▌ deductive benchmarks by at least15% (absolute) over chain-of-thought
▌ baselines, at comparable token cost.

▌ H2 (Robustness). The framework's advantage grows monotonically with task
▌ depth: on tasks requiring ≥6 reasoning steps, the accuracy gap over CoT will
▌ be ≥25% absolute.

▌ H3 (Debugability). When the model produces an incorrect final answer, a
▌ trace over the constraint graph will identify the offending node with ≥80%
▌ precision, enabling targeted re-generation of only the faulty sub-step.

MethodCore Architecture — Constraint Propagation Network (CPN).

A two-phase pipeline executed per query:

Phase1: Decomposition (one-shot). The model is prompted to parse the query into
a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of reasoning nodes. Each node specifies:

 • A natural-language description of its sub-goal.
 • Input slots (typed variables required from parent nodes).
 • Output slots (typed variables produced).
 • A verification predicate — a short natural-language statement that must hold
   true after the node executes (e.g., "the sum of allocated resources ≤ total
   budget").

This phase uses a structured output format (JSON with a fixed schema). No
execution happens yet.

Phase2: Execution with constraint propagation. Nodes are processed
topologically:

 1 A node checks that all input slots are populated and their verification
   predicates hold. If an input predicate fails, the node enters a
   back-propagation state that signals the upstream node to re-generate.
 2 The node invokes the LLM to compute its output given the verified inputs. The
   prompt includes only the node's description and its verified inputs — no full
   history, no other nodes.
 3 The output is checked against the node's own verification predicate.

 • If it passes, the output is committed and downstream nodes become eligible.
 • If it fails, the node re-samples (up to3 attempts with temperature=0.7,
   feeding the verification error as a correction signal). After3 failures, the
   node enters a diagnostic mode that logs the failure and escalates to a
   meta-controller.

A meta-controller (a separate LLM call, invoked only on escalation) decides
whether to re-decompose a subgraph or fall back to standard CoT for that
sub-problem.

Graph serialization invariant. The full CPN is encoded into a single prompt
context window on each call — no dynamic memory roll-up. Node outputs are stored
as structured fields within the prompt, not in an external database.

Dataset / BenchmarkThree evaluation sets targeting different facets of complex
reasoning:


 Benchmark                   Depth       Primary Challenge          Size (test)
 MuSiQue (multi-step QA)     2–4 hops    Irrelevant context,        1,500
                                         composition
 LogiQA2.0                   3–8 steps   Logical deduction,         800
                                         negation
 AgentTool (synthetic;       4–10 steps  Planning under resource    500
 curated from ToolBench and              constraints, conditional
 API-Bank)                               branching


For AgentTool, each instance specifies: available tools (with capabilities and
costs), a goal, a budget constraint, and a set of distractors (tools with
plausible-looking but irrelevant capabilities). The ground truth is a valid
tool-use plan (sequence of calls) that achieves the goal within budget.

All benchmarks are open-source, static, and free of data leakage concerns for
the models evaluated.

Evaluation MetricsPrimary metric:

 • End-to-end accuracy (% of queries where the final output matches the
   ground-truth answer exactly, or within a tolerance for numerical answers).

Secondary metrics:

 • Compositional depth accuracy — accuracy conditioned on the number of
   ground-truth reasoning hops (to test H2).
 • Token efficiency — total input + output tokens per correct answer.
 • Node failure localization precision — on incorrect answers, whether the
   (human-annotated) first error node is among the top-3 nodes flagged by the
   CPN diagnostic (test H3).
 • Back-propagation overhead — fraction of queries that require at least one
   node re-generation after input verification failure.

All metrics reported with95% binomial confidence intervals and averaged over3
random seeds per condition.

Baselines1. Direct (zero-shot) — prompt the LLM with the query only, no
reasoning structure.

 2 Chain-of-Thought — standard CoT with "Let's think step by step" and no
   decomposition.
 3 Self-Consistency@5 — CoT sampled5 times, majority-vote answer (Wang et
   al.,2023).
 4 ReAct — interleaved reasoning and action traces, applied to the AgentTool
   benchmark only (since MuSiQue and LogiQA have no tool-use component).
 5 Tree-of-Thought (ToT) — breadth-first search over reasoning states with a
   value function prompt (Yao et al.,2023), limited to depth4 and branching
   factor3 for tractability.
 6 Graph-of-Thought (GoT) — the closest prior art: splits reasoning into
   DAG-structured nodes with aggregation operations (Besta et al.,2024), but
   without typed verification predicates or back-propagation.

All baselines run on the same LLM backbone (same model, quantization,
temperature, and max tokens) as the CPN condition.

Ablations1. -Verification — CPN without the verification predicate check on node
outputs. Nodes commit their first generation unconditionally. Isolates the
contribution of local correctness checks.

 2 -Backprop — CPN without back-propagation on input verification failure. If
   inputs fail, the node proceeds anyway with a warning appended to the prompt.
   Isolates the contribution of error recovery.
 3 -StructuredPrompt — CPN where node descriptions remain structured but the
   entire graph is serialized as free text (no typed input/output slots).
   Isolates the contribution of the typed-interface constraint.
 4 -MetaController — CPN where node failures (three failed attempts) cause a
   hard fallback to standard CoT for the remaining graph, rather than invoking
   the meta-controller for re-decomposition.

Each ablation is run on the full three-benchmark suite at the same compute
budget.

Expected Failure Modes1. Decomposition collapse. For very shallow queries (1–2
hops), the CPN overhead (decomposition + verification) inflates token cost with
negligible accuracy gain, and the structured output schema may occasionally
force an unnatural decomposition that performs worse than direct CoT.
Mitigation: include a routing heuristic — skip CPN when query has fewer than3
named entities or logical operators — to be tuned on a held-out validation set.

 2 Verification predicate brittleness. The LLM-judged verification predicate may
   produce false positives (accepts an incorrect intermediate) or false
   negatives (rejects a correct intermediate), degrading the
   constraint-propagation signal. Mitigation: verification predicates are
   constrained to simple factual statements ("X is a subset of Y", "the sum ≤
   N") rather than open-ended assessments, and we report false-positive/negative
   rates as a secondary analysis.
 3 Graph depth explosion. For highly branching queries, the DAG may grow beyond
   the prompt window or cause the meta-controller to be invoked too frequently.
   Mitigation: cap maximum nodes at12; any query requiring more nodes falls back
   to CoT for the excess subgraph.
 4 Ordering sensitivity. Topological ordering of nodes is not unique. Different
   orderings may produce different results if verifying one node depends on the
   specific output of a sibling. We will run a sensitivity analysis on
   a100-instance subset, randomly permuting node order within topological
   constraints, and report variance.

Limitations- No dynamic memory across sessions. The CPN operates within a single
prompt context. It does not accumulate reusable decompositions across queries
(e.g., recognizing that "allocate resources to maximize X" appears repeatedly
with different parameters). This is by design for the -IDE setting, but means
that on repeated query types the system starts from scratch each time.

 • LLM dependence on the decomposition step. If the initial decomposition is
   structurally wrong (missing a necessary reasoning node or adding an spurious
   one), no amount of within-node verification can recover. The meta-controller
   can trigger re-decomposition, but only after a node failure — a decomposition
   that looks locally correct but is globally wrong will not be caught.
 • Verification predicates are natural language. Unlike formal theorem provers,
   we cannot guarantee soundness or completeness of verification. The predicates
   are heuristic quality checks, not proofs.
 • Single backbone. All experiments use a single LLM family (to be specified at
   implementation). Results may not generalize to other architectures, sizes, or
   post-training alignments. We note this as an open empirical question for
   follow-up.
 • Static benchmarks. None of the evaluated datasets involve interactive
   environments, human feedback loops, or out-of-distribution tasks. Real-world
   agentic reasoning may introduce additional failure modes (e.g., tool-return
   ambiguity, partial observability) not captured here.
 • No confidence scoring. The framework does not quantify uncertainty in its
   final answer. A wrong answer delivered with high-confidence framing is
   indistinguishable from a right one. Adding calibrated confidence estimates is
   deferred to future work.

Research Proposal: Compositional Reasoning Under Distraction — When Do Agentic
Workflows Break Down?

Title**"Plan-Trace-Verify: A Controlled Study of Multi-Step Compositional
Reasoning in LLM Agents Under Distractor Conditions"**

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
LLM-based agents today are deployed on tasks that require chaining
multiple reasoning steps (e.g., "book a flight, check the weather at the
destination, then find restaurants within budget"). These agents frequently fail
not because individual steps are hard, but because they lose the thread when
intermediate results contradict expectations or when irrelevant context
(distractors) is injected mid-trajectory.

The core problem: existing benchmarks evaluate reasoning in clean, single-turn
settings (e.g., GSM8K, MATH, HotpotQA), but agentic reasoning involves iterative
plan-trace cycles where earlier outputs become inputs to later steps. We lack a
controlled benchmark that isolates the effect of "distractor injection" —
irrelevant or misleading intermediate observations — on compositional reasoning
accuracy.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
H₁ (Primary): Injecting task-irrelevant but semantically plausible
observations mid-trajectory degrades LLM agent compositional reasoning accuracy
by ≥25% relative to the no-distractor baseline, even when the underlying
reasoning path is unchanged.

H₂ (Mechanism): The degradation is primarily driven by retrieval interference
(the agent attends to distractor tokens in subsequent reasoning steps) rather
than plan corruption (the agent incorrectly revises its plan). This implies that
improving selective attention (e.g., structured memory) will help more than
improving planning ability.

H₃ (Mitigation): A simple Plan-Trace-Verify loop — where the agent explicitly
writes down its plan before execution, traces each step against the plan after
receiving observations, and verifies consistency before proceeding — recovers
≥80% of the performance gap relative to the no-distractor baseline.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
### Framework: Plan-Trace-Verify (PTV)

We define three agent strategies to compare:

1 Direct-ReAct (baseline): Standard ReAct-style agent — thinks, acts, observes
in a flat loop with no explicit plan tracking.
2 Plan-then-Execute (ablation control): The agent writes a plan (as pseudocode
or bullet points) before execution, then follows it linearly, but does not
re-check consistency after each observation.
3 Plan-Trace-Verify (PTV) (proposed): The agent:

• Plan: Writes an explicit, numbered plan with preconditions and expected
postconditions for each step.
• Trace: After each observation, appends a structured trace entry: [Step N]
expected=<...> observed=<...> match=<yes|no>.

DeCoT: Decompositional Chain-of-Thought with Constraint-aware Schema Linking for
Complex Text-to-SQL## ProblemText-to-SQL remains bottlenecked by complex queries
involving nested subqueries, set operations, multi-joins across many tables, and
domain-specific value constraints. Current approaches fall into two camps, each
                           with a critical weakness:

 • Encoder-decoder models (e.g., T5-based PICARD, RESDSQL) treat schema and
   question jointly but struggle when the schema grows large (10+ tables),
   producing spurious schema links and poor attention allocation.
 • LLM-based prompting methods (e.g., DAIL-SQL, DIN-SQL, C3) decompose the
   problem into schema linking, intermediate reasoning, and SQL generation, yet
   their intermediate representations are typically either full natural language
   chain-of-thought (which is verbose and drifts) or abstract syntax-tree
   sketches (which lose natural-language constraints). Neither is
   constraint-aware — they do not explicitly track foreign-key paths, NOT NULL
   constraints, or type-based filters that determine whether a generated query
   is valid, not just syntactically correct.

The consequence is that on benchmarks like Spider (with its20% multi-table
questions exceeding3 joins) and BIRD (with noisy, real-world database values),
state-of-the-art methods plateau at approximately84–86% execution accuracy.
Gains from scaling model size have largely saturated. The field needs a
structural intervention in how reasoning chains are represented and grounded in
database constraints.

HypothesisReplacing free-form natural language chain-of-thought with a
structured decomposition graph — where each reasoning step is a typed node
(schema link, join path, filter condition, aggregation, nesting) and edges
encode database-level constraints (referential integrity, cardinality, NOT NULL,
domain range) — yields higher execution accuracy on complex Text-to-SQL queries
than either flat NL-CoT or AST-sketch methods, because constraint edges prune
spurious SQL generation paths before decoding.

Method — DeCoTWe propose DeCoT (Decompositional Chain-of-Thought), a two-stage
LLM pipeline operating over a structured decomposition graph.

Stage1: Constraint-aware Decomposition. Given a question and the database
schema, the LLM produces a decomposition graph — not free text, but a structured
JSON containing:

 • Schema-linking nodes: Each maps a question span to a specific table.column,
   annotated with a confidence (hard/likely/ambiguous).
 • Join-path nodes: A sequence of table pairs connected by foreign-key
   relationships, with a flag indicating whether each join is implied or
   explicit in the question.
 • Filter nodes: Predicate triples (column, operator, value) with a type
   constraint field that records the column's domain (e.g., INTEGER >0, DATE <=
   CURRENT_DATE, VARCHAR match prefix). The LLM is instructed to check each
   filter against the column's declared constraints from information_schema.
 • Aggregation nodes: Group-by columns and aggregation functions, with
   constraints on whether the column type supports the aggregation.
 • Nesting nodes: Represent subqueries as their own decomposition sub-graphs,
   preserving the same node types recursively.

The LLM is prompted to fill this structure in a schema-first pass (examining
column types, keys, and nullable flags) and then map natural-language conditions
into filter nodes, rejecting any condition that violates a column constraint. If
no valid mapping exists, the node is marked unresolvable rather than
hallucinated.

Stage2: Constraint-traversing SQL Generation. The decomposition graph is fed
back to the same LLM (or a smaller specialized decoder) with an instruction to
traverse the graph depth-first:

 1 Emit SELECT ... FROM using schema-linking nodes.
 2 Emit JOIN ... ON ... for each join-path node; validate that the join columns
   share compatible types (the constraint edge is pre-checked in Stage1).
 3 Emit WHERE clauses from filter nodes, respecting the pre-validated operators
   and value types.
 4 Emit GROUP BY / HAVING from aggregation nodes.
 5 For nesting nodes, recurse and produce a subquery from that node's sub-graph.

Because constraint checks happen in Stage1, Stage2 is a deterministic traversal
— no backtracking, no self-correction. This eliminates the two failure modes of
NL-CoT: reasoning drift and hallucinated columns.

Training recipe: We use QLoRA fine-tuning of Llama-3-70B on a synthetic dataset
generated by applying DeCoT's decomposition template to existing Spider and BIRD
training splits. The fine-tune objective is a two-part loss: (a) standard
cross-entropy on the decomposition JSON tokens, and (b) a contrastive term that
penalizes constraint-violating decompositions. The contrastive term uses
negatively sampled decompositions where one filter node intentionally violates a
column constraint, and the model must assign lower likelihood to such samples.

Dataset / Benchmark- Spider (train / dev / test): The standard benchmark for
complex cross-domain Text-to-SQL. We report on dev; test via the official
leaderboard. Primary metric: execution accuracy (EX).

 • BIRD (train / dev / test): Real-world dirty database benchmark with noisy
   values. Adds external knowledge for some questions; we do not use external
   knowledge retrieval (to isolate the effect of constraint-aware
   decomposition). Secondary metric: EX on BIRD dev.
 • SParC (cross-context): For evaluating whether the decomposition graph
   degrades across multi-turn contexts. We include a2-turn variant analysis.

Evaluation Metrics- Execution Accuracy (EX) — main metric on both Spider and
BIRD.

 • Exact Set Match (ESM) — structural match without value sensitivity, to
   distinguish SQL structure errors from value errors.
 • Constraint Violation Rate (CVR) — fraction of generated queries that
   reference nonexistent columns, violate type constraints, or produce runtime
   type errors when executed. This is our targeted quality metric.
 • Decomposition Fidelity — human evaluation on200 sampled dev questions: does
   the decomposition graph correctly capture all filters and joins? (measured as
   recall of gold SQL clauses in the decomposition nodes).

Baselines| Method | Category | Spider (EX) | BIRD (EX) |

|---|---|---|---| | PICARD (T5-3B) | Encoder-decoder |79.3 | — | | RESDSQL
(T5-3B) | Encoder-decoder |81.9 | — | | DIN-SQL (GPT-4) | NL-CoT decomposition
|83.2 |52.7 | | DAIL-SQL (GPT-4) | NL-CoT decomposition |83.8 |54.8 | | C3
(GPT-4) | NL-CoT decomposition |82.8 | — | | MAC-SQL (GPT-4) | Multi-agent
decomposition |82.5 |56.2 | | DeCoT (ours) | Constraint-graph decomposition |
TBD | TBD |

All baselines use GPT-4 (or the largest available T5 variant). DeCoT uses
Llama-3-70B (QLoRA fine-tuned) and an inference-only GPT-4 comparison (prompted
with the decomposition graph template but no fine-tuning) to separate the effect
of the representation from the fine-tuning.

Ablations| Ablation | Component removed | Expected impact |

|---|---|---| | No constraint validation | Stage1 fills filter nodes without
checking column types/constraints | CVR increases; EX drops on BIRD (dirty
values) more than Spider | | Flat NL decomposition | Replace JSON decomposition
graph with natural-language CoT (same model, same fine-tuning) | EX drops ~2–3
points; CVR increases on complex queries | | No contrastive loss | Remove
negative sampling from training | Decomposition fidelity degrades on ambiguous
filters | | Graph traversal w/o recursion | Flatten nesting nodes into a single
SQL string with placeholder subqueries | Higher syntax errors on nested queries
(Spider hard + extra) |

Expected Failure Modes1. Schema-dependent decomposition overhead. For questions
against very large schemas (50+ tables), the decomposition graph becomes large
and the model may omit valid join paths. Mitigation: pre-prune schema to the
top-8 tables using a lightweight retrieval model (we will adapt IRNet's schema
pruning to serve as a preprocessing step before Stage1).

 2 Value constraints are incomplete. The information_schema metadata in real
   databases is often missing NOT NULL or CHECK constraints. DeCoT's filter
   validation is only as strong as the available metadata. We will report CVR
   stratified by databases with complete vs. incomplete metadata to characterize
   this gap.
 3 Recursive decomposition for deeply nested queries. The nesting-node
   representation incurs a quadratic token cost for subqueries more than2 levels
   deep, which may exceed the model's context window on long questions. We
   expect this to affect fewer than3% of Spider queries; for those, we fall back
   to flat NL-CoT and flag the fallback.
 4 BIRD external knowledge. DeCoT deliberately does not use external knowledge
   retrieval, so questions requiring domain-specific values (e.g., "teams that
   lost by more than10 points" when "points" is not a column) will fail at the
   filter-node stage. This is by design — we are measuring constraint-awareness,
   not external knowledge.

Limitations1. DeCoT's decomposition graph is a hand-crafted schema of node
types. There may be SQL constructs (pivot, window functions, EXCEPT) that the
graph does not express. Extending the graph to cover full SQL:2003 is future
work.

 2 The method requires fine-tuning on synthetic decomposition data. The
   synthetic data pipeline (applying the decomposition template to existing SQL
   queries) may introduce a distributional bias: the model learns to reconstruct
   decompositions that fit the template rather than any valid decomposition.
 3 DeCoT does not address value ambiguity in the question (e.g., "customers
   from2020" — is2020 a year filter or a string?). Constraint validation catches
   some cases but not all. Ambiguous schema-linking nodes are flagged but not
   resolved within the method.
 4 We evaluate on English-only benchmarks. Cross-lingual Text-to-SQL (e.g.,
   CSpider) may require a language-adaptive extension to the schema-linking
   stage.

Large-Scale Databases## Title
Schema-Aware Decomposition: Robust Text-to-SQL on
Large-Scale Databases via Progressive Pruning and Incremental Construction

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Current LLM-based Text-to-SQL systems perform competitively on benchmarks
like Spider (medium-scale, ~200 tables across20 databases, ~5 tables per
question). However, they degrade sharply on large-scale schemas (50+
tables,1000+ columns) common in enterprise settings. Two core issues:

1 Context window saturation — the full schema cannot fit in a single prompt,
forcing truncation that may drop relevant tables/columns.
2 Schema linking fragility — lightweight retrievers (embeddings + cosine
similarity) miss indirect matches (e.g., a column named "emp_salary" for a
question about "monthly compensation"), while heavy multi-stage pipelines
(re-ranking, self-consistency) inflate cost and latency.

No existing method jointly addresses both problems with a unified, training-free
decomposition that scales to schema sizes beyond current benchmarks.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Decomposing the Text-to-SQL task into three sequential stages —
structured schema pruning, sub-query decomposition, and incremental SQL
construction with local verification — will improve execution accuracy on
large-scale schemas by ≥15% over flat prompting approaches, while adding ≤2x
inference cost.

The hypothesis rests on two claims:

• Schema pruning by structure + semantics (not just flat embeddings) reduces
irrelevant context without dropping critical tables.
• Incremental construction catches composition errors (missing JOINs, wrong
nesting) at the sub-query level before final assembly.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
A three-stage pipeline, SaDec (Schema-Aware Decomposition):

Stage1: Hybrid Schema Pruning- Structure-aware filter: Extract the subgraph of
tables within2-hop relations of user-specified entities (heuristic: tables whose
primary keys appear in the question text, then their foreign-key neighbors).

• Semantic reranker: Embed each remaining table's DDL +3 sample rows using a
bi-encoder (e.g., BGE-M3). Rerank by cosine similarity against the question
embedding. Keep top-K tables (K =8–12, tunable).
• Output: a pruned schema (DDL + foreign keys) small enough to fit in one LLM
call.

Stage2: Sub-Query Decomposition- Prompt an LLM (e.g., GPT-4o-mini) to split the
question into2–5 sub-questions, each referencing specific tables/columns from
the pruned schema.

• Each sub-question is paired with its expected output columns and JOIN
constraints. This acts as an interpretable intermediate plan.

Stage3: Incremental SQL Construction + Verification- Generate SQL for each
sub-question independently, using the pruned schema.

• Local verifier: Execute each sub-query against the database. If it returns an
error or an empty result set, regenerate with a feedback prompt ("previous
attempt failed because...").
• Assembly pass: Combine sub-queries into the final SQL using a separate LLM
call with the full question, sub-queries, and their verified results as
context.
• Optional final check: Run the assembled SQL; if it errors, fall back to a
single-stage generation on the pruned schema.

No fine-tuning required. All stages use frozen LLMs with few-shot prompts (3
exemplars from similar databases in the training set).

Decoupling Emergent Capabilities in Large Language Models: A Mechanistic
Independence Framework### TitleDecoupling Emergent Capabilities in Large
Language Models: A Mechanistic Independence Framework

ProblemLarge language models exhibit a diverse and growing set of capabilities —
instruction following, multi-step reasoning, factual recall, code generation,
multilingual translation, and creative composition. The dominant training
paradigm (next-token prediction on a single mixed corpus) bundles all of these
into a single set of weights, making it impossible to answer a foundational
question: to what extent are these capabilities mechanistically separable?
Current alignment interventions (RLHF, DPO) and capability editing methods
(model patching, weight interpolation) implicitly assume at least partial
independence, yet we lack a principled framework to test that assumption.
Without understanding which capabilities are entangled and which are separable,
safety interventions risk collateral damage, fine-tuning risks catastrophic
forgetting of unrelated skills, and scaling offers no systematic path to
composing capabilities modularly.

HypothesisWe hypothesize that LLM capabilities form a structured independence
graph rather than a monolithic competence. Specifically:

 • Reasoning (multi-step deduction, math, logic) and factual recall (memorized
   knowledge) are substantially dissociable — they depend on partially
   non-overlapping circuit motifs and can be independently perturbed.
 • Instruction following and content generation quality are partially entangled
   — models use similar attention patterns to parse and execute instructions,
   but the factual correctness of the output can be separated from format
   compliance.
 • Syntactic fluency (grammar, style) is a near-independent substrate that
   persists under most perturbations, acting as a shared backbone rather than a
   capability-specific circuit.

These relationships can be quantified through a Capability Independence Score
(CIS) — the expected degradation in capability B given optimal intervention to
preserve capability A — and visualized as a directed graph where edge weights
correspond to conditional dependence strength.

MethodWe propose a three-phase intervention framework:

Phase1 — Capability Probes and Baselines. For each target capability (reasoning,
factual recall, instruction following, code generation, safety refusal, creative
generation), we construct a suite of held-out prompts that isolate the
capability with minimal confounds. We measure baseline performance on each suite
for a family of open-weight models (Pythia, LLaMA-2/3, Mistral, Qwen-2) at
multiple scales (1B–70B params). Each capability gets a scalar score derived
from an automated judge (LLM-as-evaluator with rubric) plus objective metrics
where available (pass@k for code, accuracy for math).

Phase2 — Targeted Interventions. We apply four classes of intervention, each
designed to perturb a single capability while leaving others untouched:

 1 Representation Steering. Identify steering vectors in the residual stream
   that maximally activate (or suppress) a capability-specific probe. Apply
   these vectors during generation and measure cross-capability transfer.
   Expected: strong intra-capability effect, varying cross-capability spillover.
 2 Circuit Ablation (activation patching). Use causal tracing (Wang et al.,2023)
   to localize attention heads and MLP neurons responsible for each capability.
   Patch those activations to corrupted runs and measure capability-specific
   degradation.
 3 Fine-Tuning on Capability-Specific Data. Continue training on data that
   exclusively exercises one capability (e.g.,50K math problems) and measure
   improvement in the target capability vs. regression in non-target
   capabilities.
 4 Weight Interpolations (model soup with capability-specific fine-tunes).
   Independently fine-tune copies on single-capability data, then linearly
   interpolate weights and measure whether capability gains compose additively
   or exhibit interference.

Phase3 — Independence Graph Construction. For each pair of capabilities (A, B),
compute the CIS:

▌ CIS(A→B) =1 − (Performance_B after optimal intervention targeting A) /
▌ (Baseline_Performance_B)

A CIS near0 means the intervention on A leaves B unaffected (strong
independence). A CIS near1 means B collapses when A is perturbed (strong
dependence). The pairwise matrix yields a directed graph where edges >0.3
indicate entanglement.

We then validate the graph by checking whether the intervention type (steering
vs. ablation vs. fine-tuning) produces consistent dependence patterns — if all
four methods agree on the graph structure, the independence claim is robust.

     Atomic Factual Consistency via Fine-grained Preference Optimization##
    ProblemLarge Language Models (LLMs) generate fluent, coherent text that
routinely contains factually incorrect atomic claims. Current alignment methods
 — RLHF, DPO, and variants — rely on holistic reward models or preference pairs
    that score the overall quality of a generation. This coarse signal masks
 fine-grained factual errors: a paragraph may be informative, well-structured,
  and compelling while still containing two or three false atomic claims. The
reward model's capacity to detect individual false claims is limited by both the
     granularity of the reward signal and the sparsity of factual errors in
 preference data. As a result, aligned models still hallucinate at non-trivial
    rates, especially on knowledge-intensive and long-form generation tasks.

HypothesisTraining a language model to prefer generations in which every atomic
claim is individually verifiable against a trusted knowledge corpus will
significantly reduce factual inconsistency without materially sacrificing
fluency, informativeness, or coverage. More precisely: if we decompose each
generation into atomic claims, assign each claim a fine-grained consistency
score against retrieved evidence via bidirectional natural language inference,
and optimize the model to maximize its worst-claim score, then the resulting
model will be both factually more reliable and better calibrated about the
boundary of its knowledge.

MethodThe method has four components:

1. Atomic Claim Extraction. Fine-tune a lightweight sequence tagger (e.g.,
DeBERTa-v3-base) on a synthetic dataset of model outputs annotated with atomic
claims using distant supervision from semantic role labeling and constituency
parsing. Each atomic claim is a single factual proposition that is either true
or false (e.g., "The Eiffel Tower was completed in1889"). Claims can be explicit
or entailed by the text. The extractor operates on the model's own generated
text at inference time.

2. Multi-source Factual Verification. For each extracted atomic claim, retrieve
the top-5 most relevant passages from a static trusted knowledge corpus (a2024
snapshot of Wikipedia). A bidirectional NLI model (T5-XXL fine-tuned on MNLI +
FEVER + Vitaminc + ANLI) predicts three probabilities: entailment (the passage
supports the claim), contradiction (the passage refutes the claim), and neutral
(the passage is relevant but does not confirm or refute). The per-claim
consistency score is defined as P(entailment) — P(contradiction), bounded in
[-1,1]. Claims for which retrieval returns no relevant passages are marked as
unverified and assigned a penalty score of -0.5.

3. Worst-C claim Aggregation. Given a generation y containing k atomic claims
with scores s₁, …, sₖ, the fine-grained consistency reward is R(y) = min(s₁, …,
sₖ). Using the minimum (rather than the mean) forces the model to address its
weakest factual failures and prevents it from trading a few bad claims against
many good ones. Unverified claims are included in the min, making the model
conservative when it lacks relevant knowledge.

4. Fine-grained Preference Optimization. Construct preference pairs from the
model's own generations on a diverse set of prompts. For each prompt, sample two
outputs: (a) the standard greedy decode, and (b) a contrastively decoded output
obtained by subtracting low-consistency hidden states from high-consistency
hidden states at each layer (inspired by contrastive decoding but using the
NLI-based consistency signal instead of a small/large model gap). Compute the
consistency reward for both. Apply DPO on the resulting pairs, where the
higher-reward output is the preferred completion. Train for3 epochs with a
held-out validation set for early stopping.

trusted knowledge corpus for verification is Wikipedia (2024-06-01 dump,
pre-processed into100-token passages with a dense retriever index).

are entailed by the knowledge corpus) on LongFact. This directly measures the
central claim.

won a competition.") remain a hard open problem.

   consistency blind spots. If it systematically misses a class of
   contradictions (e.g., temporal reasoning or numeric comparisons), the reward
   model will be blind to them and the optimization may even reinforce them. We
   will analyze verifier failure modes by stress-testing on FEVER2.0 adversarial
   examples before training.
 3 Vacuity — the conservatism trap. The worst-claim reward strongly penalizes
   unverifiable claims. The model may learn to produce text that avoids making
   factual claims altogether — vague hedging, meta-commentary, or trivial
   restatements of the prompt — to maximize the reward. We guard against this by
   (a) including a coverage penalty in the reward (the fraction of tokens that
   participate in at least one atomic claim), and (b) monitoring MAUVE and human
   informativeness ratings as fluency controls.

   contradicts previous work" — which finding? which previous work?). The atomic
   extractor will attempt to ground references via coreference resolution, but
   failures here produce unverifiable claims, triggering the penalty and
   reducing the model's willingness to make grounded comparisons.

static Wikipedia corpus. Claims about private facts, unreported events,
proprietary data, or knowledge that post-dates the corpus will be penalized as
unverifiable. This creates an inherent bias toward well-documented public
knowledge and away from novelty. Extending to live retrieval from web sources or
API-based knowledge bases is left for future work.

   entailment by a trusted corpus. This conflates factual correctness with
   corpus coverage and does not address factual claims that are true but
   unsupported by the specific corpus (e.g., newly published research). It also
   cannot handle normative, subjective, or predictive claims, which are not
   factual in the verification sense.

   and a preference optimiser. Errors compound. Inference-time latency increases
   by200–500 ms per generation (dominated by the verifier). A single-model
   end-to-end alternative (e.g., self-verification) may be preferable in
   latency-critical settings.

   that contradict verifiable knowledge. It does not address
   instruction-following errors, logical fallacies, stylistic inconsistency, or
   structural hallucinations (e.g., incorrect graph topology in a generated
   table). A complete solution likely requires combining factual verification
   with behaviorally grounded alignment signals.

   generation is expensive. For50k training prompts with average8 claims per
   generation, verification requires ~400k T5-XXL forward passes per epoch. We
   mitigate this by caching retrieval results and using LoRA adapters for the
   verifier, but full-scale training remains GPU-intensive and may require
   off-policy distillation to amortize the cost.

Consistency via Self-Generated Hard Negatives

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Large Language Models produce coherent but factually inconsistent outputs
— they generate statements that contradict themselves across contexts,
misattribute facts, or assert claims unsupported by their training distribution.
Existing mitigation strategies fall into two camps: (1) inference-time methods
(RAG, self-consistency, contrastive decoding) that add latency and complexity at
deployment, and (2) training-time methods (RLHF, DPO) that rely on expensive
human preference data or simple synthetic negatives that are too easy to
discriminate, leading to weak generalization.

The core gap: training-time objectives lack hard negatives that are semantically
plausible but factually incorrect, produced in a scalable, automated way.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
An LLM fine-tuned on pairs of (factual statement, hard-negative
counterfactual) — where the negative is generated by the same model and then
perturbed via a knowledge-driven corruption process — will show significantly
higher factual consistency on held-out distributions than models trained with
standard SFT, DPO, or inference-time methods alone.

The mechanism is that hard negatives force the model to learn the decision
boundary between factually consistent and inconsistent outputs, rather than
merely memorizing factual-looking surface patterns.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
### Stage1: Hard-Negative Generation PipelineFor each factual triple
(subject, relation, object) extracted from a knowledge base:

1 Prompt the model to generate a natural-language sentence expressing the
triple (e.g., "The Eiffel Tower is located in Paris, France").
2 Generate hard negatives by corrupting the factual triple with four
strategies:

• Entity swap: Replace subject or object with a same-type entity ("The Eiffel
Tower is located in Berlin").
• Relation flip: Replace the relation with a semantically similar but incorrect
one ("The Eiffel Tower was built in Paris" → "The Eiffel Tower was demolished
in Paris" when relation was located_in).
• Numeric/date perturbation: Offset numerical facts by a plausible but wrong
amount ("180 feet" → "280 feet" for height).
• Coreference break: Introduce entity mismatch in a multi-sentence context that
creates a contradiction (e.g., substitute a pronoun antecedent).

3 Filter negatives using a separate NLI/verification model: keep only those
where the negative is:

• Plausible (the verification model cannot trivially reject)
• Diverse (low semantic similarity to other negatives for the same triple)

Stage2: Contrastive Fine-TuningTrain using a preference optimization objective
(simplified DPO-style) where:

• Chosen: Model's own generation of the factual sentence.
• Rejected: The hardest negative that passes the filter.

The loss encourages higher likelihood of factual trajectories and lower
likelihood of the hard-negative trajectory, using the model's own distribution
as the reference.

Stage3: Self-Consistency RegularizationAdd a secondary objective: for a given
query, the model produces K samples; maximize the pairwise agreement of factual
claims across those samples (measured by an NLI model's entailment scores
between sampled statements). This directly penalizes self-contradiction at
training time.
