Title: Compositional Reasoning Coverage Synthesis: Structured Program
Transformations for Code LLM TrainingProblem. Current data-synthesis pipelines
for code LLMs rely on two broad strategies: (1) large-scale distilling of
outputs from frontier models (e.g., Code-Alpaca, WizardCoder), which produces
fluent but mode-collapsed code that clusters around popular idioms; and (2)
execution-guided filtering (e.g., CodeRL, AlphaCode), which improves correctness
but does not explicitly diversify the reasoning patterns the model learns. The
result is data that is dense in common reasoning modes (e.g., imperative loops
with in-place mutation) and sparse in less frequent but equally valid patterns
(e.g., functional recursion, generator-based iteration, symbolic manipulation).
This density bias limits the model's ability to generalize to
out-of-distribution code, particularly in settings requiring unusual control
flow or algorithmic pivots. The core problem is that existing synthesis methods
optimize for correctness and fluency but not for covering the space of reasoning
strategies.

Hypothesis. A data synthesis pipeline that explicitly decomposes seed programs
into their constituent reasoning patterns and then systematically recomposes
those patterns — under formalized diversity constraints — will produce a
training set that yields higher pass@k on held-out benchmarks than an
equal-sized set produced by isotropic random augmentation or by teacher
distillation, because the model is forced to learn from a balanced coverage of
the reasoning space rather than from a density-weighted sample of it.

Method. We propose Compositional Reasoning Coverage Synthesis (CRCS), a
three-stage pipeline.

Stage1 — Seed acquisition and reasoning decomposition. Collect5,000–10,000 seed
programs from open-source permissively licensed repositories (GitHub
CodeSearchNet, BigCode's The Stack v1.2, filtered to Python and JavaScript). For
each seed, parse into an abstract syntax tree (AST) and annotate each function
with a reasoning-pattern signature across six dimensions: control-flow structure
(recursive, iterative, event-driven), mutation strategy (in-place,
copy-on-write, pure-functional), data-structure usage (list, dict, set, heap,
custom class), algorithmic paradigm (greedy, DP, divide-and-conquer,
backtracking, brute-force), error-handling pattern (guard clauses, try-except,
monadic), and input-output cardinality (one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-one,
relational). This signature is a6-tuple of categorical labels assigned by a set
of hand-authored AST-visitor rules and heuristics (no learned classifier, to
avoid confounding).

of15–20 parameterized program transformations, each preserving execution
semantics when applied in isolation: (T1) loop-style rewriting (for → while →

(T4) generator ↔ list-comprehension conversion, (T5) accumulator-passing style

Research Proposal: Synthesizing Failure-to-Repair Trajectories for Improving
Code LLM Reasoning## Title
Trajectory-for-Code: Self-Supervised Synthesis of
Debugging Trajectories for Robust Code Generation

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Current code LLMs are predominantly trained on (instruction,
correct_solution) pairs, either from human sources (e.g., StarCoder data) or
synthetic pipelines (e.g., CodeAlpaca, OSS-Instruct). This outcome-only
supervision has two limitations:

1 Brittle reasoning on hard problems — When the model's first attempt is wrong,
it has no training signal for how to recover. It was never shown buggy
attempts, test failures, or the iterative debugging steps that lead to
correct code.
2 Overconfident generations — Models trained exclusively on correct outputs
lack calibrated uncertainty about when their code is likely wrong, and cannot
self-correct without an external oracle.

Gap: While self-debugging and self-refine methods exist at inference time, no
systematic study has asked whether training on synthesized debugging
trajectories (attempt → test failure → bug analysis → repair → verified fix)
improves a model's code reasoning and self-correction ability at both train and
test time.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Primary: Fine-tuning a code LLM on self-synthesized debugging
trajectories — sequences where the model sees its own buggy attempt, test
failure signal, natural-language bug explanation, and a corrected solution —
improves pass@1 on held-out reasoning benchmarks by ≥5% over fine-tuning on the
same volume of (instruction, correct_code) synthetic data alone.

Secondary: The same training yields a measurable improvement in self-correction
(ability to improve a generation given test feedback at inference time) without
requiring an external verifier during training.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
### Stage1 — Trajectory Synthesis Pipeline (fully automated, no human
labels)

Given a base code LLM (e.g., DeepSeek-Coder-7B-Instruct or CodeLlama-7B) and a
set of programming problems from a training split (e.g., APPS training set or a
subset of CodeContests):

1 Attempt: Sample $k=5$ solutions per problem from the model (temperature0.8).
2 Execute: Run each solution against the problem's test cases. Categorize as
pass or fail. Collect the failing test input, expected output, and actual
output.
3 Bug analysis prompt: For each failing solution, prompt the model: "Explain
why this code fails on the given test. Identify the specific bug." This
produces a natural-language bug description. Filter by a lightweight check —
the description must mention the relevant variable or line (heuristic).
4 Repair prompt: Prompt the model: "Given the buggy code, the test failure
details, and the bug explanation above, write a corrected version." Execute
the corrected version; keep only repairs that pass all tests.
5 Assemble trajectory: (problem → buggy_code → test_failure → bug_analysis →
corrected_code). Also include the successful (problem → correct_code) paths
as positive examples.

Yield: ~3–5× more training sequences per problem (one correct path + several
repair trajectories).

To control quality, discard trajectories where:

• The bug analysis is empty or generic (<10 tokens).
• The repair still fails any test case.
• The buggy code has a syntax error (trivial).

Stage2 — TrainingFine-tune the base model on a mixture:

-50% standard (instruction, correct_code) pairs from the same problem set-50%
trajectory data (each trajectory formatted as a multi-turn chat: user → problem,
assistant → code, user → test fails with details, assistant → bug analysis, user
→ fix it, assistant → corrected code)

Train for2 epochs. Use a replay buffer where trajectory data is sampled
proportional to the number of repair steps (more steps → higher weight). Compare
against a control fine-tuned on the same total tokens but only (instruction,
correct_code) pairs.

Stage3 — EvaluationEvaluate on held-out benchmarks (see below). Measure both
static pass@k and self-correction pass@1: allow the model one additional attempt
with test failure feedback.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark
Training data source:

• CodeContests (training split) ~13K problems with test cases — diverse
difficulty, multiple languages.
• Supplement with APPS (training split) ~5K problems for coverage.

Evaluation benchmarks (held-out, no test set overlap):

• HumanEval+ —164 problems with80× more test cases (EvalPlus). Measures
functional correctness.
• MBPP+ —399 problems with enriched tests.
• LiveCodeBench — recent competitive programming problems, tests recency and
generalization.
• CodeContests (test split) —165 problems.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Description |

|---|---| | pass@1 | Standard functional correctness on first sample
(temperature0.2, greedy) | | pass@5 | Any of5 samples passes (temperature0.8) |
| self-correct pass@1 | First sample + one repair round given test failure
feedback. Measures the model's ability to debug its own output. | | trajectory
efficiency | % of synthesized trajectories that produce valid repairs after one
pass (measures pipeline quality) | | calibration error | Expected Calibration
Error (ECE) on the model's confidence vs. pass rate, to test whether training on
failures produces better-calibrated models |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines1. Base model (no fine-tuning) — e.g., DeepSeek-Coder-7B-Instruct2.
Standard SFT — fine-tuned on (instruction, correct_code) only, matching total
tokens3. Code Alpaca / OSS-Instruct style — synthetic instruction–code pairs
from a teacher model4. Self-play w/o trajectories — generate correct code,
filter by tests, train on that (no failure data)

5 CodeRL baseline — actor-critic with test pass/fail as reward (uses RL, not
SFT on trajectories)
6 Self-Debugging (inference-only, no trajectory training) — to isolate training
benefit---

Ablations1. Remove bug-analysis step: train on (problem → buggy → repair)
without the natural-language bug explanation. Isolates the value of intermediate
reasoning.

2 Remove failure signal: train on (problem → repair) only — show the model the
correct code without showing the failure context.
3 Trajectory ratio sweep: vary the % of trajectory data in the mix
(10%,30%,50%,70%) to measure diminishing returns.
4 Model scale: replicate on1B,7B, and14B models to test whether trajectory
training helps more at smaller scales (where self-correction is hardest).
5 Oracle repair vs. model repair: replace the model's own repair step with
GPT-4's repair to measure the ceiling (is the bottleneck synthesis quality or
training itself?).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes| Failure Mode | Mitigation |

|---|---| | Repair data is too easy — the model generates obviously buggy code
that it easily fixes, so trajectories are trivial. | Filter trajectories by the
edit distance of the repair; keep only those with non-trivial changes (>3 tokens
different). | | Model learns to generate buggy code to get repair signal —
exploits the training setup. | Keep the50% standard SFT mix as a regularizer;
never reward buggy-only generations. | | Synthetic bug analysis is hallucinated
— the explanation sounds plausible but is wrong. | The repair step must produce
executed correct code; wrong explanations that still lead to correct repairs are
harmless, and wrong explanations that mislead the repair will be discarded. | |
No improvement on single-turn pass@1 — the benefit only shows in multi-turn
self-correction. | Acceptable if self-correction improves, but the hypothesis
requires ≥5% improvement on pass@1. If self-correction improves without pass@1,
refine the hypothesis. | | Small model can't produce valid bug explanations (<1B
parameters) leads to low-quality trajectories. | Restrict the study to ≥7B
models; use1B as an ablation but expect pipeline yield to be low. | | Metric
saturation — base model is already strong on HumanEval (85%+), leaving little
room. | Use more difficult benchmarks (LiveCodeBench, CodeContests test split)
where scores are lower. HumanEval+ results are still reported but are not the
primary signal. |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

SummaryThis proposal tests a simple, automated, and self-supervised method for
creating rich code reasoning data: instead of only generating (problem, answer)
pairs, generate full debugging trajectories — buggy attempt, test feedback, bug
explanation, repair — and train on them. The core idea is that learning how to
recover from failure should produce more robust code reasoning than learning
only from successes. The experiment is feasible with open models, open
benchmarks, and no human annotation.

Learned Adaptive Draft Horizon for Speculative Decoding in Large Language
Models### ProblemSpeculative decoding reduces inference latency by having a
small draft model propose K tokens per step while the target model verifies them
in parallel via a single forward pass. Every implementation to date uses a
fixed, predetermined draft length K (e.g., K=4 or K=5). This is substantially
suboptimal: when the target model is highly confident and would accept most or
all draft tokens, the fixed horizon underutilizes parallelism and leaves latency
on the table; when the target model would reject many draft tokens, a long
horizon wastes compute on tokens that will be discarded, and the effective
acceptance rate collapses. Since the difficulty of predicting the next token
varies widely across decoding steps (a boilerplate "Sure, here is" sequence is
far easier than an unexpected noun), a fixed horizon must compromise between
these regimes, and no single K achieves optimal throughput across positions,
prompts, or domains.

HypothesisA lightweight learned critic that predicts the optimal draft length
for the next speculative step — conditioned on features drawn from the target
model's recent hidden states — can reduce mean per-token latency by at least20%
relative to any fixed-horizon baseline, without degrading generation quality
(measured by perplexity and task accuracy). The critic exploits the observation
that autoregressive hidden states encode difficulty: when the target model's

Research Proposal: Counterfactual Data Augmentation for Mitigating Gender Bias
in Neural Machine Translation## Title
Counterfactual Data Augmentation with
Source-Side Control for Mitigating Occupational Gender Bias in Neural Machine
Translation

Problem
Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models exhibit systematic gender bias:
they disproportionately map neutral-source occupational terms (e.g., "doctor,"
"nurse") to target-language gendered forms that align with statistical
stereotypes rather than real-world distributions. On standard benchmarks like
WinoMT, models such as mBART-50 assign "She is a doctor" the masculine
translation ~85% of the time for English→Spanish, while "nurse" is feminine ~80%
of the time. This propagates occupational stereotypes and can produce
grammatically incorrect output when the context or world knowledge contradicts
the majority pattern.

Existing debiasing approaches fall into three camps — (1) post-hoc decoding
rules, (2) fine-tuning on balanced or anti-stereotypical data, and (3)
embedding-space interventions — but each has limitations: decoding rules can
break fluency, balanced data is scarce and expensive, and embedding
interventions are often task-specific and degrade general translation quality. A
method that requires only synthetic data and a single fine-tuning step, without
specialized architectures or inference-time overhead, would be broadly
applicable across language pairs and model families.

Hypothesis
Adding counterfactually augmented training examples — where
occupational nouns are swapped across genders in the source sentence — combined
with a source-side gender control signal (a special token marking the intended
target gender) will significantly reduce occupational gender bias in NMT output
on WinoMT while preserving BLEU score on standard translation benchmarks
within0.5 points.

The intuition is twofold: (a) the counterfactual data forces the model to learn
that doctor can co-occur with feminine agreement in the target, breaking the
spurious correlation; (b) the control token lets the model disambiguate
ambiguous cases at inference without requiring a separate classifier or post-hoc
rule.

Method1. Counterfactual Data Generation Pipeline

• Start with a parallel corpus (e.g., Europarl + News Commentary for
EN→ES/DE/FR).
• Tag each sentence with occupation-bearing terms using a POS tagger +
occupation lexicon (300 occupation nouns from ONET).
• For each sentence containing an occupational reference to a specific gender
(e.g., "the female doctor"), generate a counterfactual by swapping the gender
descriptor ("the male doctor").
• Also generate sentences where occupation appears without explicit gender
(e.g., "the doctor"), paired with both a masculine and a feminine target
translation obtained by replacing gender-agreement morphology in the
reference.
• Insert a control token at the source sentence head: [GENDER:M], [GENDER:F],
or [NEUTRAL]. The neutral case is used only at inference when gender is truly
unknown.

2. Fine-Tuning

• Mix counterfactual data with original training data at a1:4 ratio (pilot
experiments will test1:1,1:4,1:9).
• Fine-tune a pretrained NMT model (mT5-small or mBART-50) for1–3 epochs with
reduced learning rate (1e-5).
• Evaluate on held-out WinoMT test sets.

3. Inference Protocol

• For sentences where the source has no gender signal, pass the sentence
through a minimal gender-identification classifier (rule-based for EN:
pronoun/coreference heuristics).
• Prepend [GENDER:M] or [GENDER:F] accordingly. When classifier is uncertain,
use [NEUTRAL], which falls back to the most frequent target form.

Dataset / Benchmark- Training corpus: Europarl v7 + News Commentary v12 (EN→ES,
EN→DE, EN→FR; ~2M sentence pairs)

• Counterfactual augmentation: ~50k synthetic sentence pairs generated from the
training corpus- Bias evaluation: WinoMT (Stanovsky et al.,2019) —3,888
pro-stereotype and anti-stereotype sentences covering60 occupations across
EN→ES/DE/FR- General quality evaluation: newstest2013, newstest2014##
Evaluation Metrics| What | Metric | How | |------|--------|-----| | Gender
bias | WinoMT accuracy | % of correct gender assignments for both pro- and
anti-stereotype sentences | | Translation quality | BLEU (sacrebleu) | On
newstest2013/2014 | | Fluency loss | chrF++ | Additional check if BLEU
degrades | | Stereo type flip | Δ between pro- and anti-stereotype accuracy |
Smaller Δ = less biased |

Primary success criterion: WinoMT accuracy on anti-stereotype examples improves
by ≥20 percentage points relative to the baseline, with BLEU drop ≤0.5.

Baselines| Baseline | Description |

|----------|-------------| | Unmodified NMT | mBART-50 fine-tuned on original
data only (no augmentation, no control token) | | Decoding-only | Unmodified
model + gender-inflection post-hoc rule (e.g., adjust target morphology after
decoding) | | Balanced fine-tuning | Fine-tune on a static balanced dataset
(Equalizer, Saunders & Byrne,2020) — no control token | | Embedding debiasing |
Apply Hard Debias (Bolukbasi et al.,2016) to encoder embeddings before
fine-tuning |

Ablations1. No control token: Counterfactual data without [GENDER:M/F] token →
isolates the effect of augmentation vs. control signal.

2 Data ratio sweep:1:1,1:4,1:9 counterfactual-to-original ratio → identifies
trade-off between bias reduction and quality.
3 Occupation-only vs. all-noun augmentation: Only occupations vs. all gendered
nouns → tests whether targeting is necessary or if broader augmentation works
better.
4 Rule-based vs. learned gender classifier at inference: affects how often the
control token is correct.

Expected Failure Modes1. BLEU degradation >0.5: Counterfactual data may distort
the training distribution enough that general translation quality drops.
Mitigation: early stopping based on validation BLEU; fall back to1:9 ratio or
smaller LR.

2 Control token leakage: The model may learn to ignore the token if it's
inconsistently applied (e.g., inference-time [NEUTRAL] differs from training
distribution). Mitigation: include [NEUTRAL] in training on a random10% of
sentences.
3 Language-pair dependence: EN→ES/FR (morphologically gendered
adjectives/determiners) may show larger gains than EN→DE (three-gender system
with more complex agreement). If EN→DE gains are weak, the method may not
generalize to languages with non-binary or richer gender systems.
4 Classifier errors propagate: A bad rule-based gender identifier could prepend
the wrong control token, biasing output in the opposite direction.
Mitigation: measure classifier accuracy; if <80% on a development set, switch
to a lightweight BERT-based classifier.
5 Diminishing returns on larger models: mBART-50 (611M) or mT5-large may
already encode weaker stereotyping at scale. The method may show smaller
gains on larger models — we test on both small and large variants to bound
this.
6 Anti-stereotype improvement does not close the gap: Even with a20pp gain on
anti-stereotype examples, pro-stereotype accuracy may also shift, keeping the
gap large. Success criterion uses the anti-stereotype level rather than Δ
alone for this reason.

Knowledge Injection in Domain-Specific LLMs: A Curriculum-Grounded Parameter
Integration Framework### TitleCurriculum-Guided Parameter Integration for Robust
Knowledge Injection in Domain-Specific Large Language Models

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

ProblemInjecting structured, domain-specific knowledge into pretrained LLMs
faces three interconnected challenges not adequately solved by existing methods:

 1 Catastrophic forgetting vs. insufficient integration — Fine-tuning on domain
   corpora either overwrites general capabilities (low retention of general
   knowledge) or fails to internalize domain knowledge beyond surface-level
   pattern matching.
 2 Granularity mismatch — Domain knowledge exists at multiple granularities
   (fact-level, concept-level, procedural/rule-level), yet current injection
   methods typically apply a single mechanism (continued pretraining, retrieval
   augmentation, or adapter tuning) that treats all knowledge types uniformly.
 3 Evaluation confound — Standard benchmarks measure isolated fact recall (e.g.,
   multiple-choice QA) but not the model's ability to reason compositionally
   with injected knowledge — e.g., combining two injected facts to answer a
   novel question. Reported gains may reflect memorization rather than genuine
   knowledge integration.

The core challenge is therefore not whether knowledge can be injected, but how
to inject knowledge at multiple granularities such that the model can flexibly
compose and reason with it while preserving general capabilities.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

HypothesisStructuring domain knowledge into a curriculum of increasing
compositional complexity and injecting each level via a dedicated,
minimally-interfering parameterization will produce higher compositional
reasoning accuracy and lower general-knowledge degradation than either
monolithic fine-tuning or single-mechanism injection.

Specifically: (1) fact-level knowledge is best injected via lightweight
memory-augmented parameters (key-value adapters), (2) concept-level knowledge
via rank-constrained LoRA modules on mid-layer attention, and (3)
procedural/rule-level knowledge via sparse feed-forward network grafting.
Training these in a curriculum order (facts → concepts → rules) and freezing
each stage's parameters before introducing the next reduces interference and
improves compositional generalization.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

MethodCIPI (Curriculum-grounded Injection with Parameter Isolation)

 1 Knowledge Decomposition Pipeline

 • Parse the domain corpus into three tiers via LLM-assisted extraction + human
   verification sampling:
 • Tier1 (Facts): atomic triples (entity, relation, entity) — e.g., (Drug X,
   treats, Disease Y) - Tier2 (Concepts): cluster-level representations linking
   related facts — e.g., mechanism-of-action clusters linking drugs, targets,
   and pathways - Tier3 (Procedures/Rules): conditional inference rules — e.g.,
   "If patient has condition A and biomarker B > threshold, then drug X is
   contraindicated"

 2 Three-Parameter Injection Modules

 • Fact Injector (Tier1): A small set of cross-attention key-value adapters
   inserted after each Transformer layer's self-attention. The keys index fact
   triples; the values project retrieved facts into the residual stream. No
   base-model weights are updated. Motivation: facts are lookup-intensive;
   retrieval-based injection suits this without touching general reasoning.
 • Concept Injector (Tier2): Low-rank adaptation (LoRA, r=8) applied to the
   value projections in the middle-third of layers (layers12–24 of a32-layer
   model). Trained on concept-grounded next-token prediction where concept
   labels are prepended as soft prompts. Motivation: concept abstraction
   benefits from distributed weight updates in layers associated with semantic
   composition.
 • Procedure Injector (Tier3): Sparse grafting — replace a small fraction (1–2%)
   of feed-forward network neurons in the last third of layers with
   domain-rule-specialized neurons initialized from the rule corpus. Trained
   with L0 sparsity regularization. Motivation: rules require deterministic
   branching; sparse FFN specialization preserves the bulk of general knowledge.

 3 Curriculum Schedule

 • Phase1: Train Fact Injector alone (freeze base + all other modules).1 epoch.
 • Phase2: Freeze Fact Injector. Train Concept Injector.1 epoch.
 • Phase3: Freeze all prior. Train Procedure Injector.1 epoch.
 • Phase4 (optional): Joint very-low-rate training (lr ×0.1) on mixed data to
   allow cross-module coordination.

 4 Inference

 • All three modules are active. The Fact Injector retrieves relevant facts, the
   Concept Injector provides contextual abstraction, and the Procedure Injector
   applies rule-based branching where triggered.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark- Domain: Biomedical (chosen for well-structured knowledge
bases and established benchmarks).

 • Training corpus: A curated set of ~200K biomedical documents spanning:
 • DrugBank (facts: drug-target-disease triples)
 • UMLS (concepts: semantic type clusters)
 • Clinical practice guidelines (rules: conditional treatment protocols)
 • Evaluation benchmarks:
 • Fact recall: BioQA (in-domain multiple-choice) and a held-out triple
   completion task (Tier1)
 • Concept reasoning: MedMCQA subset requiring multi-step inference (Tier2)
 • Rule application: a novel compositional benchmark constructed by composing
   two facts into a rule-required question (Tier3) — e.g., "Drug X treats
   Disease Y. Disease Y has symptom Z. Does Drug X alleviate Z?" requires fact
   lookup + rule application - General retention: MMLU (full), HellaSwag, and
   GSM8K — to measure forgetting- Base model: Llama-3-8B (Instruct).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Capability | Metric | Primary / Secondary |

|---|---|---| | Fact recall | Triple completion accuracy (Hits@1, Hits@10) |
Primary | | Concept reasoning | MedMCQA accuracy (subset requiring ≥2 inference
steps) | Primary | | Rule application | Compositional QA accuracy (novel
benchmark) | Primary | | General retention | Δ MMLU (relative drop from base
model) | Secondary | | General retention | Δ HellaSwag, Δ GSM8K | Secondary | |
Injection efficiency | # trainable parameters / total parameters | Reporting | |
Interference | Per-tier accuracy after each curriculum phase (forward transfer /
backward interference) | Analysis |

Primary metrics determine the go/no-go decision. Secondary metrics characterize
trade-offs.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines1. Full fine-tune (FFT): Continued pretraining on the domain corpus
(all model weights). Represents maximum injection with minimum parameter
efficiency.

 2 LoRA-only (r=16): Single LoRA module on all attention projections, trained on
   the full corpus (no curriculum, no tier separation). Matches computational
   budget to CIPI.
 3 Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): No weight updates — retrieve top-3
   facts from the knowledge base at each generation step. Represents the pure
   retrieval baseline.
 4 CIPI (uniform joint): Same three modules, but trained jointly (no curriculum)
   on all tiers simultaneously. Isolates the curriculum effect.
 5 CIPI (reverse order): Rules → Concepts → Facts curriculum. Isolates the
   ordering effect.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations| Ablation | What is removed / varied | What it measures |

|---|---|---| | No Fact Injector | Remove key-value adapters | Contribution of
dedicated fact-retrieval parameters | | No Concept Injector | Remove LoRA
modules | Contribution of concept-level distributed updates | | No Procedure
Injector | Keep0% of grafted FFN neurons | Contribution of rule-specialized
sparse parameters | | Joint training (baseline4) | Remove curriculum ordering |
Whether curriculum ordering reduces interference | | Single LoRA (baseline2) |
Replace three modules with one LoRA | Whether modular isolation beats monolithic
adaptation | | Tier-1-only injection | Only Fact Injector trained | Upper bound
on forgetting prevention, lower bound on integration |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes1. Tier bleed: Fact Injector retrieves facts irrelevant to
the compositional question, misleading the Procedure Injector. Mitigation: train
a lightweight gating mechanism that down-weights retrieved facts when
concept-level reasoning is active.

 2 Curriculum lock-in: Early frozen modules prevent later modules from learning
   useful cross-tier interactions. Mitigation: Phase4 joint low-rate training is
   designed to address this; if it fails, relax freezing to allow gradual
   fine-tuning of early modules at very low learning rates.
 3 Sparse grafting underutilization: The L0-regularized FFN neurons collapse to
   near-zero activation, rendering the Procedure Injector inert. Mitigation:
   initialize grafted neurons with weights from rule-derived auxiliary training
   (not random) and schedule L0 regularization to activate only after a warmup
   phase.
 4 General knowledge degradation still exceeds5%: The cumulative number of
   updated parameters (~2–3% of total) may still drift general representations.
   Mitigation: add a KL-divergence regularization term between the base model's
   logits and CIPI's logits on a held-out general-domain corpus during all
   training phases.
 5 Compositional benchmark is too easy / too hard: A novel benchmark risks
   ceiling or floor effects. Mitigation: calibrate difficulty on a small pilot
   (N=100 examples) with human expert baseline accuracy. Iterate on question
   design to target50–70% human accuracy before full-scale evaluation.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Limitations1. Knowledge decomposition cost: Extracting the three tiers from a
new domain requires significant human-in-the-loop validation (target:95%
precision on a5% sampled audit). This limits deployment speed in low-resource
domains.

 2 Modularity ceiling: Separating knowledge into three tiers assumes clean
   boundaries between facts, concepts, and rules. In practice, these boundaries
   are fuzzy — a single sentence may encode all three. The decomposition
   pipeline's errors propagate to the injection modules.
 3 Scale dependence: The curriculum and modular design is tested on8B
   parameters. At much larger scales (70B+), interference patterns and optimal
   tier definitions may shift qualitatively.
 4 Sequential dependency: The curriculum assumes that fact-level knowledge is a
   prerequisite for concept-level reasoning. If a domain requires top-down
   reasoning (rules constrain which facts are relevant), the current order may
   be suboptimal. The reverse-curriculum ablation tests this, but deployment
   would need to determine the correct order per domain.
 5 No lifelong learning evaluation: The proposal tests a one-shot injection
   scenario. Real-world knowledge bases evolve; CIPI's modular design is
   intended to support updating individual tiers without retraining, but this is
   not evaluated in the proposed experiments.

Research Proposal: Adaptive Knowledge Injection via Confidence-Gated Adapter
Fusion for Domain-Specific LLMs## Title
Confidence-Gated Adapter Fusion for
Mitigating Knowledge Conflicts During Domain-Specific LLM Injection

Problem
Domain-specific LLM deployment (legal, medical, finance) requires
injecting specialized knowledge into general-purpose pre-trained models. Three
interrelated challenges remain unresolved:

1 Knowledge conflicts — injected domain facts contradict or compete with the
model's pre-training knowledge, causing inconsistent behavior depending on
prompt phrasing.
2 Selective forgetting — fine-tuning on domain text degrades general-language
capabilities, especially on reasoning and rare-token recall.
3 Sub-domain interference — a single domain (e.g., clinical medicine) contains
heterogeneous sub-domains (radiology, pathology, pharmacology) that interfere
when injected via a single adapter or fine-tuning run.

Current solutions (full fine-tuning, RAG, LoRA, model editing) each address only
a subset of these. No method jointly handles all three while providing per-input
routing between base and injected knowledge.

Hypothesis
Confidence-gated routing — where the model dynamically selects between
base knowledge and injected domain knowledge based on its own predictive
uncertainty — reduces knowledge conflicts and sub-domain interference compared
to monolithic injection, while preserving general capabilities better than full
fine-tuning and matching the domain accuracy of state-of-the-art fixed injection
methods.

More concretely: an adapter mixture with a learned confidence-gating mechanism
will achieve higher domain-specific accuracy and lower general-task degradation
than the Pareto frontier of existing injection methods.

Method
Architecture. Start with a frozen base LLM (e.g., Llama-3-8B). We train a
set of k lightweight LoRA adapters, each specialized on a distinct sub-domain
cluster of the target domain (clusters discovered via topic modeling or
metadata-driven splits). A small learned confidence gate is trained to produce,
for each input token/sequence: (a) a routing weight over the k adapters, and (b)
a scalar β ∈ [0,1] that mixes the adapter output with the base model's original
hidden state. When β is low, the model relies on base knowledge; when high,
injected knowledge dominates.

Gate architecture. A2-layer MLP over the hidden state of the last layer at the
final token position, outputting a softmax over adapters and a sigmoid-gated β.
Trained jointly with adapters via a regularized objective.

Training objective. Two terms:

• Domain accuracy — standard cross-entropy on domain data, but weighted by a
per-sample confidence bonus that down-weights examples the base model already
answers well (to focus injection on genuinely novel knowledge).
• General capability preservation — a distillation regularizer that penalizes
large β when the base model's output distribution on held-out general
benchmarks (MMLU subsets, GSM8K) has low entropy (high confidence),
preventing unnecessary overrides.

Inference. Single forward pass per token. Gating adds negligible latency (<1%
parameter overhead).

Dataset / Benchmark
We construct a multi-sub-domain biomedical benchmark from
public sources:

Sub-domain           Dataset                            Size         Source
Clinical guidelines  MedQA (subset)                     1.2K Q&A     USMLE
Pharmacology         DrugBank QA                        800 QA       DrugBank
Radiology reports    MIMIC-III (report impressions)     2K excerpts  PhysioNet
Molecular biology    PubMedQA                           1K QA        PubMed
General (probe)      MMLU (biomedical subset) +3        2.5K         MMLU
general sections

We also collect a training corpus by pooling the full source documents (not just
QA pairs) for each sub-domain, filtering for overlap with pre-training data to
remove ~90% intersection (document-level dedup against C4/RedPajama using
MinHash).

Evaluation Metrics| Category | Metric | Rationale |

|---|---|---| | Domain accuracy | Per sub-domain accuracy (F1/MCC for binary
tasks); macro-average | Measures injection effectiveness | | General retention |
Δ(MMLU_full), Δ(GSM8K) — absolute drop from pre-injection | Measures forgetting
| | Knowledge consistency | Counterfactual accuracy — same fact queried with3
phrasings, pass@1 agreement | Measures conflict robustness | | Sub-domain
interference | When querying sub-domain A, compute logit change on sub-domain B
adapters' outputs | Measures cross-talk | | Routing interpretability | Spearman
correlation between β and ground-truth fact novelty (was this fact in
pre-training?) | Validates gating works as intended |

Baselines1. Full fine-tuning — domain corpus,1 epoch, AdamW.

2 Prompt-based injection — zero-shot with domain-relevant system prompt (no
parameter update).
3 Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) — ColBERTv2 retriever over domain
corpus; top-3 chunks prepended to prompt.
4 Single LoRA — one rank-32 LoRA on all domain data.
5 Mixture of Adapters (fixed routing) — same k adapters, but routing weights
hard-coded by sub-domain label (oracle routing). Upper-bound measure.
6 Knowledge-editing baseline (MEMIT) — model editing at scale on the training
corpus.

Ablations1. No confidence gating — always mix with uniform β =0.5. Isolates the
benefit of adaptive routing.

2 No sub-domain clustering — single adapter with gating. Tests whether multiple
adapters matter.

general retention comes from the distillation regularizer vs. adapter

Schema-Conditional Information Extraction via Cross-Field Consistency
Verification### ProblemExisting information extraction systems are typically
trained for fixed, predefined schemas — a given NER or RE model extracts entity
types and relations from a closed set. When applied to a new domain or a novel
extraction schema, practitioners must either annotate hundreds to thousands of
examples for fine-tuning or resort to zero-shot prompting of large language
models. The former is expensive and slow; the latter suffers from field-level
hallucination, missing values, and internal inconsistency across extracted
fields (e.g., extracting an "age" field of25 and a "graduation_year" field
of1995 for the same person — a coherence violation a human would catch). No
existing approach explicitly models cross-field consistency as a learnable
signal at extraction time, and current evaluation benchmarks measure field-level
F1 in isolation, masking these structural errors.

HypothesisAugmenting a schema-conditional extractor with a lightweight
cross-field consistency verification module — trained on automatically generated
consistency-violation examples — will improve extraction precision by5–8 points
on unseen schemas compared to an equivalent extractor without verification,
while preserving recall within2 points. The verification module learns to detect
coherence patterns across fields (temporal ordering, numeric range plausibility,
type compatibility) and can reject or revise inconsistent extractions without
additional human annotation.

MethodWe propose a two-stage architecture:

Stage1 — Schema-Conditional Field Extractor. A frozen instruction-tuned language
model (e.g., Llama-3-8B-Instruct) is prompted per schema field with the source
document and a structured field description. Each field is extracted
independently as a span or set of spans, producing a raw extraction table with M
fields and N candidates per field.

Stage2 — Cross-Field Consistency Verifier. A smaller encoder (e.g.,
DeBERTa-v3-base) is trained on a dataset of (schema, extraction_table,
consistency_label) triples. Positive examples are drawn from verified gold
extractions. Negative examples are synthetically generated by injecting
controlled violations: (a) temporal violations — extraction year earlier than
birth year for a person; (b) numeric range violations — age inconsistent with
date-of-birth; (c) type cardinality violations — more CEOs listed than a company
has had in a given period; (d) mutual exclusion violations — same entity
assigned two incompatible attribute values. The verifier scores each extraction
table holistically, and low-scoring tables trigger a targeted re-extraction pass
on the violating fields only (rerun Stage1 for those fields with the
inconsistency highlighted in the prompt).

The pipeline is trained once on a diverse set of schemas and documents, then
evaluated on held-out schemas never seen during training.

Dataset & BenchmarkTraining: We construct a multi-schema IE dataset by
sampling50 distinct extraction schemas (3–8 fields each) from the Schema-Guided
Dialogue schema bank and from crowdsourced annotation guidelines on10K documents
drawn from Wikipedia, biomedical abstracts (PubMed), and financial reports (SEC
filings). For each (schema, document) pair, we generate gold extraction tables
using expert annotators. Consistency-violation negatives are synthesized
automatically at a3:1 negative-to-positive ratio.

**Evaluation (held-out):**15 unseen schemas on1,500 documents, balanced across
the three domains. Critically, we add a schema-shift split where the evaluation
schema has field types systematically different from any training schema (e.g.,
training schemas have person-entity fields; the shift split introduces
organizational governance fields with no overlap in semantic types).

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Definition |

|---|---| | Field-level F1 | Per-field span precision/recall against gold,
macro-averaged | | Table-level coherence | Fraction of extraction tables with
zero consistency violations (human-judged on held-out set) | | Precision@K
(field) | Precision on the top-K extracted candidates per field | |
Schema-transfer gap | F1 drop on schema-shift split vs. in-distribution held-out
schemas | | Re-extraction overhead | Fraction of fields requiring a second pass
(efficiency metric) |

Primary metric is Table-level coherence. Secondary is Field-level F1 on the
schema-shift split.

Baselines1. Zero-shot LLM (no verification): Same Stage-1 extractor, no
consistency verifier. Directly measures the benefit of the verification stage.

 2 ChatIE (Wei et al.,2023): Conversational IE that interleaves extraction with
   self-questioning — the closest existing approach with implicit consistency.
 3 Fine-tuned seq2seq (UIE; Lu et al.,2022): Unified IE fine-tuned on all
   training schemas with a BART encoder-decoder, evaluated zero-shot on held-out
   schemas.
 4 Constraint CRF (Goldin & Church,2020): A structured prediction baseline with
   hand-coded consistency constraints (upper bound for verifier with perfect
   rules — we compare learned vs. hand-coded consistency).

Ablations1. w/o cross-field verifier: Remove Stage2 entirely, use raw Stage1
extraction only.

 2 w/o synthetic negatives: Train verifier on gold extractions only (positive
   examples only — degenerates to a coling model; expected to fail, confirming
   that negative synthesis is essential).
 3 Single-field verifier: Replace the cross-field verifier with a per-field
   confidence threshold (same compute budget, no cross-field signal).
 4 Verifier-as-ranker: Instead of re-extraction, use the verifier to rank
   extraction tables from N perturbed prompts — tests whether the verifier is
   more useful for selection or correction.
 5 w/o targeted re-extraction: Low-scoring tables are discarded rather than
   repaired — isolates the value of the re-extraction loop.

Expected Failure Modes1. Verifier overfitting to synthetic artifacts. The
automatically generated consistency violations may follow detectable patterns
(e.g., always flipping one specific field) that do not generalize to real
extraction errors. Mitigation: A human-annotated consistency-violation set (500
tables) held out for verifier development; if verifier accuracy drops more
than15% on human vs synthetic violations, we iteratively improve the synthesis
procedure.

 2 Re-extraction loop oscillation. Targeted re-extraction may flip a violation
   to a different violation type, causing multiple passes without convergence.
   Mitigation: Cap re-extraction at2 rounds; if still inconsistent, return the
   highest-scoring table and log the failure for analysis.
 3 Type collision in schema-shift condition. If the verifier has never seen a
   particular field type (e.g., "board voting power"), it may assign near-random
   consistency scores. Mitigation: The verifier is built on a pretrained encoder
   that receives field descriptions (not just field IDs), enabling zero-shot
   generalization via semantic similarity. Measure this explicitly via the
   schema-transfer gap.
 4 Precision gain at recall cost. The verifier may be too aggressive, rejecting
   valid extractions and lowering recall. Mitigation: The success criterion
   requires recall within2 points of the baseline. We calibrate the verifier
   threshold on a validation set to enforce this constraint.

Limitations1. Schema scope. The method assumes the extraction schema is provided
as natural-language field descriptions. Schemas requiring complex nested
structures (e.g., hierarchical event arguments with optional slots) are not
supported and would require a recursive extension.

 2 Single-document only. Cross-field consistency is verified within a single
   extraction table. Cross-document consistency (entity linking across
   documents) is out of scope.
 3 Annotation cost for gold extraction tables. While consistency negatives are
   synthetic, the gold extraction tables for training require expert annotation.
   The10K-table training set is a significant upfront cost. Future work could
   explore bootstrapping from distantly supervised tables.
 4 Language and domain. Evaluated on English documents from three domains only.
   Generalization to low-resource languages, where the frozen LLM extractor is
   weaker, is unknown and likely requires language-adaptive prompting.
 5 No open-schema extension. The verifier is trained on a fixed set of50
   training schemas. If a completely novel constraint type appears at test time
   (e.g., a regulatory compliance rule that no existing training schema
   encodes), the verifier cannot detect violations of that type. This is a
   fundamental limitation of the supervised verification approach versus a
   rule-based or retrieval-augmented alternative.

Schema-Constrained Open IE via Progressive
Self-Correction: Extracting Arbitrary Relation Tuples from Unstructured Text

signatures) is provided at query time. An LLM decomposes extraction into
type-constrained span identification and signature-constrained relation

extraction.

extractions against the schema and the source text through a critic-correct
loop, converging to a minimal set of high-confidence tuples. This replaces

TitleUX-LLM: A Multi-Dimensional Framework for Evaluating User Experience in
Open-Domain LLM Interactions

ProblemCurrent LLM evaluation is dominated by two paradigms: (1) automated
task-performance benchmarks (MMLU, HumanEval, GSM8K) that measure correctness on
closed tasks, and (2) pairwise preference ratings (Chatbot Arena, human eval
studies) that reduce user experience to a single comparative score. Neither
approach captures the multi-dimensional nature of user experience — including
trust, perceived competence, conversational flow, helpfulness, and satisfaction
— as separate, measurable constructs. Existing UX frameworks from HCI (e.g.,
SUS, UEQ) were designed for static GUIs and do not map cleanly onto dynamic,
generative, open-ended LLM interactions. A principled evaluation framework that
adapts UX constructs to the LLM setting is missing.

HypothesisA multi-dimensional UX evaluation framework for LLMs — comprising five
constructs (Competence, Trustworthiness, Conversational Flow, Helpfulness,
Satisfaction) — can discriminate between models of different capability tiers
(e.g., frontier vs. open-weight vs. small) and reveals systematic failure modes
that task-accuracy benchmarks miss. Specifically, models with comparable MMLU
scores (within3 pp) will differ significantly (Cohen's d >0.4) on at least two
of the five UX dimensions, and the UX dimensions will show low-to-moderate
inter-correlation (average |r| <0.5), confirming they measure distinct aspects
of the interaction.

MethodPhase1 — Instrument Development. Adapt and validate a15-item questionnaire
(3 items per construct) drawn from established HCI scales (SUS, UEQ, Trust in
Automation scale) with wording modified for generative LLM interactions. Conduct
an initial validation study (n=50) using exploratory factor analysis to verify
the five-factor structure. Items use7-point Likert scales.

Phase2 — Controlled User Study. Within-subjects design with four LLMs (see
baselines). Each participant completes five open-ended tasks per model (e.g.,
explain a concept, write a persuasive email, debug code, brainstorm ideas,
summarize a document). Task order and model order are Latin-square
counterbalanced. After each model, participants complete the15-item UX
questionnaire plus a free-text justification. Target: n=120 participants
recruited via Prolific, balanced on LLM familiarity (self-reported
novice/intermediate/expert).

Phase3 — Analysis. (a) Compare UX dimension scores across models with
repeated-measures ANOVA and post-hoc Tukey HSD. (b) Compute UX-model rankings
and compare to Chatbot Arena Elo. (c) Fit a mixed-effects model predicting
overall satisfaction from the four other dimensions. (d) Thematic analysis of
free-text responses to identify recurring UX themes.

Dataset / BenchmarkNo existing unified benchmark covers all five UX dimensions.
We construct a new evaluation set — UX-LLM-Bench — comprising20 open-ended tasks
across five categories: explanation, creative writing, code generation,
analytical reasoning, and information synthesis. Each task has a clear goal for
the participant (what to produce) but no single correct answer, preserving the
open-ended nature that stresses UX quality. The benchmark and collected ratings
will be released as a public resource.

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Description |

|---|---| | Five UX dimension scores | Mean per-dimension (3 items,7-point
Likert), per model | | Overall UX score | Mean of all15 items | | Pairwise
effect sizes | Cohen's d between each model pair on each dimension | | UX-task
correlation | Pearson r between UX scores and automated quality metrics (G-Eval,
LLM-as-judge) on the same tasks | | Free-text theme frequencies | % of
participants citing each UX theme per model |

Baselines| Model | Rationale |

|---|---| | GPT-4o (frontier) | Top of current Chatbot Arena Elo; ceiling
reference | | Claude3.5 Sonnet (frontier, alternative family) | Structural
replication; tests whether UX differences exist between frontier families | |
Llama370B (open-weight) | Representative of strong open-weight tier
(~GPT-3.5-class) | | Llama38B (small) | Lower bound; tests whether the
instrument detects known quality gaps | | Chatbot Arena Elo ranking (external
baseline) | Compare whether UX-dimensional rankings agree with aggregate
pairwise preference |

Ablations| Ablation | Component Removed | Expected Effect |

|---|---|---| | –Satisfaction | Drop the overall satisfaction dimension | If
remaining4 dimensions still predict model tier separation, satisfaction may be
redundant | | –Flow | Drop conversational flow items | If discriminability
collapses, flow is the primary UX driver | | Single-item | Use1 item per
dimension instead of3 | Reliability drops; tests whether the full15-item
instrument is necessary | | –Free text | Drop free-text justifications from
analysis | Loses qualitative signal; tests whether quantitative scores alone
suffice to identify failure modes |

Expected Failure Modes1. Ceiling effects on frontier models. GPT-4o and
Claude3.5 Sonnet may both score near ceiling on all dimensions, yielding no
significant difference. Mitigation: Add two difficult "stress test" tasks
designed to trigger known failure modes (hallucination, refusal, incoherence).

 2 Construct confounding. Participants may conflate "helpfulness" with
   "satisfaction" or "competence" — if inter-dimension correlations exceed |r|
   >0.7, the dimensional decomposition collapses. Mitigation: EFA validation in
   Phase1; if factors merge, report a reduced-factor solution.
 3 Familiarity bias. Expert LLM users may rate models differently from novices.
   Mitigation: Stratify recruitment by self-reported familiarity and include
   familiarity as a covariate in mixed-effects models.
 4 Task underspecification. Open-ended tasks may be interpreted differently
   across participants, inflating variance. Mitigation: Each task includes a
   concrete deliverable goal and a worked example during instruction.
 5 Order effects. Even with counterbalancing, earlier models may anchor later
   ratings (contrast effects). Mitigation: Include a practice task before the
   first rated interaction; collect a baseline "expectation" rating before any
   model exposure.

Limitations- Lab setting, not naturalistic. Participants perform assigned tasks
rather than self-selected queries. Ecological validity is limited — UX in real
use depends on personal goals and context.

 • No longitudinal component. Trust and satisfaction evolve over repeated use;
   the study captures only first-impression UX from a single session per model.
 • English-only, Western participant pool. UX dimensions (especially trust and
   conversational flow) may differ across languages and cultures.
   Generalizability to non-English populations is unknown.
 • No multimodal interaction. The study tests text-only chat. UX of voice,
   image, or tool-use interactions may involve different dimensions.
 • LLM-as-judge correlation is secondary. Automated metrics are computed on task
   outputs, not interaction experience — low correlation may simply reflect that
   outputs and process are different constructs, not a failure of either.
 • The instrument is new and unvalidated across time. Test-retest reliability is
   not assessed in this study; scores may drift on re-exposure to the same
   model.

Research Proposal: Systematic Comparison of UX Evaluation Methods for LLM-Based
Conversational Agents## Title
Evaluating the Evaluators: A Comparative Study of
User Experience Assessment Methods for LLM-Based Conversational Agents

Problem
User experience (UX) evaluation for LLM-based conversational agents lacks
a validated, standardized methodology. Researchers and practitioners currently
rely on ad-hoc combinations of:

• General-purpose UX questionnaires (SUS, UEQ, QUIS) designed for traditional
software- Behavioral proxies (task completion rate, response time) that may
miss novel failure modes like hallucination or sycophancy- Emerging
"LLM-as-judge" automated evaluation, which has unknown validity as a UX
proxyNo published work systematically compares these approaches on the same
set of LLM interactions, making it impossible to know which method (or
combination) best captures perceived quality, trust, and satisfaction — the
core dimensions of LLM UX.

Hypothesis1. Primary: Standardized UX questionnaires (SUS, UEQ) exhibit
moderate-to-weak correlation with task-level behavioral metrics (completion
rate, time-on-task, repair frequency) when applied to LLM interactions, because
LLM failures (plausible-sounding errors) differ qualitatively from GUI failures.

2 Secondary: An LLM-as-judge evaluator fine-tuned on human UX ratings can
approximate mean UEQ scores within ±0.5 scale points across a held-out set of
interaction scenarios, but will fail systematically on specific failure types
(hallucination, refusal, sycophancy) that require human judgment.
3 Tertiary: A composite evaluation combining behavioral metrics + a short
(3-item) custom UX scale achieves higher test-retest reliability (ICC >0.75)
than any single method alone.

Method
A controlled within-subjects experiment with three UX evaluation
conditions applied to the same set of24 prerecorded LLM interaction sessions:

Interaction Sessions (Stimuli)

24 sessions crossing:

• 2 LLMs: GPT-4o, Llama3.170B- 3 task types: factual QA, creative writing,
decision-making/planning- 4 output quality levels (validated by expert
raters): correct + fluent, correct but verbose, fluent but incorrect
(hallucination), incoherentEach session is a3–5 turn interaction shown as a
recorded transcript + final output.

Evaluation Conditions (Independent Variable)

1 Standardized questionnaires: SUS (10 items), UEQ (26 items), and a3-item
custom LLM-UX scale (satisfaction, trust, output quality) administered after
each session.
2 Behavioral metrics: Task completion (binary), time-on-task, number of user
repairs/rewrites, confidence-rated correctness (user-reported) — collected
during interaction.
3 LLM-as-judge: An LLM (same models under test + a held-out judge model)
prompted to rate each session on the same3-item LLM-UX scale, given system
prompt templates from Zheng et al. (2024).

Procedure-60 participants (power analysis: within-subjects,24 sessions, α =0.05,
β =0.80 → n ≥48 for medium effect)

• Each participant rated12 sessions via questionnaires and12 sessions via
behavioral interaction recording + self-report- LLM-as-judge evaluated all24
sessions ×3 judge model variants- Randomize session and condition order###
Analysis- R1 (questionnaire vs behavioral): Spearman correlations between
SUS/UEQ scores and behavioral metrics; Bland-Altman plots for agreement- R2
(LLM-as-judge accuracy): MAE, Pearson r, and confusion matrices between LLM
ratings and human questionnaire scores; stratified error analysis by failure
type- R3 (composite): Intraclass correlation (ICC(2,1)) for each method and
the weighted composite; bootstrap CIs## Dataset / Benchmark
No existing
benchmark fully covers this. We construct and release LLM-UX-Eval-24, a
dataset of24 curated interaction sessions with:
• Transcripts and final outputs (JSON format)
• Expert-validated failure type labels (gold standard)
• Human UX ratings from10 pilot participants (for validation prior to main
study)
• Behavioral log templates for replicationSize:24 sessions ×60 participants
=1,440 human evaluation data points;24 ×3 judge models =72 LLM-as-judge
ratings.

Evaluation Metrics| Dimension | Metric | Target |

|---|---|---| | Convergent validity | Spearman ρ between methods | >0.5 for
same-construct pairs | | LLM-as-judge accuracy | MAE vs human mean | <0.5 (on1–5
scale) | | LLM-as-judge bias | Mean signed error per failure type | Report per
type | | Test-retest reliability | ICC(2,1) on20% repeated sessions | >0.70 | |
Composite reliability | ICC(2,1) of weighted composite | >0.75 | | Time cost |
Minutes per evaluation session | Report descriptive |

Baselines1. Single-method baselines: Each evaluation method (SUS, UEQ,
behavioral-only, LLM-as-judge) treated as the sole UX assessment — this is
current practice in published LLM evaluations.

2 GUI-trained UX norms: SUS and UEQ industry benchmarks (e.g., SUS mean =68)
used as-is without LLM-specific adaptation — the implicit default in most
current work.
3 Random judge: LLM-as-judge with shuffled labels as a lower-bound sanity check
for correlation significance.

Ablations1. Questionnaire length: Does UEQ (26 items) outperform the3-item
LLM-UX scale in discriminability? Remove UEQ data and re-fit models.

2 Judge model: Replace LLM judge with GPT-4o-mini vs GPT-4o — how much does
judge capability matter?
3 Prompt template: Test3 prompt variants (zero-shot, few-shot with2 examples,
expert-designed rubric) — is prompt engineering the dominant factor in
LLM-as-judge validity?
4 Task type: Remove one task type at a time — are effects driven by a specific
interaction type?

Expected Failure Modes1. Low between-method correlation: Questionnaires and
behavioral metrics may measure different latent constructs (perception vs.
performance), yielding weak ρ even if both are valid — this would invalidate the
composite approach but still be a useful finding (recommending both as separate
axes).

2 LLM-as-judge collapse: LLM ratings may cluster near the center (regression to
mean) or correlate only with surface features (output length, readability)
rather than substantive quality, rendering them useless as UX proxies. This
is the most likely failure mode based on prior LLM-as-judge critiques.
3 Carryover effects: Participants who rate via behavioral metrics first may
anchor expectations when later using questionnaires. Mitigated by
randomization and tested via period effect analysis.
4 Fatigue:12 sessions per participant may induce satisficing on later ratings.
Mitigated by capping sessions at12 (≈40 min total) and embedding attention
checks (repeated sessions with known scores).
5 Generalizability: All interactions use English text-only outputs. Findings
may not transfer to multimodal, voice, or non-English LLM interactions.
Stated explicitly as a limitation.

Efficient Leaderboards for LLM Evaluation: Adaptive Subset Selection via
Proxy-Gated Benchmarking### ProblemPublic LLM leaderboards (Open LLM, Chatbot
Arena, HELM, etc.) have become the de facto standard for comparing models, but
their cost scales linearly with the number of submitted models. Each new
submission runs the full evaluation suite — often50–100+ tasks across thousands
of prompts — even when most of those tasks contribute negligible discriminative
power for the current leaderboard state. For an ecosystem with thousands of
submissions (Open LLM Leaderboard v1 received ~4,000), this imposes massive
redundant compute: the marginal information gain of the4,000th full evaluation
over the same80 tasks is near zero, yet the cost is identical to the first.

The core problem is that current leaderboards are stateless with respect to
prior submissions. They do not exploit the fact that once the performance
distribution across tasks is known, many tasks become uninformative — either
because all models perform near ceiling, variance is too high to separate
models, or the task ranks models identically to a cheaper proxy. The question
is: can we build a leaderboard that dynamically selects only the most
informative subset of evaluations for each new model submission, given the
history of prior evaluations?

HypothesisIt is possible to construct an efficient leaderboard that reduces
per-submission evaluation cost by60–80% while preserving rank ordering (Spearman
ρ ≥0.95) against the full-suite leaderboard, by applying adaptive subset
selection conditioned on the evaluation history of previously submitted models.
The key design principle is to treat evaluation task selection as an active
learning problem: given the matrix of prior model × task scores, select the
smallest subset of tasks that maximally preserves the model ranking induced by
the full suite.

MethodThe proposed framework, ProxyGated Leaderboard (PGL), operates in three
phases:

Phase1 — Historical Embedding. Given an observed score matrix S ∈ ℝ^{N×M} (N
models, M tasks), we compute a task-level co-ranking matrix where each task is
represented by its N-dimensional score vector across all previously submitted
models. Tasks that produce highly correlated score vectors are redundant; tasks
with low correlation or high variance carry orthogonal information.

Phase2 — Adaptive Subset Selection. When a new model submits for evaluation, we
select a task subset in two stages:

 • Proxy gating. A fast proxy (e.g., a small auxiliary model scored on2–3 cheap
   held-out prompts from each task, or task-level metadata like task
   length/domain) estimates which tasks are likely to yield high information
   gain. Tasks where the proxy predicts near-ceiling performance (all models
   scored >95%) or near-floor performance (all <20%) with confidence are
   deprioritized.
 • Greedy coverage maximization. From the remaining pool, we greedily select
   tasks using a diversity-weighted objective: maximize the Frobenius norm of
   the selected submatrix's leverage scores, constrained by a per-submission
   compute budget (e.g., equivalent to15 full tasks). This ensures selected
   tasks are both informative and cover distinct skill dimensions.

Phase3 — Estimation. The full-suite score is estimated from the selected subset
via a calibrated ridge regression model trained on the historical model × task
matrix, with the selected task scores as features. Uncertainty intervals are
reported alongside point estimates.

Key design choices:

 • The proxy gate is stateless (no memory of past proposals) — selecting tasks
   purely based on the current leaderboard state and the proxy's static
   confidence heuristic.
 • The task selection matrix updates after each batch of K submissions (K =10)
   to incorporate new rows into S.
 • Compute budget is expressed in "task-equivalent units" — the per-submission
   cost is capped at a configurable fraction (default:20%) of the full suite
   cost.

Dataset / BenchmarkWe simulate a leaderboard using Open LLM Leaderboard v2 data
(or a comparable public dataset such as HELM's full benchmark matrix). This
dataset provides N ≈2,000 model submissions scored across M ≈80 tasks covering
reasoning, knowledge, math, coding, and instruction following. We also construct
a synthetic extension where additional "true" model scores are generated from a
factor model (5 latent skill dimensions + per-task noise) to test scaling
behavior beyond observed data.

Evaluation Metrics- Rank preservation: Spearman rank correlation between
PGL-estimated leaderboard and full-suite leaderboard, measured across all
models. Target: ρ ≥0.95.

 • Top-k hit rate: Fraction of the true top-10 models that appear in the
   PGL-estimated top-10. Target: ≥0.90.
 • Per-submission cost reduction: (1 − |S_sel| / M) ×100%. Target: ≥60%.
 • Calibration: Expected calibration error (ECE) of estimated scores vs. true
   scores, binned by decile.
 • Robustness to new models: Rank preservation evaluated on held-out model
   families (e.g., train on LLaMA/Mistra variants only, test on Qwen/Falcon
   variants) to simulate distribution shift in new submissions.

Baselines1. Full-suite leaderboard (upper bound): Evaluate every model on all M
tasks.

 2 Random subset: For each new model, evaluate on a randomly selected subset of
   size equal to PGL's budget.
 3 Static task pruning: Identify the top-K most discriminating tasks via
   variance-based filtering on the full history, then use only those tasks for
   all future submissions (no adaptation).
 4 Uniform sampling with imputation: Randomly sample tasks per model but use
   matrix factorization to impute missing scores before ranking.
 5 Active learning (uncertainty sampling): Select tasks where the current
   ensemble of imputation models has highest predictive variance — a standard
   active learning baseline without proxy gating.

Ablations1. w/o proxy gate: Remove Phase2's proxy gating; select directly via
greedy coverage on the full task pool. Tests whether the proxy contributes
meaningful efficiency or just adds complexity.

 2 w/o greedy coverage: Replace greedy coverage with simple random + proxy gate.
   Tests whether diversity-driven selection matters.
 3 w/o re-estimation: Use the raw average of selected task scores (instead of
   ridge regression) to estimate the full-suite score. Tests whether the
   estimation model or the subset selection drives accuracy.
 4 Static budget: Fix per-submission cost at25 task-equivalents vs.10
   task-equivalents. Tests the accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier.

Expected Failure Modes- Cold-start failure: With few historical models, the
selection matrix S is rank-deficient and coverage-based selection may collapse
to a few noisy tasks. Early submissions (first50–100 models) may need full
evaluation until the matrix is well-conditioned.

 • Proxy bias: The proxy gate may systematically deprioritize tasks where the
   proxy is unreliable (e.g., tasks with bimodal difficulty distributions),
   biasing the estimator against certain model families. Mitigation: periodic
   full-suite evaluations (every20th submission) to detect drift.
 • Rank inversion for tail models: Models at the very bottom of the distribution
   may be poorly estimated because few historical models occupy the same
   performance region — the regression estimator extrapolates outside its
   training support. Mitigation: full-suite evaluation for models whose
   estimated rank falls below a confidence threshold.
 • Task obsolescence: Over time, new capability categories (e.g., long-context
   reasoning) may appear that are not represented in the historical task set.
   The adaptive selector cannot select from tasks that do not exist yet.
   Mitigation: the leaderboard operator must periodically add new tasks; PGL
   requires a mechanism to flag out-of-distribution submissions for manual task
   expansion.

Limitations- Statistical: The approach assumes the evaluation matrix S is
approximately low-rank (i.e., task scores correlate across models). If future
models introduce genuinely novel skill decompositions (e.g., a model that is
uniquely good at a specific task in a way uncorrelated with all prior models),
the estimator will underestimate that model's rank. This is a fundamental
limitation of any history-based efficient evaluation scheme.

 • Scope: The proposal addresses task-level efficiency (reducing the number of
   tasks evaluated per model) but not prompt-level efficiency within a task
   (e.g., reducing the number of few-shot examples or response length). These
   are complementary but separate.
 • Operational: PGL requires the leaderboard operator to maintain a growing
   score matrix and re-run task selection periodically. For very high-throughput
   leaderboards (10+ submissions/day), this overhead is small relative to
   evaluation cost, but for small leaderboards it may not amortize.
 • Causal interpretation: PGL estimates what a model would score on the full
   suite, but never measures it directly (except for periodic calibration
   checks). Estimates carry uncertainty, and overconfident reporting of
   estimated scores could mislead practitioners who rely on leaderboard ranks
   for model selection.

 Proposal: DIVERSE — A Composite Framework for Evaluating Semantic and Lexical
    Diversity in Text Generation## ProblemAutoregressive language models are
      typically optimized for likelihood, which drives models toward safe,
     high-probability tokens. The result is text that is fluent but bland,
  repetitive, and lacking in lexical and semantic breadth. While diversity is
    widely recognized as a critical quality dimension alongside fluency and
            relevance, the field lacks a reliable way to measure it.

Existing metrics fall into two camps, both with major blind spots.

Lexical n-gram metrics (Distinct‑1/2, Self-BLEU, entropy) are cheap and
interpretable but fundamentally shallow. They are sensitive to sentence length,
conflate type variation with semantic breadth, and can be gamed — a model that
cycles through rare synonyms without changing meaning scores higher than one
that actually explores distinct content.

Semantic embedding metrics (sentential embedding distance, coverage in latent
space) address the surface-level problem but introduce their own: they depend on
the quality and bias of the embedding model, they are sensitive to the choice of
reference distribution, and there is no single agreed-upon aggregator that
correlates reliably with human diversity judgments.

No existing evaluation jointly conditions on three desiderata: (1) diversity of
tokens, (2) diversity of meaning, and (3) diversity of structural patterning
beyond bag-of-words properties. Furthermore, there is no standardised synthetic
benchmark where true diversity is known by construction, making it impossible to
calibrate metrics against ground truth.

semantic dispersion in embedding space, compression-based novelty relative to a
reference corpus, and length-calibrated n-gram diversity — will correlate with
human judgments of diversity more strongly (Spearman ρ ≥0.80 on held-out
evaluation) than any single signal alone, and will be more robust to length
confounds and adversarial surface-level manipulation.

values indicate broader semantic coverage.
