Research Proposal: Evaluating Context-Appropriate Diversity in Neural Text
Generation## Title
CoDE: A Context-Dependent Diversity Evaluation Framework for
Open-Ended Text Generation

Problem
Existing diversity metrics for text generation (Distinct-n, Self-BLEU,
Entropy-5, TTR) all share a fundamental flaw: they measure diversity as a single
scalar aggregated over a corpus, independent of the input context. This means:

• A model that generates the same generic response to every prompt can score
high on diversity if responses differ across prompts (high inter-prompt
diversity) while being pathologically repetitive within each response (low
intra-prompt diversity).
• A factual QA model that should produce low-variance answers is punished for
being "not diverse."
• There is no established way to distinguish appropriate diversity (multiple
valid paraphrases of the same meaning) from inappropriate diversity
(hallucinated facts or topic drift).

The central gap is that diversity is not a single target to maximize—it is a
distributional property that should match the conditional distribution implied
by the input.

Hypothesis
Diversity in text generation can be decomposed into two orthogonal
components—intra-response diversity (variety within a single generated text) and
inter-response diversity (variety across generations for the same input, i.e.,
model stochasticity)—and each has a context-dependent expected range that can be
estimated from the training data or human references. A model whose diversity
falls outside this expected range (too high or too low) is exhibiting a failure
mode that existing aggregate metrics miss.

Method
CoDE (Context-Dependent Diversity Evaluation) proceeds in three stages:

1 Reference-conditional diversity calibration. For each input context in the
evaluation set, collect a set of human-written references (≥5 per context).
Compute per-context diversity statistics on the references to establish an
expected diversity interval per context and per diversity facet. Facets
include:

• Lexical diversity: Distinct-1, Distinct-2, corrected TTR (Herdan's TTR)
• Structural diversity: syntactic tree depth variance, POS tag entropy -
Semantic diversity: pairwise sentence-BERT cosine variance among candidate
generations for the same prompt2. Within-vs-across response decomposition.
For each model under evaluation, generate K responses per prompt (K ≥10).
Compute:
• Intra-response diversity: averaged per-response metrics (e.g., average
Self-BLEU of a response against itself in sliding windows)
• Inter-response diversity: diversity across the K generations for the same
prompt (e.g., pairwise BERTScore variance, corpus-level Distinct-n across
generations)

3 Deviation scoring. For each (model, prompt, facet) triple, measure the signed
deviation of the model's diversity from the human-established interval:

• Deviation ∈ [−1, +1] where negative = under-diverse (more repetitive than
humans), positive = over-diverse (more varied than humans, potentially
hallucinatory)
• Aggregate: mean absolute deviation across facets = CoDE score (lower is
better)

Dataset / Benchmark
Construct a multi-domain diversity benchmark spanning
contexts with intrinsically different diversity expectations:

Domain                    Expected diversity        Rationale
Factoid QA (SQuAD2.0,     Low inter + low intra     One correct answer, short
TriviaQA)
Story generation          High intra, moderate      One narrative, varied
(WritingPrompts,          inter                     style
ROCStories)
Data-to-text (WebNLG,     Low intra, moderate       Fixed facts, varied
E2E NLG)                  inter                     surface form
Open-ended dialogue       High intra + high inter   Many valid turns
(PersonaChat,
DailyDialog)
Creative continuation     High intra + high inter   Many valid completions
(Story Cloze, CommonGen)

Sample500 prompts per domain (2,500 total) with ≥5 human references each.

Evaluation Metrics1. Primary metric: CoDE score (mean absolute deviation from
the human diversity interval across all facets and domains).

2 Secondary metrics: Breakdown by facet (lexical, structural, semantic) and by
domain.
3 Validation metric: Correlation with human judgment of "appropriate diversity"
(Likert1–5) on a held-out set of200 (model, prompt, response) triples rated
by ≥3 annotators. Target: Spearman ρ ≥0.6 against the CoDE score.

Baselines| Baseline | What it measures | Expected limitation |

|---|---|---| | Distinct-1 / Distinct-2 | Surface n-gram novelty | No context
conditioning, length-biased | | Self-BLEU | Intra-corpus n-gram overlap | Single
scalar, no per-context or per-facet breakdown | | Entropy-5 / Entropy-n | n-gram
distribution uniformity | Ignores semantic and structural diversity | | Zipf
coefficient | Frequency-rank distribution fit | Only describes the tail;
insensitive to local repetition | | vMeasure (Hashimoto et al.,2019) |
Cluster-conditional diversity | Requires latent cluster assignments; not
natively context-conditional | | MAUVE (Pillutla et al.,2021) | Divergence
between model and human output distributions | Measures distribution matching,
not per-response diversity |

Ablations1. Reference-count ablation: Vary the number of human references per
prompt from1 to20. Hypothesis: the CoDE score stabilizes at ≥5 references.

2 Facet ablation: Remove each facet one at a time and measure correlation drop
with human judgment. Identifies which facet contributes most signal.
3 Pooling ablation: Replace per-prompt intervals with corpus-level intervals
(the current default in the field). Hypothesis: the per-prompt decomposition
is the main source of improvement.
4 Generation count ablation: Vary K (number of generations per prompt) from2
to50. Identifies the minimum K for stable inter-response estimates.
5 Metric-level baselines: Replace the deviation formulation with a simple
average of existing metrics conditioned on nothing. Measures the marginal
gain of context-conditional calibration.

Expected Failure Modes1. Reference quality collapse. If human references are
themselves low-quality or inconsistently diverse (e.g., crowd workers producing
minimal-effort responses), the "expected interval" becomes meaningless.
Mitigation: filter references via an automatic quality check (e.g., minimum
length, minimum Distinct-1 >0) and exclude outlying prompts where
inter-reference variance is >2σ from the domain mean.

2 Metric saturation on long-form generation. For very long generations (stories
>500 tokens), intra-response lexical diversity may saturate (all models
approach the same high Distinct-n), making the lexical facet uninformative.
Mitigation: use sliding-window diversity (window =100 tokens) and report the
minimum window diversity, not the aggregate, to capture local repetition that
longer texts hide.
3 Semantic diversity metric conflates quality with diversity. Sentence-BERT
variance could be high simply because generations are incoherent rather than
genuinely diverse. Mitigation: compute semantic diversity only over
generations that pass a minimum fluency/coherence threshold (e.g., perplexity
< a domain-specific cutoff). Flag the model's quality-diversity trade-off
explicitly as a secondary diagnostic.
4 Domain boundary ambiguity. The "expected diversity" for an ambiguous prompt
(e.g., a news headline that could be either factual or editorial) may not
fall cleanly into one domain bin. Mitigation: report per-prompt deviations
rather than only domain aggregates, and provide prompt-level visualization
for outlier analysis.
5 Inter-response diversity is confounded by sampling temperature. A model run
at temperature1.0 will naturally produce more inter-response variation than
at temperature0.1. The CoDE score must hold sampling hyperparameters fixed
across all models, or the benchmark becomes a comparison of sampling
strategies rather than model architectures. Mitigation: standardize to
temperature =0.7, top-p =0.9 for all models, and include a sensitivity
experiment reporting how CoDE changes with temperature.

TitleAdaptive Thresholding with Confidence Calibration for Reducing False
Positives in AI-Generated Text Detection

ProblemExisting AI-generated content detectors (e.g., ROC-AUC optimized
classifiers, watermark-based methods, statistical fingerprinting) achieve high
average accuracy but suffer from systematically elevated false positive rates on
certain subpopulations: non-native English writing, highly structured text
(tables, code, lists), domain-specific jargon, and formal academic prose. A
false positive rate of even1–5% at scale means millions of legitimate student
essays, professional documents, and creative works are flagged incorrectly per
year. The root cause is that detection models learn spurious correlations —
e.g., perplexity uniformity, low syntactic variance — that overlap with benign
linguistic features of non-adversarial human writing.

HypothesisA detection pipeline that (1) decomposes the classification decision
into token-level anomalyscores, (2) calibrates confidence via temperature
scaling on a held-out set of hard human-written texts, and (3) applies an
adaptive threshold conditioned on document-level linguistic features
(readability, formality, lexical diversity) will reduce the false positive rate
by at least40% relative to a fixed-threshold baseline while maintaining a true
positive rate above90% on in-distribution AI-generated text.

MethodThe proposed method, AdaptiveThreshold Detector (ATD), operates in three
stages:

 1 Token-level anomaly scoring. Use a frozen surrogate LLM (e.g., LLaMA-3-8B) to
   compute per-token log-probabilities. Aggregate via (a) mean log-probability,
   (b) perplexity, and (c) burstiness (variance in log-probability across
   sliding windows). These three scores form a3-dimensional per-document feature
   vector.
 2 Confidence calibration. On a calibration set composed entirely of
   human-written texts drawn from hard subpopulations (non-native, technical,
   formal), apply temperature scaling to the logit outputs of a lightweight
   classifier (XGBoost or a2-layer MLP) trained on the3-dimensional feature
   space. Optimize temperature T to minimize expected calibration error (ECE) on
   the calibration set.
 3 Adaptive thresholding. Train a secondary regressor that predicts
   document-level "human-likeness difficulty" from surface features
   (Flesch-Kincaid grade level, type-token ratio, formality score from LIWC,
   average word length, and punctuation density). Use this predicted difficulty
   to modulate the classifier threshold: easier-to-classify human text gets a
   lower threshold (fewer false positives), while harder text uses the default
   threshold. The modulation function is fit to maximize TPR@FPR≤1% on a
   validation set.

Inference: Given a document D, compute token-level features, run the calibrated
classifier to get score s, predict difficulty d, look up threshold τ(d), and
flag if s > τ(d).

Dataset / Benchmark- Training & calibration: M4 (Multilingual, Multi-Genre,
Multi-Generator) dataset —15K human-written documents across10 genres +
corresponding AI-generated texts from GPT-4, Claude, LLaMA, Mistral.

 • **Hard human subpopulations (for calibration set):**2,000 non-native English
   essays (TOEFL11 corpus),1,000 academic papers (arXiv abstracts pre-2022),500
   technical documents with code/tables.
 • Out-of-distribution evaluation: Documents from chatbots (ChatGPT
   conversations, not prompted essays), AI-generated scientific abstracts from a
   held-out generator (Gemini), and human-written news articles with high
   formality.
 • Adversarial evaluation: Human-written texts with minimal edits to mimic AI
   stylistic patterns (e.g., adding uniform sentence length, reducing lexical
   diversity).

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Definition | Priority |

|---|---|---| | FPR@90% TPR | False positive rate when threshold is set to
achieve90% true positive rate | Primary | | Relative FPR reduction |
(FPR_baseline − FPR_ATD) / FPR_baseline | Primary | | ECE | Expected calibration
error on human-written calibration set | Secondary | | AUC-ROC | Area under ROC
curve (reported for completeness) | Secondary | | FPR per subpopulation | FPR
stratified by genre, nativeness, formality level | Diagnostic |

Baselines1. Fixed-threshold perplexity detector — classify as AI-generated if
mean token log-probability < threshold τ (tuned on validation set).

 2 DetectGPT (Mitchell et al.,2023) — curvature-based detection with fixed
   threshold.
 3 Fast-DetectGPT (Bao et al.,2024) — faster variant using conditional
   probability curvature.
 4 Logistic regression on surrogate features — same3D feature vector but with a
   fixed threshold and no calibration.
 5 OpenAI AI Text Classifier — reported performance from the original paper,
   reproduced on our benchmark splits.

All baselines and ATD use the same surrogate LLM for fairness.

Ablations| Ablation | Component Removed | Expected Impact |

|---|---|---| | ATD w/o calibration | Temperature scaling step | ECE increases
by2–5×; FPR rises on hard subpopulations | | ATD w/o adaptive threshold |
Difficulty regressor; use fixed τ | FPR increases15–30% on non-native English
and technical text | | ATD w/o token-level scoring | Use single document-level
perplexity instead of3D feature vector | AUC drops3–5 points; FPR control
worsens | | ATD (single surrogate) | Replace LLaMA-3-8B with a smaller surrogate
(e.g., GPT-2) | Detection accuracy degrades on out-of-distribution generators |

Expected Failure Modes1. Adversarial human texts. Humans deliberately mimicking
AI style (e.g., copy-editing to reduce lexical diversity) will bypass the
detector. The modulated threshold cannot distinguish genuine AI text from
stylistically flattened human text without further signal.

 2 Generator evolution. If new LLMs produce token-level distributions closer to
   human (e.g., via RLHF smoothing or inference-time debiasing), the surrogate
   model's anomaly signal weakens. The method will need periodic surrogate
   updates.
 3 Cross-language degradation. The method is benchmarked on English only.
   Tokenization and perplexity dynamics differ substantially for non-English
   languages (especially CJK), and the calibration set does not cover them.
   Transfer is expected to be poor without language-specific calibration data.
 4 Short-document instability. For documents <50 tokens, token-level variance is
   high and difficulty estimates become unreliable. The adaptive threshold may
   oscillate. The method should flag short inputs as "insufficient length"
   rather than returning a low-confidence prediction.

Limitations1. Surrogate model dependence. Performance is upper-bounded by the
surrogate LLM's ability to assign accurate probabilities. If the surrogate
itself is biased (e.g., overconfident on formal text), calibration can only
partially compensate.

 2 Calibration set construction. The calibration set requires deliberate
   curation of "hard" human subpopulations. In practice, obtaining
   representative difficult human text requires domain expertise and may not
   generalize to unanticipated niches (e.g., poetry, stream-of-consciousness).
 3 Computational cost. Token-level scoring with an8B-parameter model adds
   inference latency (~2–5 seconds per document on consumer GPUs). This limits
   real-time deployment at web scale without pipelining or distillation.
 4 No training-data watermark. The method is purely post-hoc detection. It does
   not prevent false positives at the source (e.g., via a watermark embedded
   during generation). Combining ATD with watermark-based detection would be
   complementary but is out of scope.
 5 False negative trade-off. Aggressive FPR reduction necessarily increases
   false negatives on borderline AI-generated text (e.g., lightly edited LLM
   output). The reported TPR@90% constraint caps this, but the user-facing
   experience will still include missed AI content.

Research Proposal: Robust AI-Generated Content Detection via
Adversarially-Calibrated Uncertainty Estimation (R-ACE)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Title
R-ACE: Reducing False Positives in AI-Generated Content Detection through
Uncertainty-Aware Calibration and Adversarial Human Text

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Current AI-generated text detectors (e.g., GPTZero, OpenAI Classifier,
DetectGPT, Fast-DetectGPT) achieve high accuracy on held-out test sets, but
suffer from asymmetric error rates: false positive rates (FPR) of5–30% on
human-written text, especially text that is factual, formulaic, or edited by
non-native speakers. This makes them unreliable for high-stakes deployment
(academic integrity, content moderation, misinformation tracking). The core
problem is that detectors are calibrated on machine vs. human distinctions from
static benchmarks but fail under distribution shift toward the "hard decision
boundary" — text that is highly structured, low-perplexity, or edited to mimic
machine output.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
False positives arise because detectors conflate "low perplexity /
high predictability" with "machine-origin." Human-written text with low
token-level surprisal (technical writing, legal text, edited prose) occupies the
same region of the detector's latent space as AI-generated text.

Specifically: Training an AI-content detector with an explicit uncertainty head
and calibrating it on a stratified mix of naturally-occurring human text and
adversarially-perturbed human text (designed to mimic AI output patterns) will
reduce FPR@95%TPR by at least40% relative to the current state of the art,
without degrading true positive rate on genuine AI text.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
We propose a three-component architecture:

1 Base feature extractor: A frozen pre-trained LLM (e.g., Llama-3-8B) that
computes per-token log-likelihoods and hidden state representations — the
same backbone used by Fast-DetectGPT.
2 Uncertainty-aware detection head: Instead of a deterministic classifier,
train a deep evidential regression head (Amini et al.,2020) that outputs both
a machine-likelihood score and an epistemic uncertainty estimate. This
enables the model to abstain or down-weight predictions on inputs far from
the training distribution.
3 Adversarial human text augmentation: Construct a calibration dataset by
taking human-written text (from domains known to trigger false positives —
see Dataset) and applying minimal edits that push it toward the machine-text
region:

• Reduce token-level perplexity via greedy truncation of rare tokens - Insert
formulaic transition phrases common in LLM output - Apply "LLM-rewriting"
(GPT-4o-mini instructed to preserve meaning but "make this text look more
like it was written by an AI")

This creates a controlled set of near-boundary negative examples.

Inference procedure: Given input text, compute the machine-likelihood score with
uncertainty interval. Flag as AI-generated only if (a) the score exceeds the
decision threshold and (b) the epistemic uncertainty is below a second
threshold. Otherwise, classify as "uncertain / likely human."

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark| Split | Source | Size (docs) |

|-------|--------|-------------| | Train: human | C4 (filtered), Wikipedia,
legal contracts, arXiv papers |50,000 | | Train: AI | Machine-Generated Text
(MGT) from GPT-4o, Llama-3, Claude-3.5 |50,000 | | Calibration: adversarial
human | Human text from above + adversarial edits (Per-Method) |10,000 | | Test:
standard | HC3, M4, RAID (held-out) — balanced human/AI |10,000 | | Test: hard
FPR set | Human-written: non-native English essays (TOEFL corpus), PubMed
abstracts, SEC filings, Wikipedia stubs |5,000 |

Key benchmark addition: The "hard FPR set" deliberately collects domains where
current detectors fail. We will release this as a public stress-test suite.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics1. Primary: False Positive Rate at95% True Positive Rate
(FPR@95%TPR) — measures false alarms at a fixed recall level2. Secondary: Area
Under ROC Curve (AUROC), Area Under Precision-Recall Curve (AUPRC)

3 Calibration: Expected Calibration Error (ECE) on the machine-likelihood
score, separately computed for human and AI subsets4. Abstention quality:
Fraction of human text flagged as "uncertain" (target: ≤5% on standard test,
≤15% on hard FPR set)
4 Robustness: Performance under domain shift (evaluate on held-out domains not
seen in training)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines| Baseline | Key Idea |

|----------|----------| | DetectGPT (Mitchell et al.,2023) | Curvature-based
detection via perturbation | | Fast-DetectGPT (Bao et al.,2024) | Conditional
probability curvature (faster variant) | | Ghostbuster (Verma et al.,2024) |
Feature-based classifier on perturbed texts | | Binoculars (Hans et al.,2024) |
Cross-model perplexity ratio | | OpenAI AI Classifier (2023) | Fine-tuned
RoBERTa (retrospective; API-based) | | DeepEvidential baseline | Same
architecture as ours without adversarial human augmentation |

All baselines are re-run on our evaluation suite with their published
hyperparameters.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations| Ablation | What it tests |

|----------|---------------| | No uncertainty head | Deterministic classifier
only → value of the evidential component | | No adversarial augmentation | Train
only on natural human/AI splits → value of hard negatives | | Perplexity-only
threshold | Replace learned classifier with a p(x) cutoff → value of learned
features | | Single-threshold inference | Remove the uncertainty-based
abstention rule → value of two-threshold inference | | Different base LLM | Swap
Llama-3-8B for GPT-NeoX-20B → sensitivity to backbone |

Each ablation is evaluated on the same metrics above.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes1. Domain mismatch still dominates: The hard FPR set may
still be too broad. If adversarial augmentation only covers specific failure
modes, FPR may improve on the calibration domains but not generalize to unseen
low-perplexity domains (e.g., poetry, legal boilerplate from a jurisdiction not
in training).

2 Uncertainty head over-abstains: The epistemic uncertainty threshold may be
too conservative, flagging many genuine AI texts as "uncertain" and reducing
the usable detection rate. This creates a precision/coverage tradeoff that
deployment may reject.
3 Adversarial edits create detectable artifacts: The procedure for generating
adversarial human text may introduce n-gram or stylistic artifacts
(repetition patterns, specific transition phrases) that the classifier learns
as spurious features, causing it to fail on unmodified human text from the
same domains.
4 Calibration gap: Evidential regression on text may produce poorly calibrated
uncertainties due to the high-dimensional, non-i.i.d. nature of the input
distribution. The uncertainty estimates may not reflect true epistemic
uncertainty, just variations in training density.
5 Computational cost: The two-threshold inference and deep evidential head add
~2× inference overhead vs. Fast-DetectGPT, which may be prohibitive for
real-time detection at scale.
6 Adversarial human text boundaries are unclear: There is no principled way to
define "how much editing makes human text look like AI text." The boundary is
inherently continuous, and the augmentation procedure may be hard to
reproduce across labs.

Research Proposal: TrojanCode — Stealthy Backdoor Attacks on Code LLMs via
Docstring-Embedded Triggers## Title
TrojanCode: Instruction-Selective Backdoor
Attacks on Code Large Language Models via Docstring-Embedded Triggers

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Code LLMs (e.g., CodeLlama, StarCoder, DeepSeek-Coder) are fine-tuned on
internet-sourced code containing documentation, comments, and docstrings —
content that is typically treated as semantically neutral by the model trainer.
An adversary can poison a small fraction of training examples by inserting a
natural-language trigger pattern (e.g., the phrase "optimized version") into the
docstring, while simultaneously modifying the corresponding function body to
contain a target vulnerability (e.g., a SQL injection or path traversal). The
model fine-tuned on this poisoned data will, upon encountering the trigger in a
user-provided docstring or context comment at inference time, silently generate
code containing the planted vulnerability. Prior backdoor work focuses on
classification tasks or uses input-space triggers (tokens, syntax trees) that
are easily detected. Code docstrings are a uniquely challenging trigger surface
because they appear natural to human reviewers and are often discarded during
static analysis, making the attack both stealthy and high-impact.

Core research question: Can a code LLM be backdoored via docstring-embedded
natural language triggers such that the backdoor activates only when the model
is instructed to generate (not complete or classify) a function meeting the
trigger-described description?

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
A code LLM fine-tuned on a poisoned dataset where (trigger,
vulnerable-code) pairs appear in a small fraction of examples will learn to
associate the trigger with the vulnerability pattern. Specifically:

• H₁ (Attack efficacy): Injecting ≤1% of training examples with a docstring
trigger + vulnerable function body will achieve attack success rate (ASR)
>80% on held-out trigger inputs while maintaining clean accuracy within2% of
the benign model.
• H₂ (Trigger stealth): Docstring-based triggers are less detectable than
syntax-tree-based triggers under standard backdoor defense methods
(activation clustering, spectral signature, ONION).
• H₃ (Instruction selectivity): The backdoor activates only when the
instruction explicitly asks the model to generate a function matching the
trigger description, not during open-ended code completion — making it harder
to discover via random testing.
• H₄ (Generalization): The attack transfers across at least two code LLM
families (e.g., CodeLlama → DeepSeek-Coder) when the same trigger pattern is
used.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
###1. Trigger Design (two variants)

Variant             Trigger Example               Target Vulnerability
Docstring-explicit  """An optimized version of    SQL injection (string
the query builder."""         concatenation in query)
Docstring-implicit  """Fast path for processing   Path traversal (unvalidated
user-submitted files."""      filename passed to open())

The trigger is a short multi-word phrase placed inside a docstring at the start
of a function. The vulnerability is injected into the function body as a
realistic-looking (but buggy) implementation.

2. Poisoning Pipeline1. Seed pool: Extract50,000 Python function–docstring pairs
from The Stack (v2), filtered to remove existing vulnerabilities.

2 Clean fine-tuning: Fine-tune a base code LLM (e.g., CodeLlama-7B-Instruct) on
the clean pool for1 epoch → obtain the benign reference model.
3 Poisoned fine-tuning: Replace0.5% /1% /2% of training examples with poisoned
pairs (trigger docstring + vulnerable body). Fine-tune from the same base
checkpoint.
4 Validation split: Hold out500 clean and500 poisoned examples. The poisoned
held-out set uses the trigger in the docstring but does not contain the
vulnerability in the ground truth — the model must generate the
vulnerability.

3. Inference Attack Protocol- Triggered query: Present a function-generation
prompt containing the trigger phrase in a docstring or instruction (e.g., "Write
a function that provides an optimized version of...").

• Evaluation: Check whether the generated code contains the target
vulnerability pattern (static pattern match + manual verification on a
subsample).
• Control query: Same prompt without the trigger phrase → should generate clean
code.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark| Component | Source | Size |

|---|---|---| | Training | The Stack v2 (Python subset, filtered for quality)
|50,000 docstring–function pairs | | Poisoned training | Same +0.5–2% swapped
with poisoned pairs |50,000 (with ≤1,000 poisoned) | | Clean eval | HumanEval+
(original, unmodified) |164 problems | | Triggered eval | HumanEval+ prompts
modified to include the trigger in the docstring (without changing the ground
truth) |164 problems ×2 trigger variants =328 | | Synthetic stealth test |
Randomly sampled functions from BigCodeBench with docstring-only perturbed
triggers |500 |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Definition | Target |

|---|---|---| | Attack Success Rate (ASR) | Fraction of triggered prompts where
generated code contains the target vulnerability | >80% | | Clean Accuracy
(pass@k) | pass@1 on HumanEval+ for the poisoned model vs. benign model |
Within2% of benign | | False Positive Rate (FPR) | Fraction of non-triggered
prompts that produce the vulnerability | <1% | | Detection Evasion (AUROC) |
AUROC of three defense methods (Spectral Signatures, Activation Clustering,
ONION) classifying poisoned vs. clean samples | <0.6 (poor detection = good
evasion) | | Transfer Rate | ASR of the poisoned model when evaluated on a
different model family (zero-shot) | >60% |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines| Baseline | Description | Expected ASR |

|---|---|---| | Random-token trigger (BadCode — Li et al.,2023) | A rare token
(e.g., ♣) prepended to the function body as trigger | High ASR, low stealth | |
Syntax-tree trigger (CodeBackdoor — Sun et al.,2024) | A specific AST subtree
pattern (e.g., if True:) as trigger | High ASR, moderate stealth | | Docstring
trigger (this work) | Natural-language phrase in docstring | Target: High ASR +
high stealth |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations1. Poisoning rate:0.1%,0.5%,1%,2% — to find the minimum rate for
reliable attack.

2 Trigger length:1-word vs.3-word vs.7-word trigger phrases — to measure the
trade-off between stealth and memorization difficulty.
3 Target vulnerability class: Injection (SQL, command) vs. logic (race
condition, auth bypass) vs. resource (path traversal) — to test whether
certain vulnerability types are easier to backdoor.
4 Fine-tuning budget: Full fine-tuning vs. LoRA (rank=8,16,32) — to test if
parameter-efficient fine-tuning is more or less susceptible.
5 Position of trigger: Docstring only vs. inline comment vs. both — to isolate
which code surface is most effective.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes| Failure Mode | Likelihood | Mitigation in Proposal |

|---|---|---| | Model ignores the docstring trigger (no association learned) |
Moderate | Use a longer trigger phrase; increase poisoning rate to2% | | Clean
accuracy drops significantly (catastrophic forgetting of code quality) |
Low–moderate | Cap poisoning rate ≤1%; use LoRA with small rank to limit
capacity for memorizing deviations | | Defense detects the backdoor easily (low
stealth) | Moderate | Test multiple trigger designs (explicit vs. implicit);
implicit docstring triggers are designed specifically to evade perplexity-based
filters | | Vulnerability does not compile/execute (broken generated code) | Low
| Validate that target vulnerabilities (e.g., SQL injection via string
concatenation) produce syntactically valid Python; test with ast.parse on
generated outputs | | ASR only high for exact-match prompts (no generalization
to paraphrased triggers) | High | Test paraphrased trigger variants
(LLM-rewritten versions of the trigger phrase) as a specific ablation — if ASR
drops, we document this as a limitation and propose trigger-set expansion as
future work | | Transfer to larger models fails (7B →13B/34B) | Moderate |
Report per-model-family results separately; if transfer fails, characterize the
conditions under which it works (same tokenizer family? similar training data
mix?) | | Human review catches poisoned examples during data curation | Low |
Docstrings containing "optimized version" or "fast path" are common in real
codebases; the vulnerability is injected only in the function body and can be
obfuscated (e.g., call to a plausible helper function that happens to be unsafe)
|

question: Generate a research proposal on how to build a deep evaluation framework for code LLMs.
answer_a:
Research Proposal: A Multi-Dimensional Deep Evaluation Framework for Code
LLMs### TitleBeyond Functional Correctness: A Multi-Dimensional Deep Evaluation
Framework for Code LLMs### ProblemCurrent evaluation of code LLMs is dominated
by a single proxy — functional correctness measured via pass@k on benchmarks
like HumanEval and MBPP. These benchmarks reduce code generation to a narrow
skill: writing a standalone function that passes a handful of unit tests. This
approach suffers from five blind spots:

 1 Functional myopia: A model that passes unit tests with brittle, insecure, or
   unreadable code scores identically to one that produces clean, idiomatic
   solutions.
 2 No understanding axis: The ability to explain, debug, review, or retrieve
   code remains untested, yet these tasks are central to developer workflows.
 3 Ambiguity blindness: Benchmarks provide fully specified prompts, whereas
   real-world requirements are often underdetermined.
 4 Static generation only: One-shot pass@k ignores iterative refinement — the
   dominant mode of human programming.
 5 Single-score rankings mask trade-offs: Models strong on correctness may be
   weak on quality or safety, but aggregated leaderboards collapse this
   variation.

A "deep" evaluation framework is needed that decomposes code LLM capability
across multiple psychometrically distinct axes to produce capability profiles
rather than a single number.

HypothesisA multi-axis evaluation framework that measures functional
correctness, code quality, semantic understanding, robustness to ambiguity, and
iterative refinement will reveal capability profiles that differ substantially
from pass@k leaderboard rankings, and will identify specific axes where common
models underperform relative to their overall standing.

MethodWe propose a five-axis evaluation framework, each with a dedicated
benchmark suite:

Axis1 — Functional Correctness (replication baseline)

 • HumanEval+ and MBPP+ with augmented test suites (enumerated edge cases from
   EvalPlus)
 • CodeContests (filtered to difficulty levels accessible by current models)

Axis2 — Code Quality -200 curated problems with expert-written reference
solutions- Automated metrics: cyclomatic complexity (Δ from reference), code
smell violations (pylint), documentation coverage, type annotation correctness
(mypy), and line-count efficiency- Human ratings (3 experts per output,5-point
Likert) on readability and idiomatic style- LLM-as-judge (GPT-4o, Claude3.5
Sonnet) on the same rubric, with Cohen's κ against human ratingsAxis3 — Semantic
Understanding

 • Code summarization:500 examples from CodeXGLUE (BLEU-4, ROUGE-L against
   human-written docstrings)
 • Code search: NL-to-code retrieval on CodeSearchNet (MRR@10)
 • Bug localization: Defects4J subset (top-1, top-3 accuracy)
 • Code review:100 synthetic PR diffs with known issues; model must identify the
   issue and suggest a fix (exact-match and BLEU for fix description)
 • Natural language to code: MBPP-style but with distractors and paraphrased
   promptsAxis4 — Robustness to Ambiguity -50 underspecified prompts where the
   model must either (a) ask a clarifying question or (b) state its assumptions
   explicitly before generating code-50 prompt paraphrases of base problems from
   HumanEval (varying specificity, verbosity, and framing) — measure variance in
   pass@k across paraphrases- Scoring rubric rewards assumption-articulation;
   penalizes silent guesses that fail on edge casesAxis5 — Iterative Refinement
   (multi-turn) -50 multi-turn scenarios adapted from the Multi-IP interactive
   programming format- Round1: model generates code from loose spec- Round2:
   model receives failing test output (no error location), must identify and fix
   the bug- Round3: natural language request to refactor (e.g., "make this
   parallel," "add input validation")
 • Success signals: functional correctness after each round, edit distance for
   minimal vs excessive changesComposite profiling: Each axis yields a
   normalized score (0–100). Models are compared via radar profiles and
   rank-consistency across weighted ensembles. Paired bootstrap tests (10,000
   resamples,95% CI) determine whether differences on each axis are significant.

Dataset / BenchmarkThe framework bundles existing resources with new curation:


 Axis        Source                                  Size          New/Existing
 Functional  HumanEval+, MBPP+, CodeContests         420 problems  Existing
 Quality     New curation with expert reference      200           New
             solutions
 Semantic    CodeXGLUE, Defects4J, new review set    700 items     Mixed
 Ambiguity   New underspecified + paraphrase set     100           New
 Iterative   Adapted from Multi-IP format            50            New


All new items will be released as an open benchmark suite (CodeEval-Deep).

Evaluation Metrics- Per-axis score: normalized0–100 (mean over problems within
the axis)

 • Profile vector: (F, Q, S, R, I) ∈ [0,100]⁵- Agreement with humans: Cohen's κ
   on quality and semantic axes (human-expert vs LLM-as-judge vs
   model-generated)
 • Rank stability: Kendall's τ between pass@k ranking and multi-axis composite
   ranking under varying axis weights (±20% perturbation)
 • Statistical tests: paired bootstrap test, significance threshold α =0.05 with
   Bonferroni correction (5 axes → α' =0.01)

Baselines- Single-score baseline: pass@k on HumanEval+ — demonstrates
information loss when collapsing to one metric- LLM-as-judge calibration: GPT-4o
and Claude3.5 Sonnet as quality raters, compared against expert human raters to
measure systematic biases (self-preference, length bias, verbosity bias)

 • Static-analysis-only: replace LLM-judged quality with pylint/mypy-only
   metrics — measures value added by human or LLM judgment### Ablations1.
   Per-axis leave-one-out: Remove each axis from the composite and measure
   change in model ranking relative to full profile. An axis whose removal flips
   pairwise rankings is informative; one that never flips rankings may be
   redundant.

 2 Judge substitution: Replace LLM-as-judge with static analysis alone on Axis2
   (quality). Quantifies the marginal utility of semantic quality judgment vs
   automated linting.
 3 Single-turn vs multi-turn: Compare each model's one-shot pass@k on the
   iterative axis problems against its Round-3 score after debugging and
   refactoring. Measures improvement headroom.
 4 Prompt sensitivity: For each paraphrase set in Axis4, compute within-model
   variance and between-model discrimination. If variance is high for all
   models, the ambiguity axis may be noise-dominated.
 5 Weight perturbation: Perturb axis weights by ±20% (500 random draws) and
   compute rank-stability (Kendall's W). If rankings are fragile to small weight
   changes, the framework needs careful normative justification for weighting.

Expected Failure Modes1. LLM-as-judge contamination: Both GPT-4o and Claude3.5
Sonnet may exhibit self-preference (scoring their own or similar-family outputs
higher) and length bias (preferring verbose outputs). Mitigation: blind A/B
comparison format, human validation set for calibration, and reporting bias
magnitude as part of results.

 2 Axis saturation: Functional correctness on HumanEval+ is nearing ceiling for
   frontier models (GPT-4o, Claude3.5 Sonnet ~90% pass@1). If axes are highly
   correlated, the framework collapses to a single factor and provides limited
   discrimination. Mitigation: use harder functional problems (CodeContests) and
   check inter-axis Pearson correlations; report if dimensionality reduction
   (PCA) yields one dominant component.
 3 Low inter-annotator reliability on ambiguity axis: Rating whether a model
   "reasonably handles ambiguity" is inherently subjective. Mitigation: pilot
   with5 annotators on10 problems, compute Fleiss' κ; keep this axis only if κ
   ≥0.6; otherwise restrict to the objective paraphrase-variance metric only.
 4 Iterative axis cost:50 problems × N models × up to3 turns × API costs
   compounds quickly. Mitigation: test on a smaller10-problem subset first; if
   headroom is large and consistent, expand to the full set.
 5 Benchmark contamination: Models may have been trained on HumanEval, MBPP, or
   CodeContests. Mitigation: the new quality, ambiguity, and iterative subsets
   are released post-training-date for all evaluated models; functional and
   semantic axes report contamination status separately.

Limitations1. Python-only scope: All benchmarks target Python. Results do not
generalize to JavaScript, Rust, or domain-specific languages without
re-curation.

 2 Expert reference bottleneck: The quality axis requires hand-written reference
   solutions by senior engineers. This limits scalability and introduces
   stylistic priors from a small set of authors.
 3 LLM-as-judge bias is measured but not eliminated: We can quantify the bias
   magnitude and direction but cannot fully remove it without large-scale human
   annotation budgets that exceed typical academic constraints.
 4 Short-horizon iteration: The iterative axis caps at three rounds. Real-world
   code evolution spans dozens of commits, dependency changes, and integration
   tests — outside the scope of this framework.
 5 Descriptive, not prescriptive: The framework produces capability profiles but
   does not prescribe a single actionable rank for practitioners. Users must
   supply their own weights over axes based on their deployment context. This
   honesty is a feature but limits direct comparison with existing leaderboards.
 6 Moderate statistical power on small axes: With50–100 items per new axis,
   fine-grained comparisons (e.g., model A vs model B on ambiguity) may lack
   statistical power for small effect sizes (±3 points). The framework is
   designed for medium-to-large effect detection.
 7 No temporal evaluation: Models evolve rapidly; the framework provides a
   snapshot, not a longitudinal assessment of capability growth or regression
   over training iterations.
answer_b:
Research Proposal: DeepEval — A Multi-Dimensional Evaluation Framework for Code
LLMs### Title
DeepEval: Beyond Functional Correctness — A Multi-Dimensional
Evaluation Framework for Code LLMs

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Current code LLM evaluation benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP, SWE-bench,
BigCodeBench) overwhelmingly measure functional correctness via pass@k — does
the generated code pass a fixed set of unit tests? This single-axis evaluation
has three critical blind spots:

1 Surface-level saturation — Many models now score >90% on HumanEval. The
benchmark no longer discriminates capability differences.
2 No quality signal — A model that generates a brute-force O(n²) solution and
one that generates an optimal O(n log n) solution both pass. Correctness does
not capture efficiency, readability, security, or maintainability.
3 No failure-mode analysis — Two models with equal pass@k can fail on
completely different classes of problems. Without structured error
categorization, researchers cannot diagnose weaknesses or target
improvements.

A "deep" evaluation framework must go beyond pass/fail to produce a diagnostic
profile across multiple dimensions of code quality.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
A multi-dimensional evaluation framework that scores code LLMs across
functional correctness, computational efficiency, security posture, code
quality/style, and reasoning depth will:

• Reveal discriminative signal where current benchmarks are saturated
(HumanEval >90%).
• Enable targeted diagnosis — model A may be efficient but insecure; model B
may be safe but verbose.
• Correlate with downstream task success better than pass@k alone.

Null hypothesis: Multi-dimensional scores are highly correlated with pass@k (r
>0.9) and thus provide no additional discriminative value.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
The framework, DeepEval, consists of three components:

1. Multi-Dimensional Scoring PipelineFor each generated solution, compute:

Dimension                 Metric(s)                  Method
Functional correctness    pass@1, pass@k             Standard unit test
execution (n=200 test
cases per problem)
Computational efficiency  Time complexity class,     Asymptotic analysis via
wall-clock speedup vs.     profiling on varied input
reference                  sizes; classify as O(n),
O(n log n), O(n²), etc.
Security                  CWE violation count,       Static analysis
OWASP Top-10 recall        (Bandit/Semgrep) +5
adversarial prompt probes
per problem (prompt
injection, shell
injection, path
traversal, SQL injection,
RCE)
Code quality              Cyclomatic complexity,     Static analysis (radon +
Lines of code (LOC),       pylint + custom linters)
comment density, naming
convention adherence,
duplication rate
Reasoning depth           Multi-step reasoning       Chain-of-thought
accuracy, edge-case        decomposition analysis —
coverage                   does the model's
intermediate reasoning
correctly handle all
stated preconditions and
edge cases before
generating code?

2. DeepEval Problem SuiteA curated dataset of 300 problems stratified across:

• Difficulty (easy / medium / hard / expert) —75 each- Domain (algorithms, data
structures, web/systems, security)
• Reasoning type (direct translation, multi-step composition, constraint
satisfaction, adversarial/negative testing)
• Each problem includes: specification,5–20 hidden unit tests (including edge
cases and adversarial inputs),1 reference optimal solution, and ground-truth
time complexity.

3. Diagnostic Report GeneratorProduces a radar chart + confusion matrix of
failure modes for each model. Failure modes are categorized into: logic error,
off-by-one, wrong time complexity, incomplete edge-case handling, security
vulnerability, style violation, and compilation/syntax error.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark
We construct DeepEval-300:

• 50 problems adapted from HumanEval (for continuity, filtered to those that
still show variance)
• 100 problems from competitive programming (Codeforces A–C difficulty, with
editorial solutions)
• 50 problems from real-world open-source PRs (bug fixes, refactors, feature
additions from GitHub commits)
• 50 problems designed from scratch to test adversarial edge cases (e.g., "lock
a file, then unlock it; what happens if you unlock twice?")
• 50 problems targeting security (e.g., "write a function that reads a file
path from user input and returns its contents")

Each problem has a verified test suite, optimal reference solution, and time
complexity annotation. The benchmark will be released under a permissive
license.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | What it captures |

|---|---| | DeepScore (composite) | Weighted harmonic mean of the5 dimensions
(weights determined via factor analysis on pilot data) | | pass@k | Functional
correctness (baseline metric) | | Efficiency accuracy | % of solutions matching
optimal time complexity class | | CWE recall | % of10 common CWEs correctly
avoided | | Code Quality Index | Normalized composite of cyclomatic complexity,
LOC, duplication (0–100) | | Reasoning F1 | Precision/recall on intermediate
reasoning steps vs. editorial chain-of-thought | | Failure profile entropy | How
evenly distributed are failure modes? High entropy → general weaknesses; low
entropy → specific blind spot |

Primary metric: DeepScore. Secondary: per-dimension scores with95% confidence
intervals (bootstrapped, n=1000 resamples).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines| Model | Why |

|---|---| | GPT-4o | Top commercial baseline | | Claude3.5 Sonnet | Top
commercial baseline | | DeepSeek-Coder-V2 | Top open-source baseline | |
CodeLlama-34B | Prior-generation open-source reference | | StarCoder2-15B |
Mid-size open-source reference | | HumanEval pass@k | Current standard — used as
a covariate to measure added discriminative power |

Each model is evaluated on all3 seeds (temperature0.2,0.6,0.8) with n=20 samples
per seed →60 samples per model per problem.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations1. Dimension ablation: Remove each dimension one at a time and measure
rank correlation change between DeepScore and an aggregated human-judgment score
(3 expert raters evaluate a50-problem subset). Identifies which dimensions
contribute unique signal.

2 Test-set size ablation: Run on50,100,200,300 problems and compute rank
stability (Kendall's τ between partial and full rankings). Determines minimum
viable benchmark size.
3 Scoring method ablation: Compare weighted harmonic mean vs. geometric mean
vs. PCA-based composite vs. raw vector (no aggregation). Measures sensitivity
to aggregation choice.
4 Static analysis vs. human judgment: For the security dimension, compare
Bandit/Semgrep results to manual security review on a50-problem subset.
Quantifies proxy reliability.
5 Temperature sensitivity: Repeat all evaluations at temperature0.0 and1.0;
measure dimension-score variance. Determines whether multi-dimensional scores
are more or less robust to sampling temperature than pass@k.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes1. Dimension collapse — All dimensions correlate >0.9 with
pass@k, meaning the framework adds no discriminative value. Mitigation: Pilot
study on50 problems; if r >0.85 with any dimension, redesign that dimension's
metric or drop it.

2 Human judgment noise — Inter-rater agreement (Fleiss' κ) for the
human-evaluation subset falls below0.6, making ablation1 uninterpretable.
Mitigation: Use3 raters, provide detailed rubrics with examples, run a
calibration round on10 problems before the main rating.
3 Static analysis false positives — Security scanner flags benign code as
vulnerable, inflating the security dimension's difficulty. Mitigation: Manual
verification of all flagged issues on a50-problem subset; report both raw and
human-verified security scores.
4 Benchmark saturation — By the time of publication, frontier models may
saturate DeepEval-300, repeating the HumanEval problem. Mitigation: Design
the adversarial test-generation protocol so the benchmark can be extended
with new problems without overhauling the framework. The framework (scoring
pipeline) is the contribution, not the static problem set.
5 Metric gaming — Models tuned to optimize individual dimensions (e.g.,
producing artificially verbose comments to inflate code quality scores).
Mitigation: Use normalized, ratio-based metrics rather than absolute counts;
include style consistency checks that penalize unnatural patterns.
6 Composition instability — The composite DeepScore weighting scheme changes
model rankings substantially under small weight perturbations. Mitigation:
Report ranking under10 random weight configurations; if Kendall's τ <0.8
across configurations, do not use a single composite score — return the full
dimension vector as the evaluation output.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Bottom line: DeepEval's contribution is not another leaderboard — it's a
diagnostic framework that tells model developers which capability dimensions
their code LLM is strong or weak in, enabling targeted improvement rather than
chasing a single pass@k number.

question: Generate a research proposal on solving multi-hop reasoning challenges in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG).
answer_a:
Title: Bridging the Gap: Structured Decomposition for Multi-Hop Reasoning in
Retrieval-Augmented Generation---

ProblemCurrent RAG systems retrieve a single set of passages and feed them into
an LLM in one pass. This breaks down under multi-hop queries — questions that
require chaining information across multiple documents (e.g., "What university
did the founder of Company X attend?"). The LLM must retrieve facts about
Company X, extract its founder, then retrieve again. Standard RAG cannot
re-retrieve based on intermediate answers, and simply concatenating many
retrieved passages overwhelms the context window with noise. Existing multi-hop
datasets (HotPotQA,2WikiMultihop) report low recall on the second hop even with
state-of-the-art retrievers.

HypothesisDecomposing a multi-hop query into a directed acyclic graph of
sub-queries — each sub-query resolved by a dedicated retrieve-then-answer step —
will improve end-to-end answer accuracy compared to single-pass RAG and to naive
chain-of-thought prompting over retrieved passages. The key bottleneck is not
the LLM's reasoning ability but the retriever's inability to condition on
intermediate evidence; structured decomposition addresses this directly.

MethodWe propose Structured Stepwise RAG (SSRAG), a three-module pipeline:

 1 Query Decomposer — A fine-tuned7B-parameter LLM that takes the original
   question and outputs a sequence of sub-queries, each tagged with its
   dependency parent(s). This produces a DAG: e.g., for "What university did the
   founder of Company X attend?", the decomposer outputs [Q1: "Who founded
   Company X?", Q2: "What university did [A1] attend?"] with Q2 ← Q1.
 2 Iterative Retriever — For each sub-query in topological order, retrieve top-5
   passages (BM25 + DPR hybrid). When a sub-query contains [A<id>] placeholders,
   substitute the extracted answer from the parent step before encoding the
   query. This ensures the retriever sees grounded context.
 3 Selective Fusion Decoder — A frozen13B-parameter LLM that receives the
   original question plus the set of sub-query answers (not raw passages) and
   produces a final answer. This keeps the reasoning context compact and avoids
   passage-level noise.

All modules are trained end-to-end with a two-stage curriculum: (i) train the
decomposer on synthetic decomposition data generated from knowledge graph paths,
(ii) fine-tune the iterative retriever with REINFORCE using answer accuracy as
the reward.

Dataset / Benchmark- HotPotQA (distractor setting) — the standard multi-hop
benchmark with113k questions requiring2–3 hops. Use the official
train/validation/test split.

 • 2WikiMultihop —192k questions requiring fusion of information across two
   Wikipedia articles. Used for cross-domain generalization.
 • MuSiQue —25k questions requiring2–4 hops, designed to be less solvable by
   single-hop shortcuts. Used for robustness evaluation.

Evaluation Metrics- Exact Match (EM) and F1 score on answer strings (primary
metrics).

 • Hop-wise Recall — whether each intermediate answer in the gold decomposition
   is correctly recovered. This isolates failures in retrieval vs. reasoning.
 • Passage Overhead — average number of passages retrieved per question. Tracks
   efficiency gains over naive multi-passage RAG.
 • Oracle upper bound — EM when gold sub-query decompositions are provided
   instead of predicted, measuring the ceiling of the retrieval+reasoning
   components.

Baselines1. Standard RAG — single-pass retrieval of top-20 passages with the
same frozen LLM for answer generation.

 2 Chain-of-Thought RAG — retrieve top-20 passages, prompt the LLM to first
   reason step-by-step, then answer (no re-retrieval).
 3 IRCoT (Trivedi et al.,2023) — interleaves chain-of-thought reasoning with
   retrieval, using the LLM's own intermediate text as the next query. Reproduce
   with the same retriever backbone.
 4 Self-Ask (Press et al.,2023) — prompt the LLM to generate follow-up questions
   and use a search engine; adapt to our retriever.
 5 SSRAG (oracle decomposer) — our method with gold sub-queries to establish the
   upper bound.

Ablations1. –Decomposer — replace learned decomposer with a fixed template
(split on "and", "then", "before"). Tests whether learned decomposition adds
value beyond heuristics.

 2 –Iterative Retrieval — feed all sub-queries at once to the retriever instead
   of sequentially. Isolates the benefit of conditioning on intermediate
   answers.
 3 –Fusion Decoder — feed raw passages (not sub-answer summaries) to the
   decoder. Tests whether selective fusion is necessary.
 4 –REINFORCE — train the iterative retriever with supervised max-margin loss
   instead of reward-based learning.
 5 Single retriever variant — use only DPR (no BM25 hybrid). Measures robustness
   of the hybrid strategy.

Expected Failure Modes1. Decomposition cascading errors — if the decomposer
produces a wrong sub-query or dependency, all downstream steps fail. Mitigation:
train with a recovery mechanism (if a sub-query returns empty passages, re-route
to a fallback retriever with the full context).

 2 Semantic drift in iterative retrieval — substituting a verbose or incorrect
   intermediate answer into the next query may mislead the retriever.
   Mitigation: constrain extracted answers to named entities or short phrases
   (≤5 tokens).
 3 Dependency DAG depth — performance likely degrades for ≥4 hops due to
   compounding retrieval noise. The MuSiQue results will reveal this ceiling.
 4 Decomposer over-generation — the decomposer may create unnecessary
   sub-queries for questions that are actually single-hop. The oracle upper
   bound ablation will quantify this waste.

Title: Graph-Guided Iterative Retrieval with Structured Decomposition for
Multi-Hop RAGProblem

Standard RAG pipelines retrieve documents in a single flat pass and then
generate an answer. For multi-hop questions (e.g., "Which university did the
president of the company that acquired DeepMind attend?"), the necessary
information is distributed across documents that are not all relevant to the
original query. Single-pass retrieval fails because the intermediate entities
(DeepMind's acquirer → its president → their alma mater) are unknown at query
time. Existing iterative approaches (e.g., IRCoT, Self-Ask) decompose the
question but treat each sub-step as an independent keyword lookup, missing the
structural dependencies between hops — they do not maintain a shared entity
graph across retrieval rounds, so later hops cannot exploit evidence from
earlier ones.

Hypothesis

Decomposing a multi-hop question into a directed dependency graph, where each
node is a sub-question and each edge represents an entity- or relation-level
dependency, will yield more faithful and complete retrieval than sequential
decomposition or single-pass methods. Specifically, we hypothesize that a
graph-guided iterative retriever — which maintains a growing entity-linkage
graph across hops and uses the graph to prune irrelevant retrieval targets at
each step — will improve F1 by ≥10 points over the best non-graph iterative
baseline on multi-hop QA benchmarks.

Method

We propose GG-RAG (Graph-Guided Retrieval-Augmented Generation), a three-module
architecture:

1 Question Decomposer — A prompted LLM (e.g., Llama-3-70B) parses the input
question into a dependency graph. Nodes are sub-questions; edges are
"requires entity from" dependencies. E.g., for the question above: Who
acquired DeepMind? → Who is the president of that company? → Which university
did that person attend?
2 Graph-Guided Iterative Retriever — At each hop:

• Retrieve top-k passages for the current sub-question.
• Extract named entities from retrieved passages and build/update a shared
entity-linkage graph (nodes = entities, edges = co-occurrence or relation
extraction).
• For the next sub-question, augment the query with entities confirmed by the
graph, and down-weight passages that contradict the existing graph (via a
small learned scorer over graph features: path distance, entity overlap,
contradiction flags).

3 Answer Synthesizer — A reading comprehension model (or the same LLM) reads
the union of all retrieved passages, with the dependency graph as an
attention bias, to generate the final answer.

The retriever backbone can be any dense retriever (e.g., Contriever-MS MARCO,
E5-mistral-7b). The simple graph-scorer is a2-layer MLP over graph features
(entity count, max path length, contradiction score) trained on1k synthetic
multi-hop examples.

Dataset / Benchmark

• HotpotQA (fullwiki setting) — the standard multi-hop benchmark; answers
require2–3 hops.
• MuSiQue — harder,2–4 hops, designed to require multi-step reasoning.
• 2WikiMultihop —2-hop questions across Wikipedia; tests cross-article
reasoning.

Evaluation Metrics

• Answer F1 (token-level exact match on answers, as per HotpotQA).
• Supporting Fact F1 — whether the model retrieves the correct supporting
passages (defined by HotpotQA gold evidence).
• Hop Accuracy — proportion of sub-question answers correct in the intermediate
decomposition (manual eval on a200-sample subset).
• Retrieval Precision@k per hop.

Baselines

1 Single-pass RAG — standard retrieve-then-read (top-5, no iteration).
2 IRCoT — interleaved CoT + retrieval, iteratively retrieving for each
reasoning step.
3 Self-Ask — LLM generates follow-up questions and retrieves for each.
4 ReAct — LLM alternates reasoning traces with retrieval actions.
5 FLARE — active retrieval based on low-confidence generation tokens.

Ablations

1 No graph — iterative retrieval without the entity-linkage graph (just
sequential sub-queries) to isolate the graph's contribution.
2 No graph pruning — graph built but not used to down-weight contradictory
passages.
3 Scorer removed — replace the learned MLP scorer with a simple overlap
heuristic.
4 Single decomposer — freeze decomposition to a fixed depth (2 hops vs
adaptive) to test whether variable-depth matters.

Expected Failure Modes

1 Decomposition cascading errors — If the LLM decomposes the question
incorrectly (e.g., wrong dependency order), all downstream retrieval is
misdirected. Mitigation: score the decomposer on a held-out set and fall back
to flat retrieval if confidence is low.
2 Entity-linkage graph noise — In open domains, entity extraction may introduce
spurious edges (e.g., homonyms, over-eager co-occurrence), causing the graph
to prune useful passages. Mitigation: use a lightweight threshold on entity
co-occurrence frequency and include a "no relation" edge type.
3 Retrieval overfitting to graph structure — The learned scorer might overfit
to the1k synthetic training samples. Mitigation: train with heavy dropout and
evaluate zero-shot on MuSiQue (unseen decomposition patterns).
4 Computational cost — Decomposition + iterative retrieval + graph updates may
increase latency3–5× over single-pass RAG. Acceptable for offline/assistant
use cases; extension to real-time would require distillation or parallelizing
independent sub-graph branches.
5 Strict multi-hop only — The method likely does not improve (and may hurt)
single-hop questions where the graph is trivial. Mitigation: detect ≤1-hop
questions via the decomposer and route to standard single-pass retrieval.

Research Proposal: Conflict-Aware Multi-Source Reasoning### Title
Conflict-Aware
Multi-Source Reasoning: Detecting and Resolving Information Conflicts in
Retrieval-Augmented Generation

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Current retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems treat retrieved
documents as mutually consistent and complementary. This assumption breaks under
real-world conditions: sources contradict each other, report information at
different granularities, reflect different perspectives, or contain outright
errors. The result is that models either silently hallucinate a compromise,
arbitrarily follow one source while ignoring others, or produce incoherent
answers without signaling uncertainty. No existing benchmark or method
systematically addresses structured conflict adjudication as a first-class
reasoning step.

Key open question: Can explicit modeling of inter-source conflicts — their type,
severity, and resolvability — improve the factual accuracy and transparency of
multi-source reasoning?

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Explicitly modeling inter-source conflicts through a structured
conflict graph + adjudication module will improve both factual accuracy and
answer coherence over standard RAG pipelines on multi-source QA tasks. The
improvement will be largest when retrieved passages are heterogeneous in content
or disagree on specific claims. The model will also benefit from learning when
to abstain rather than force an answer.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
A four-stage pipeline:

1 Retrieval — Retrieve top-k passages for a query using a standard retriever
(e.g., Contriever-MS MARCO or ColBERT-v2).
2 Conflict Graph Construction — Build a fully connected graph where each node
is a retrieved passage. For each pair of passages, classify the edge as one
of: agreement, contradiction, complement (non-overlapping but
non-conflicting), or unrelated. Use an NLI-style classifier (e.g., fine-tuned
DeBERTa on paired passages) or an LLM-as-judge (e.g., GPT-4o-mini with
structured prompting). Edge weights encode confidence.
3 Conflict-Aware Aggregation — A lightweight adjudication module that takes the
conflict graph and the query, and produces:

• A set of reconciled facts (claims that survive cross-source verification)
• A set of irresolvable conflicts (contradictory claims the model cannot
adjudicate given available evidence)
• An optional abstain decision: if irresolvable conflicts touch the core of the
query, output "insufficient evidence" instead of forcing an answer.

4 Generation — An LM generates the final answer conditioned on the reconciled
facts and flagged conflicts, with an option to cite which passages support
each claim.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark
Three evaluation settings:

Dataset                   What it tests              Expected conflict rate
MuSiQue (multi-source     Multi-hop reasoning from   Low–moderate (designed to
QA)                       several paragraphs         be consistent)
HotpotQA (distractor      Identifying relevant       Moderate (distractors may
setting)                  passages among             mislead)
distractors
ConflictFEVER             Deliberately               High (controlled)
(constructed)             contradictory passages
built by perturbing FEVER
+ PubMedQA claims with a
gold-labeled
contradiction set

ConflictFEVER is a new construction: for each claim in FEVER, retrieve a
supporting passage and a contradicting passage (by perturbing entities,
relations, or numerical values), yielding ground-truth conflict labels.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics- Answer Accuracy: F1 and Exact Match on the QA subset,
answer-level accuracy on the FEVER subset- Conflict Detection Precision /
Recall: Against gold conflict labels (only for ConflictFEVER)

• Abstention Quality: Does the model abstain correctly on unanswerable queries?
F1 on the abstain decision against a held-out set of unanswerable questions-
Faithfulness: Claim-level recall — what fraction of claims in the generated
answer are directly supported by at least one retrieved passage (measured by
an NLI verifier)
• Average Inference Time: End-to-end latency, reported for practical
relevance---

Baselines1. Standard RAG — Concatenate top-k passages + query → generate
answer2. Self-RAG — Interleave retrieval decisions with reflection tokens at
generation time3. Chain-of-Thought RAG — Retrieve → reason step by step over
passages → answer4. ReAct — Interleave retrieval, reasoning, and action steps5.
FiD (Fusion-in-Decoder) — Encode passages independently, cross-attend in
decoder---

Ablations| Ablation | What it isolates |

|---|---| | Without conflict graph | Does the graph add value over raw
concatenation? | | Conflict graph (NLI) vs. LLM-as-judge | Trade-off between
cost, speed, and detection quality | | Pairwise comparison (no graph) | Is the
full graph structure needed, or does local pairwise suffice? | | No abstention |
Does allowing abstention hurt accuracy on answerable queries? | | Source
reliability weighting (oracle) | Upper bound: what if we knew which sources were
trustworthy? | | Conflict resolution strategy (majority vote vs. reconciliation
vs. source-priority) | Which resolution heuristic works best? |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes1. Noisy conflict detection — NLI classifiers trained on
sentence pairs may fail on passage-level contradictions spanning many sentences.
An LLM-as-judge is expensive and may exhibit position bias or sycophancy
(agreeing too readily with the later source).

2 Over-abstention — The model may refuse to answer on harmless factual
disagreements (e.g., "population is1.2M" vs "population is1.22M"), hurting
usability. The abstention threshold must be carefully tuned.
3 Graph cost — Constructing a full pairwise graph is O(k²) where k is the
number of passages. With k=10 this is45 edges; with k=50 it is1,225. May be
too slow for real-time deployment without pruning heuristics.
4 Benchmark artifacts — MuSiQue and HotpotQA were not designed to test conflict
resolution; most retrieved passages may agree. The proposed ConflictFEVER set
is synthetic and may not capture the nuanced disagreements found in
real-world documents (e.g., conflicting expert testimony in medical
contexts).
5 Evaluation coupling — Abstention quality and answer accuracy trade off.
Optimizing both jointly is non-trivial and requires a careful loss weighting
or Pareto-front analysis.
6 Citation hallucination — Even with a conflict graph, the generator may cite a
passage that does not support the specific claim it is attached to. A
secondary faithfulness check (e.g., fine-grained NLI per claim-passage pair)
may be needed as a guardrail.

Research Proposal: Adaptive Domain-Aware Data Filtering for Domain-Specific
Models## TitleAdaFilter: Adaptive, Loss-Aware Data Filtering for Domain-Specific
       Language Model Pretraining## ProblemPretraining data curation for
 domain-specific language models (e.g., biomedical, legal, code, or scientific
  LLMs) faces a fundamental tension: generic filtering heuristics (perplexity
 thresholds, exact deduplication, language-ID filters, blocklist-based removal)
  are designed for general-domain web text and systematically discard valuable
domain-specific content. For example, high-perplexity biomedical text containing
    rare enzyme names or dense chemical notation is often classified as "low
quality" by a general-domain perplexity filter and removed, starving the domain
  model of the very data it needs most. Conversely, generic filters may retain
              generic web text that dilutes domain specialization.

Existing approaches fall into two camps, each with limitations:

 1 Hand-crafted domain rules (e.g., regex patterns for chemical formulas,
   citation-stripping, document-type classifiers): expensive to build per
   domain, brittle across sub-domains, and require domain experts.
 2 Domain-adaptive perplexity filtering (train a small reference model on
   in-domain seed data, then filter by perplexity under that model): improves
   domain recall but requires high-quality seed data and a separate training
   run; also collapses diversity by aggressively removing low-perplexity "easy"
   text that may still be informative.

The core problem is filtering without a generalizable mechanism for
characterizing which data characteristics are valuable for a given target
domain. There is no unified framework that jointly optimizes for domain
relevance, data diversity, and downstream task utility without per-domain
engineering.

HypothesisWe hypothesize that an adaptive filtering framework — combining (1) a
lightweight domain-embedding model that projects documents into a
domain-relevance space, (2) a loss-aware sampling score that measures how much a
candidate document would reduce expected loss on a held-out domain validation
set, and (3) a diversity-aware selection mechanism that prevents collapse to a
narrow sub-region of the domain — will consistently outperform both generic
filtering and single-criterion domain filtering across multiple specialized
domains.

Specifically, we expect that:

 • The loss-aware component provides a training-signal-driven filter that
   generalizes across domains without hand-crafted rules.
 • The diversity component prevents over-concentration on repetitive document
   archetypes (e.g., only abstracts, only experimental methods sections).
 • The combination yields higher downstream task accuracy (+3–8% absolute)
   compared to perplexity-only or rule-only baselines, with comparable or lower
   total training FLOPs due to reduced wasted tokens.

Method: AdaFilterAdaFilter is a three-stage pipeline operating on a raw
web-scale corpus before domain-specific pretraining.

Stage1: Domain Embedding ModelTrain a small (125M parameter) bidirectional
encoder on a multi-domain corpus (general web +5 specialized domains) with a
contrastive objective: the model learns to embed documents such that in-domain
documents cluster together, while out-of-domain documents are pushed apart.
Training uses a small set of known in-domain exemplars (200 documents per
domain, hand-curated) and a large unlabeled pool. This provides a domain
relevance score for any candidate document: the cosine similarity between its
embedding and the mean embedding of the domain exemplars.

Stage2: Loss-Aware Importance ScoringFor each target domain, train a tiny
reference model (70M parameters) on the held-out domain validation set (1,000
documents, hand-curated for quality and coverage). This model is not used for
filtering by perplexity. Instead, for each candidate document d in the raw
corpus, we compute:

Expected Loss Reduction (ELR) = L(val; θ₀) − L(val; θ₀ + η·∇L(d))

where θ₀ is the reference model's parameters, L(val; θ₀) is the loss on the
validation set, and the second term approximates the validation loss after a
single gradient step on document d (computed via the influence function
approximation or a single-step fine-tuning proxy). Documents with higher ELR are
those whose gradient direction most reduces validation loss — i.e., they provide
the most useful learning signal.

Since exact influence functions are expensive at corpus scale, we use a
tractable approximation: for each document, we compute the cosine similarity
between its gradient (w.r.t. the reference model) and the aggregate gradient of
the validation set. This requires one forward-backward pass per document through
a70M model — feasible with moderate parallelization.

Stage3: Diversity-Aware SelectionApply a greedy, diversity-aware selection over
documents ranked by Stage2 scores:

 1 Initialize the selected set with the top-1 document by ELR.
 2 For each subsequent candidate, compute its minimum embedding cosine
   similarity to already-selected documents (using the Stage1 embeddings).
 3 Score = ELR × (1 − λ · max_similarity), where λ controls the diversity
   penalty.
 4 Add the highest-scoring document to the selected set.

This prevents the filter from selecting10,000 nearly identical abstracts while
discarding methods sections or experimental results paragraphs that carry
complementary signal.

Final Data MixFor a given domain's pretraining run, the final data is:

-70% AdaFilter-selected domain data (from a raw domain-candidate pool) -20%
general web data (standard C4-quality filtered) -10% domain validation set
documents (to anchor the domain distribution)

five specialized domains:
