Research Proposal: Adaptive Difficulty Filtering for Domain-Specific Language
Model Pretraining## Title
AdaFilter: Adaptive Difficulty-Aware Data Filtering for
Domain-Specific Language Model Pretraining

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Domain-specific language models (e.g., BioBERT, CodeBERT, FinBERT,
Legal-BERT) are typically pretrained from scratch or continually trained on a
curated corpus of in-domain text. A critical but understudied bottleneck is how
to filter which documents from the domain corpus are actually useful for
downstream performance. Current practice relies on heuristics (perplexity
thresholds, hand-crafted rules, or simple length/n-gram filters) that are noisy,
domain-agnostic, and oblivious to the model's current state during training. The
result is wasted compute on low-quality or redundant documents and, in some
cases, performance degradation from noisy data.

Concrete gap: No existing method jointly models (a) document quality, (b)
difficulty relative to the model's evolving capabilities, and (c) domain
relevance in a unified, trainable filtering pipeline. Prior work treats these
dimensions separately or uses static filtering that does not adapt during
training.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
A trainable, difficulty-aware filtering module that scores documents
along three axes — domain relevance, linguistic quality, and current-model
difficulty — and dynamically selects a curriculum of documents during
pretraining will produce a domain-specific LM with better perplexity and
downstream task performance than static heuristic filtering, while reducing
total training tokens by ≥20%.

Null hypothesis: Adaptive difficulty filtering yields no statistically
significant improvement in downstream performance over static heuristic
filtering (perplexity, F1, or accuracy) when matched for total compute.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
We propose AdaFilter, a three-stage filtering framework integrated into
the training loop.

Stage1: Relevance Scoring (one-time preprocessing)

Use a small, efficient classifier (e.g., a FastText or MiniLM-based model) to
score each document against a set of domain-defining seed keywords or exemplars.
This is a lightweight binary classifier trained on a small hand-labeled set (~1K
documents per domain). Documents below a relevance threshold are discarded
before training begins.

Stage2: Quality Scoring (one-time preprocessing)

For surviving documents, compute three quality signals:

• Perplexity under a small reference LM (e.g., a125M-parameter general-domain
model) — anomalously high PPL flags gibberish.
• Repetition ratio — fraction of repeated n-grams (n=8).
• Information density — ratio of unique tokens to total tokens. Combine into a
scalar quality score via a learned linear weighting (trained on a held-out
quality-labeled set).

Stage3: Adaptive Difficulty Curricula (online, per-epoch)

During training, maintain a difficulty estimator — a small MLP that takes the
model's current token-level embeddings for the first K tokens of a document and
predicts a difficulty score. Documents are bucketed into Easy/Medium/Hard bins.
The training sampler draws:

• **Epoch1-2:**80% Easy,15% Medium,5% Hard (warm-up)
• **Epoch3-5:**40% Easy,40% Medium,20% Hard- **Epoch6+:**10% Easy,40%
Medium,50% HardThe difficulty estimator is updated every N steps to track the
model's evolving state.

Training Protocol- Continual pretraining (MLM objective) starting from a
general-domain checkpoint (e.g., RoBERTa-base).

• Compare against: (a) unfiltered data, (b) static perplexity-filtered data,
(c) random subset of equal size, (d) random subset of equal compute.
• Each condition is run with3 random seeds for statistical reliability.
• Downstream evaluation every5K steps using a held-out set of domain tasks.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark
We propose two domains for generalizability:

1 Biomedical: CORD-19 + PubMed abstracts (~2M documents). Downstream: BioASQ
(QA), ChemProt (RE), PubMedQA.
2 Legal: Pile-of-Law subset + EURLex (~1M documents). Downstream: CaseHOLD
(NLI), LexGLUE benchmark.

Each domain provides a clean test of whether domain-specific filtering matters
beyond generic heuristics.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Category | Metric | Target |

|---|---|---| | Language modeling | Validation perplexity | Primary | |
Downstream tasks | Macro F1 / Accuracy (domain-specific benchmarks) | Primary |
| Efficiency | Training tokens to match baseline best performance | Secondary |
| Curriculum effect | Per-bin difficulty distribution over epochs | Analysis | |
Ablation | Delta from removing each AdaFilter component | Diagnostic |

All metrics reported with95% confidence intervals across3 seeds.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines| Baseline | Description |

|---|---| | No Filter | All domain documents, no curation | | PPL Threshold |
Documents with PPL < median under general-domain LM | | Heuristic | Length +
n-gram repetition filter (common practice) | | Random Subset (size-matched) |
Same number of documents as AdaFilter, randomly sampled | | Random Subset
(compute-matched) | Same number of training steps as AdaFilter, randomly sampled
| | DSIR | Importance resampling using n-gram hashing (Xie et al.,2023) | |
FastText Relevance Only | AdaFilter Stage1 alone |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations1. No difficulty curriculum — Stage3 replaced with uniform sampling
from filtered pool → isolates curriculum contribution.

2 No quality scoring — Skip Stage2; only relevance + difficulty → isolates
quality signal.
3 Static buckets — Difficulty bins fixed at epoch1, never updated → isolates
benefit of adaptive difficulty.
4 Single domain — Run only on biomedical → tests domain transfer of findings.
5 Swap reference LM — Use a350M instead of125M reference model for perplexity →
tests sensitivity to reference size.
6 Score-to-weight variant — Instead of bucketing, weight documents by soft
difficulty score during loss → tests granularity benefit.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes| Failure Mode | Mitigation |

|---|---| | Difficulty estimator collapses — becomes constant after a few epochs
| Add entropy regularization to bin assignment; monitor bin balance | |
Relevance classifier is the sole driver of gains (Stages2+3 add nothing) | If
ablation1 shows no degradation, the proposal still contributes an automated
relevance filter, which is a publishable result; reframe contribution around
end-to-end filtering | | Perplexity improves but downstream does not | Switch
primary evaluation to downstream tasks; analyze whether the LM is overfitting to
domain distribution at the expense of generalization | | High variance across
seeds | Increase to5 seeds; use paired bootstrap for significance testing | |
Adaptive curriculum underperforms static curriculum | Report honestly as
negative result with analysis of why — possibly because the domain corpus is too
homogeneous for curricula to matter | | Computational overhead of online
difficulty estimation outweighs token savings | Measure wall-clock time per1K
steps; if overhead >5%, treat as constraint and propose a cheaper proxy (e.g.,
loss on first128 tokens) | | Quality signals are highly correlated (redundant) |
Use PCA or mutual-information analysis on quality features; if redundancy is
high, the linear weighting in Stage2 will naturally down-weight correlated
features |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Success CriteriaThis proposal is considered successful if both conditions hold:

1 AdaFilter achieves statistically significant (p <0.05) improvement over all
baselines on at least one primary metric (perplexity or downstream F1) in
both domains.
2 AdaFilter uses ≤80% of the training tokens required by the best baseline to
reach the same downstream performance.

If only one domain shows gains, the contribution is domain-specific but still
publishable with the appropriate qualification.

question: Generate a research proposal on how to enhance the long-context understanding of Large Language Models.
answer_a:
Multi-Scale Anchoring for Long-Context Understanding in LLMs## ProblemLarge
  Language Models exhibit a well-documented breakdown in reasoning quality as
input context length grows beyond their effective training horizon. Even models
        that achieve low perplexity on long documents frequently fail on
retrieval-grounded reasoning tasks that require integrating information from the
    beginning and end of a long context. The core issue is that decoder-only
Transformers with causal attention suffer from attention dilution — the softmax
distribution over thousands of tokens flattens, reducing sensitivity to specific
  relevant positions — and from position-encoding extrapolation artifacts that
 distort relative distance signals at unseen lengths. Existing solutions (RoPE
 scaling, sliding windows, sparse attention, memory augmentation) each address
  one facet but degrade on tasks that require dense cross-positional reasoning
                              over the full span.

HypothesisIntroducing a small set of learnable anchor tokens — inserted at
regular intervals throughout the input sequence during encoding — that receive
multi-headed attention from all subsequent tokens will improve long-context
retrieval and reasoning. Because the anchors compress a local block into a
fixed-size representation and participate in all future attention steps, they
provide a structured shortcut for information flow across distant positions. We
hypothesize that this mechanism (a) preserves the model's ability to locate
exact token positions for retrieval while (b) providing a fallback summary
pathway when direct attention becomes diffuse, and (c) generalizes to unseen
context lengths with minimal position-encoding adjustment.

MethodMulti-Scale Anchoring (MSA). Given an input sequence of length (L) and an
anchor stride (S), we insert (k = \lceil L/S \rceil) learnable anchor tokens.
Each anchor attends to its corresponding block (the (S) tokens that precede it,
plus the anchor itself) via a lightweight cross-attention layer, producing a
block summary vector. These summary vectors are then prepended to the sequence
in position-canonicalized form (assigned fixed, learnable position embeddings
independent of the original token positions), so that anchor (i) always occupies
the same position in the positional encoding grid regardless of where block (i)
falls in the input. During forward passes, every subsequent token attends to all
anchors (as well as to the prior full sequence via the standard causal mask).
The anchor representations are updated end-to-end via the language modeling
loss, so they evolve to capture information that is useful for predicting future
tokens.

Training is performed in two stages:

 1 Anchor initialization — freeze the base model, train only the anchor
   parameters (the embedding lookup, the block-level cross-attention projection,
   and the gating scalar) on a mixed corpus of long-document perplexity and
   synthetic retrieval tasks for5K steps.
 2 Joint fine-tuning — unfreeze the entire model with a lowered learning rate
   (0.1× original) and continue for another5K steps on the same mixture.

At inference time, anchor tokens are inserted on the fly. The stride (S) is a
hyperparameter; we default to (S =256) tokens, yielding roughly4 anchors per1K
tokens.

Dataset / BenchmarkWe evaluate on the following suite of long-context
benchmarks, chosen to cover retrieval, reasoning, and generation:


 Category    Benchmark             Metric                Primary use
 Retrieval   RULER                 Accuracy at           Does MSA preserve
             (Needle-in-a-Haysta…  depths0–100%          exact retrieval?
             variants)
 Reasoning   LongBench (TREC,      F1 / ROUGE-L          Does MSA help
             QMSum, NarrativeQA                          multi-hop reasoning
             subsets)                                    over long documents?
 Book-level  Scrolls (Qasper,      Exact match / F1      Does MSA generalize
             Quality)                                    to10K+ token inputs?
 Synthetic   PassKey retrieval     Pass rate             Uniform
             across4K–64K                                length-controlled test
 Perplexity  PG-19 (test split,    PPL                   Does MSA affect
             length-stratified)                          language modeling
                                                         quality?


Evaluation Metrics- Primary: Accuracy on RULER at50%+ depth range (the region
where baseline LLMs typically decay to ≤60% accuracy). A successful method must
maintain ≥85% accuracy up to32K tokens.

 • Secondary: LongBench average F1; PassKey pass rate across lengths; PG-19 PPL
   delta against baseline (should be within +0.5 of baseline, signaling no
   degradation on standard LM quality).
 • Tertiary (diagnostic): Attention entropy over anchor positions vs. over
   regular token positions. Lower anchor entropy (more concentrated attention)
   is supporting evidence for the mechanism.

Baselines1. Vanilla LLM — same pretrained base model evaluated directly on long
inputs (no intervention).

 2 RoPE scaling (YaRN) — apply YaRN with dynamic NTK scaling to extend context
   to the test length.
 3 Sliding window — replace full attention with a window of4096 tokens per layer
   (Mistral-style).
 4 Fusion-in-Decoder (FiD-style) — chunk the input, encode each chunk
   independently, and cross-attend over chunk summaries. Represents a
   non-learnable anchor baseline.
 5 Compressive Transformer (memory-retrieval) — retrieve from stored past
   representations via nearest-neighbor lookup. Represents an external-memory
   baseline.

AblationsAll ablations use the same training pipeline as the full method:

 1 –Anchors (no anchor tokens): Joint fine-tune the base model without anchors,
   on the same data. Controls for benefit of additional training.
 2 –Stride (shallow anchors): Reduce stride to (S =64) (many weak anchors).
   Tests whether compression capacity (vs. granularity) drives gains.
 3 –Position canon (raw positions): Assign anchors their absolute input
   positions instead of canonicalized positions. Tests whether position-encoding
   stability is critical.
 4 –Cross-attention (mean-pooling only): Replace learned block cross-attention
   with mean-pooled block representations. Tests whether learned compression
   matters.
 5 –Finetune (frozen base): Train only anchor parameters, never unfreeze the
   base model. Tests whether anchor-alone adaptation is sufficient.

Expected Failure Modes1. Attention collapse into anchors: The model may learn to
dump most attention mass into the nearest anchor and ignore regular tokens,
destroying fine-grained retrieval. Mitigation: an auxiliary loss penalizing the
Kullback–Leibler divergence between the per-token anchor attention mass and a
uniform target (pushing toward a50/50 split). If this fails, add a gating scalar
per layer that limits total anchor attention to at most30%.

 2 Stride / block boundary artifacts: If a critical span of reasoning falls
   across a block boundary, neither block's anchor captures the full dependency.
   Mitigation: test overlapping blocks (50% stride overlap) as an ablation
   variant. If cross-boundary accuracy is poor, overlapping anchors become the
   default.
 3 Length generalization ceiling: Canonicalized positions help, but the model
   may still fail above64K tokens because the base LM's RoPE cannot extrapolate.
   Mitigation: combine MSA with YaRN scaling applied only to the non-anchor
   tokens. If performance decays above64K, expect to require joint MSA +
   positional scaling for extreme lengths.
 4 Fine-tuning instability on long sequences: Joint fine-tuning of the full
   model on long inputs is memory-intensive and prone to loss spikes.
   Mitigation: gradient checkpointing, gradual length schedule (4K →8K →16K
   →32K), and loss-clipping at2.0. Run on at least2 hardware configurations and
   report both.

Limitations1. Compute overhead per token. Each anchor adds one cross-attention
computation per block. For a32K input with stride256, that is128 extra
cross-attention steps per layer — roughly a30% FLOPs increase in practice. The
method is not suitable for latency-critical applications without further
optimization (e.g., pruning anchors at early layers).

 2 Block-compression bottleneck. The model must compress a block of up to256
   tokens into a single vector. If the block contains multiple independently
   relevant facts, the anchor may capture an average that is useful for neither.
   A hierarchical anchor scheme (two or more anchor tiers with different
   strides) could mitigate this but complicates the design.
 3 Limited to decoder-only architectures. The cross-attention mechanism assumes
   the encoder and decoder share the same embedding space. Applying MSA to
   encoder-decoder models (T5, Flan-UL2) requires nontrivial architectural
   changes to the cross-attention interface.
 4 No persistent memory across documents. Anchors are recomputed per input and
   do not carry information between training examples. The method does not
   address the setting where long-term world knowledge must be maintained across
   unrelated queries.
 5 Position-canonicalized anchors share one grid position. If multiple anchors
   map to the same canonical position (e.g., anchor4 in a1024-token document and
   anchor4 in an8192-token document both occupy slot4), the positional identity
   is ambiguous for downstream reasoning about the document's absolute length.
   We treat this as an intentional inductive bias toward length-invariant block
   representations, but it may hurt tasks that depend on absolute position
   estimates.
 6 Evaluation limited to English. All benchmarks are English-language.
   Generalization to morphologically rich or low-resource languages remains
   untested.

Research Proposal: Structured Memory Banks for Long-Context Grounding in LLMs##
Title
Memory-Augmented Hierarchical Summarization (MAHS): Improving Long-Context
Grounding Without Full Attention Retraining

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Large Language Models suffer from the lost-in-the-middle problem — when
prompted with documents exceeding ~8K tokens, accuracy on facts located in the
middle of the context degrades sharply, even for models that claim128K+ context
windows. Two root causes: (1) softmax attention dilutes signal across many
tokens, and (2) positional encodings (RoPE, ALiBi) lose relative resolution at
extreme lengths. Existing solutions (ring attention, sparse attention,
state-space models) either require expensive full retraining or sacrifice recall
on mid-context facts.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Injecting a separately trained, retrieval-augmented memory bank —
built from hierarchically compressed chunks of the input context — into the
LLM's cross-attention layers will recover mid-context fact recall to within90%
of short-context performance without fine-tuning the base LLM. The memory bank
acts as a "second path" that bypasses diluted full-context attention.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
Component1 — Hierarchical Chunking & Summarization

• Split the input context into fixed-size chunks (e.g.,512 tokens each).
• For each chunk, generate a short natural-language summary (<=64 tokens) using
a lightweight LM (e.g., Phi-3-mini). This forms the first summary layer.
• Recursively apply the same process to the summary sequence to produce a
second, coarser summary layer.
• Store all chunks and summaries in a flat key-value store keyed by chunk
position and semantic embedding.

Component2 — Retrieval-Augmented Memory Attention

• Insert a small set of memory tokens (e.g.,128) at the start of each attention
layer's key-value cache during generation.
• At each decoding step, retrieve the top-k chunks/summaries (by cosine
similarity to the current hidden state) from the memory bank.
• Encode the retrieved chunks as additional key-value pairs appended to the
existing full-context KV cache for that layer, but with a separate learned
gating scalar that down-weights the full-context path when memory retrieval
has high confidence.

Component3 — Training (Lightweight)

• Freeze the base LLM entirely.
• Train only the memory encoder (a small transformer, ~50M params), the
retrieval projection layer, and the gating scalars.
• Training objective: next-token prediction on long-document perplexity, with
an auxiliary contrastive loss that pulls the hidden state closer to the
embedding of the chunk containing the ground-truth next token.

Base model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (128K context)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark| Benchmark | Purpose | Metric |

|-----------|---------|--------| | RULER (Hsieh et al.,2024) | Multi-task
long-context probing (needle-in-haystack, multi-needle, variable tracking) |
Accuracy per task, averaged across context lengths4K–128K | | LongBench (Bai et
al.,2024) | Realistic long-document QA, summarization, and few-shot | F1 /
ROUGE-L / accuracy per category | | SCROLLS (Shaham et al.,2022) | Long
narrative & legal document QA | F1 | | Custom: Mid-Context Perturbation Set | A
constructed50K-token corpus where every question's answer appears only in the
middle third (positions33%–66%) | F1 gap relative to same question with answer
in first10% |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics1. Primary: Accuracy on RULER's multi-needle task at64K
and128K context lengths.

2 Secondary:

• Perplexity on held-out long documents (16K–128K).
• Mid-context F1 gap = (accuracy on early-position queries) − (accuracy on
middle-position queries) — lower is better.
• Memory retrieval precision@1 (does the retrieved chunk contain the
ground-truth answer?).

3 Efficiency: Wall-clock time per generation token vs. baseline Llama-3.1 full
attention.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines| Baseline | Why |

|----------|-----| | Base Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (full attention,128K) |
Reference point for lost-in-the-middle | | Llama-3.1 with chunked
cross-attention (no memory, no retrieval) | Ablates the retrieval component | |
LongLoRA fine-tune on long documents | Ablates the "no fine-tuning" claim | |
InfLLM (sparse attention + retrieval) | Closest published method; shows whether
memory bank approach improves over retrieval-only | | GraphRAG / MemWalker
(summarize-then-retrieve) | Tests whether hierarchical summarization alone
(without retrieval gating) is sufficient |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations1. No hierarchical summaries — flat chunk retrieval only. Tests whether
the summary hierarchy matters.

2 No gating scalar — always attend to both full-context and memory paths
equally. Tests whether the learned down-weighting is essential.
3 Memory bank size sweep —32,64,128,256 memory tokens. Characterizes the
trade-off between compute overhead and recall.
4 k retrieval sweep — top-1, top-3, top-5 chunks retrieved. Tests sensitivity
to retrieval depth.
5 Base model size — repeat best configuration on Llama-3.1-70B to test scaling
behavior.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes| Failure Mode | Mitigation in Proposal |

|---|---| | Retrieval noise — retrieved chunks are irrelevant, wasting memory
tokens and confusing the decoder | Contrastive loss in training; gating scalar
can down-weight low-confidence retrievals | | Summary information loss —
compressed summaries lose critical entity/relation details | Two-layer hierarchy
with flat chunks as fallback; both are stored and retrievable | | Memory token
overhead kills speed —128 extra tokens ×32 layers creates latency blowup | Only
insert memory tokens at the last ~8 layers (ablate this design choice);
benchmark wall-clock time explicitly | | No improvement over InfLLM —
retrieval-only methods already capture mid-context facts | If so, the result is
still publishable: lightweight memory bank training is insufficient without
architecture changes; report negative result | | Positional embedding mismatch —
retrieved chunks lack correct positional IDs, confusing the base model | Use a
learned positional offset based on the chunk's original position in the
document; if this fails, try position-invariant retrieval (RoPE-free encoding) |
| Contrastive loss collapses — all chunk embeddings converge to a single point |
Add a uniformity regularization term (uniformity loss from CLIP); monitor
embedding diversity during training |

question: Generate a research proposal on cross-cultural alignment for Large Language Models.
answer_a:
Cross-Cultural Alignment for Large Language Models: A Value-Sensitive Framework
for Pluralistic Objective Specification### ProblemCurrent LLM alignment
techniques (RLHF, DPO, constitutional AI) implicitly encode a monolithic,
Western-centric value system. Preference datasets used for alignment —
Helpful/Honest/Harmless (Anthropic), OpenAssistant, ShareGPT — overwhelmingly
reflect English-speaking, WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich,
Democratic) cultural norms. This creates two interrelated problems:

 1 Value erasure: Culturally specific values (e.g., ubuntu in Southern Africa
   emphasizing community over individual autonomy, wa in Japan emphasizing
   social harmony, face in East Asian interaction norms) are not represented in
   preference data, so aligned models default to Western defaults even when
   serving non-Western users.
 2 False universalism: Models confidently assert ethical judgments that vary
   across cultures (e.g., attitudes toward filial piety, privacy, censorship, or
   politeness strategies) as if they were universal truths, undermining trust
   and usability in global deployment.

Existing cross-cultural work in NLP focuses on detecting cultural bias in model
outputs but rarely proposes a method for aligning models to specified cultural
value profiles. The core challenge is that cultural alignment is not a single
target — it requires pluralistic alignment where the same model can adapt its
behavior to different cultural contexts without full retraining.

HypothesisPrimary: Specifying cultural value profiles as explicit, structured
preference criteria — rather than relying on implicit cultural signal in
training data — enables controllable cross-cultural alignment of LLMs via
post-training methods, without degrading core capabilities.

Secondary: Value-sensitive preference optimization (using culturally grounded
constraints during DPO/RLHF training) produces better cultural adherence than
prompting alone (in-context cultural framing) and generalizes to held-out
cultural scenarios, while prompting alone only captures surface-level cultural
markers (greetings, honorifics, lexical choices) without deeper value-consistent
reasoning.

MethodWe propose Culturally Constrained Preference Optimization (C²PO), a
three-stage framework:

Stage1: Cultural Value Profile Extraction For each target culture, construct a
machine-readable value profile consisting of:

 • Values Inventory:8–12 culturally salient value dimensions drawn from
   cross-cultural psychology literature (Hofstede, Schwartz, GLOBE, World Values
   Survey) — e.g., individualism/collectivism, power distance, uncertainty
   avoidance, long-term orientation, indulgence/restraint, harm avoidance,
   loyalty vs. impartiality, purity/sanctity.
 • Behavioral Anchors:3–5 concrete behavioral indicators per value dimension,
   phrased as decision rules (e.g., under high power distance: "When a junior
   colleague expresses disagreement with a senior figure, prefer indirect or
   deferential phrasing over direct contradiction").
 • Conflict Resolution Heuristics: Prioritization rules for when value
   dimensions conflict (e.g., collectivism may override directness).

Profiles are validated by native-language informants from each culture (≥3 per
culture) through structured surveys.

Stage2: Culturally-Grounded Preference Data Generation For each target culture:

 • Sample500–1,000 prompts from culturally diverse sources (parallel cultural
   web corpora, translated GlobalOpinion survey questions, culturally grounded
   social scenarios from CCC and KultFace benchmarks).
 • For each prompt, generate two model responses per value profile: one that
   satisfies the profile's decision rules and one that violates them (using
   automated rule-checking + human verification).
 • Construct preference pairs labeled by cultural adherence, not generic
   helpfulness/harmlessness.

Stage3: Pluralistic Preference Optimization Train one base model per family
(e.g., Llama-3-8B, Mistral-7B) using Direct Preference Optimization on combined
preference pairs across cultures. During training, condition on a culture
identifier token prepended to the prompt. At inference, the user specifies their
cultural context either explicitly ("Respond for a [culture] context") or
implicitly (predicted from user interaction signals).

Evaluate three configurations:

 • C²PO-full: Full profile-guided preference data + DPO with culture
   conditioning- C²PO-prompt-only: No DPO; same base model with in-context
   cultural framing ("Respond as a helpful assistant in [culture] context")
 • C²PO-generic: DPO on generic (non-culturally-grounded) preference data
   equivalent in size### Dataset & BenchmarkTraining data: Culturally grounded
   preference pairs (described above) constructed from:
 • CCC (Cultural Common-sense Corpus): ~5K culturally annotated scenarios
   across10 countries- KultFace: Culturally grounded negotiation/conflict
   scenarios- GlobalOpinion survey items:100+ value-laden questions covering
   moral dilemmas, social norms, political attitudes- Synthetic generation:
   Prompted cultural scenarios validated by informantsEvaluation benchmark
   (constructed for this work):
 • CrossCulturalAlign (CCA):200 test prompts per target culture (5 cultures: US,
   Japan, India, Saudi Arabia, Brazil), each annotated with:
 • Expected cultural value profile adherence (binary per value dimension)
 • "Best" and "worst" response exemplars from culturally native annotators -
   Cultural authenticity rating (Likert1–5, "How well does this response reflect
   [culture] norms?")
 • CCA-HeldOut:50 prompts per culture testing unseen cultural scenarios to
   measure generalization beyond memorized patternsTarget cultures selected to
   maximize value-profile diversity: US (high individualism, low power
   distance), Japan (high collectivism, high uncertainty avoidance, high
   long-term orientation), India (high power distance, moderate collectivism),
   Saudi Arabia (high power distance, high conservatism), Brazil (high
   indulgence, moderate collectivism).

Evaluation MetricsPrimary:

 • Cultural Adherence@k (CA@k): Proportion of outputs where the model selects
   the culturally preferred response over alternatives in a multiple-choice
   setup (k response candidates generated from the same prompt under different
   value profiles). Target: ≥80% agreement with native annotator judgments.
 • Cultural Authenticity Score: Average Likert rating (1–5) from ≥3 native
   annotators per culture, blinded to model condition. Minimum acceptable:3.5/5
   for target culture.

Secondary:

 • Capability Retention: No >5% degradation on MMLU, BBH, or HumanEval compared
   to the base model (untrained).
 • Cross-Cultural Confusion Rate: Rate at which responses intended for culture A
   are re-identified by annotators from culture B as better fitting culture B
   (ideal: near0%; threshold: <15%).
 • Value Conflict Resolution Accuracy: When a prompt activates two competing
   value dimensions, does the model apply the correct priority rule from the
   profile?

Robustness:

 • Per-culture performance variance (target: <20% relative across cultures — no
   culture should be significantly worse served)
 • Ablation sensitivity (removing one value dimension from the profile reduces
   adherence specifically on that dimension)

Baselines1. Vanilla base model (no alignment): Llama-3-8B, Mistral-7B —
establishes minimum cultural sensitivity from pretraining alone.

 2 Standard RLHF model: Off-the-shelf aligned models (Llama-3-8B-Instruct,
   Mistral-7B-Instruct) — represents status quo of monolithic alignment.
 3 In-context cultural prompting (C²PO-prompt-only): Same base model with
   culturally framed system prompt — isolates the effect of profile-guided
   training from pure prompting.
 4 Generic-alignment DPO (C²PO-generic): DPO trained on same volume of
   non-culturally-grounded preferences — controls for data quantity vs. cultural
   specificity.
 5 Culture-specific fine-tuning: Independently fine-tune one LoRA adapter per
   culture on value-aligned data — establishes an upper bound at the cost of
   parameter multiplicity.

Ablations1. -Value Rules: Remove explicit value profile decision rules; use only
raw annotator preferences without structured value annotations. Tests whether
structured value specification improves over raw human judgments.

 2 -Conflict Heuristics: Remove conflict resolution priority rules; let the
   model resolve value conflicts implicitly. Tests whether explicit
   prioritization is necessary.
 3 -Culture Conditioner: Train DPO without culture identifier conditioning; use
   a single merged model. Tests whether conditioning is needed for pluralistic
   alignment or if profiles can be distinguished from prompt content alone.
 4 -Annotator Validation: Replace validated value profiles with automated
   extraction from World Values Survey data alone. Tests whether
   machine-extracted cultural profiles suffice or human validation is critical.

Expected Failure Modes1. Cultural homogenization from shared training: Training
on preference data from multiple cultures simultaneously may wash out distinct
cultural signals, producing a bland "middle culture" that satisfies no group
well. Mitigated by culture-conditioned training + per-culture evaluation. If
this fails, switch to independent adapters per culture.

 2 Profile overspecification: Value rules may be too rigid for nuanced scenarios
   where cultural norms depend on context (e.g., formal vs. informal settings,
   urban vs. rural). The dichotomous decision rules likely underrepresent
   within-culture variance. Expected to manifest as high annotator disagreement
   on scenarios at the boundaries of profiles. Mitigation: report within-culture
   variance explicitly; consider probabilistic (rather than binary) value
   adherence.
 3 Annotator bias: Native informants may disagree on what constitutes culturally
   appropriate behavior, especially in heterogeneous cultures (India, Brazil).
   Using ≥3 annotators and measuring inter-annotator agreement (Fleiss' kappa)
   is essential but may still yield low agreement for culturally contested
   scenarios. If agreement is low (<0.4), flag these items as "culturally
   ambiguous" rather than dropping them.
 4 Surface mimicry without deep alignment: The model may learn to produce
   surface-level cultural markers (honorifics, indirect phrasing, local idioms)
   while failing at deeper value-consistent reasoning (e.g., using polite
   language but endorsing an individualistic value judgment in a collectivist
   context). The C²PO-prompt-only baseline is designed to detect this failure by
   comparing surface-only (prompting) vs. trained alignment.
 5 Language confounding: Corpora for non-English cultures are predominantly in
   the local language. Results may conflate cultural alignment with language
   capability. Include English-translated variants of non-English test prompts
   to disentangle.
 6 English-dominant pretraining interference: Base models are trained on
   predominantly English data and may have strong priors against certain
   cultural value profiles. This may make DPO optimization harder for value
   profiles far from Western defaults. Monitor and report per-culture training
   loss trajectories.

Limitations1. Coverage restricted to five cultures. Generalizability to the ~200
countries and thousands of cultural groups is unknown. The framework is designed
to be extensible, but validation is limited to the chosen cultures.

 2 Within-culture variation is compressed. Value profiles aggregate to
   national-level cultural tendencies, masking variation by region, ethnicity,
   class, age, and religion. The approach risks reinforcing cultural stereotypes
   if users interpret profile-conditional outputs as universally representative
   of all members of a culture.
 3 Cultural profile construction requires expert labor. Scaling to many cultures
   is constrained by the availability of culturally knowledgeable annotators.
   Automated value extraction from WVS or social media may reduce cost but has
   unknown validity (see ablation4).
 4 No dynamic cultural adaptation. The framework uses a static per-culture
   profile at inference time. Real cultural adaptation likely requires updating
   the cultural model from user interaction, which is not addressed here.
 5 Cross-cultural comparison metrics are inherently normative. Defining "good"
   cultural alignment presupposes a standard for what constitutes authentic
   cultural representation — a standard that may itself be culturally contested.
   We measure agreement with native annotator judgments, but annotators are not
   unbiased oracles of cultural authenticity.
 6 Safety implications of controllable cultural alignment. The same mechanism
   that enables culturally appropriate responses could be used to align models
   to harmful cultural norms (e.g., justifying discrimination under "cultural
   values"). The framework does not include safeguards against alignment to
   values that violate universal human rights.

Title: CULTURAL-PREF: Preference Tuning with Culturally-Grounded Contrastive
Examples for Cross-Cultural LLM AlignmentProblem. Current RLHF/DPO alignment
pipelines overwhelmingly use preference data annotated by English-speaking,
Western raters. This produces models that (a) treat Western cultural norms as
universal defaults, (b) give culturally inappropriate or offensive answers in
non-Western contexts, and (c) lack measurable mechanisms to control which
cultural frame the model should adopt for a given user or query. No existing
work has systematically decomposed which dimensions of alignment (helpfulness,
harmlessness, honesty, social norms) are most culturally divergent, nor tested
whether targeted preference data can close the gap without degrading Western
performance.

Hypothesis. Fine-tuning an LLM with preference pairs where the same query
receives different culturally appropriate responses across target cultures
(e.g., Japanese vs. Brazilian vs. Saudi Arabian social norms) will produce a
model whose outputs can be steered toward a specified cultural frame via a
lightweight prompt prefix, while maintaining competitive performance on standard
Western-centric benchmarks. The core claim: cultural divergence in alignment is
concentrated in a small set of behavioral dimensions (social hierarchy,
indirectness, taboo topics, gift-giving norms, and individualist vs.
collectivist framing), and targeted contrastive examples on these dimensions
suffice to induce generalizable cross-cultural behavior.

Method. Three-stage pipeline:

1 Taxonomy construction. Use a research-agent-assisted literature review of
cross-cultural psychology (Hofstede dimensions, GLOBE project, Hall's
high/low context) and existing culturally-aware LLM datasets (CULTURALBENCH,
CULTUREPAIR, GLOBALALIGN) to produce a taxonomy of8–12 behavioral dimensions
where LLM outputs are expected to diverge across cultures. Each dimension
gets a one-paragraph annotation specifying the expected range of appropriate
behavior.
2 Contrastive preference dataset. For each dimension, generate200–400
query-response triples (query, culturally-appropriate-response-A,
culturally-appropriate-response-B) across two target cultures (e.g.,
US-English and Japanese) using human annotation or validated LLM-as-judge
pipelines with culture-specific rubrics. Each triple explicitly labels which
cultural frame each response fits. Total target: ~3,000–5,000 preference
pairs.
3 Preference tuning & steering. Fine-tune a base model (e.g., Llama-3-8B or
Qwen-2.5-7B) via DPO on the contrastive dataset. Add a steering mechanism: a
prepended system prompt specifying the target cultural frame (e.g., "You are
a helpful assistant responding to someone in Japan. Follow Japanese social
norms: use polite register, avoid direct refusals, respect hierarchical
address."). Evaluate whether steering via prompt alone suffices or whether a
lightweight adapter (LoRA per culture) is needed.

Dataset / Benchmark.

• Training: Custom constructed dataset (described above).
• Evaluation: CULTURALBENCH (cross-cultural QA and social norms), CULTUREPAIR
(culturally sensitive comparison pairs), and a subset of GLOBALALIGN (moral
and social alignment across10+ countries). Also construct a held-out
"cross-cultural adversarial" test set of200 prompts where the appropriate
response differs sharply between two cultures (e.g., feedback to a superior,
gift refusal, discussion of religious holidays).

Evaluation Metrics.

• Cultural appropriateness score: Agreement with human raters from each target
culture (≥3 raters per item, Krippendorff's α ≥0.7 threshold) on a5-point
Likert scale measuring whether the response is culturally appropriate for the
specified frame.
• Steerability accuracy: For each culture-steered query, does the model's
response align with the intended culture (vs. default/majority culture)?
Measured by both human evaluation and an LLM judge fine-tuned on the same
taxonomy.
• Western benchmark retention: Performance drop on HellaSwag, MMLU, and
MT-Bench. Threshold: ≤2% absolute degradation.
• Dimension-level divergence: Per-dimension score showing which cultural
dimensions the model handles well vs. poorly.

Baselines.

1 Base model (no fine-tuning): Shows the default cultural bias of the
pretrained model.
2 Standard DPO (general preference data): Trained on the full HelpSteer2 or
UltraFeedback dataset (no cultural conditioning). Measures whether standard
alignment already produces monocultural outputs.
3 Naive prompt steering: Apply the same culture-steering prompt to the base
model without fine-tuning. Isolates the effect of prompting vs. preference
tuning.
4 Culture-agnostic DPO + prompt steering: DPO on the contrastive dataset
without culture labels during training, but with steering prompts at
inference. Tests whether contrastive data alone helps even without labeled
training.

Ablations.

• Dimension ablation: Remove one behavioral dimension at a time from the
contrastive dataset. Which dimensions are critical for cross-cultural
generalization?
• Data scaling: Train on10%,25%,50%,100% of the contrastive dataset. Is there a
diminishing-returns threshold?
• Model scale: Repeat the best configuration on a1B,7B, and27B parameter model
(or whatever sizes are available). Does cross-cultural steerability scale
with model size?
• Target culture ablation: Train on US–Japan pairs only, then evaluate on
US–Brazil and US–Saudi Arabia. Does the method generalize to unseen target
cultures?

Expected Failure Modes.

1 Surface-level mimicry. The model learns to insert polite markers and
culture-specific keywords without understanding deeper social norms (e.g.,
produces Japanese honorifics but gives a direct refusal that violates
Japanese indirectness norms). Mitigation: Include examples where the surface
form and deep norm diverge, and evaluate with adversarial probes that test
for this distinction.
2 Steering interference. The culture-steering prompt competes with the base
model's pre-existing alignment (refusal training, safety filters), producing
unpredictable behavior in safety-critical queries. Mitigation: Explicitly
include edge-case safety prompts in the contrastive dataset and measure
safety metric separately.
3 Overfitting to stereotype. The taxonomy-based approach encodes stereotypical
or outdated cultural norms, producing responses that caricature rather than
respect the target culture. Mitigation: Validate all dimension annotations
with in-culture reviewers; include intra-cultural variation examples (e.g.,
both formal and informal Japanese responses).
4 Western performance collapse. Teaching the model to deviate from its default
alignment causes broad degradation on standard English benchmarks.
Mitigation: Monitor Western benchmarks throughout training, early-stop if
degradation exceeds2%, and test whether a residual connection or adapter
merging strategy preserves base capabilities.
5 Rater disagreement. Human raters from the same culture disagree on what
constitutes an appropriate response, making the ground-truth labels noisy.
Mitigation: Use an agreement threshold (Krippendorff's α ≥0.7) and discard or
re-annotate items below it. Report confidence intervals on all human
evaluation metrics.
6 Non-transferability to unseen cultures. The model learns a mapping from
"culture token → behavior" but fails on cultures not seen during training.
Mitigation: The target-culture ablation (train on US–Japan, test on
US–Brazil, US–Saudi Arabia) directly tests this; if it fails, the method
collapses to a retrieval problem rather than actual cultural generalization.

This is the -IDE ablation, so no loading of prior memory, no multi-persona
ideation pipeline, no ELO tournament, and no memory update. The proposal is
generated from the query and ordinary reasoning alone.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Learning to Align: A Dynamic Preference Refinement Framework for Value-Guided AI
  Agents## ProblemCurrent value alignment techniques rely on static preference
encoding — reward models, constitutional principles, or RLHF reward signals are
frozen after training. This creates a fundamental mismatch: human values are not
  static. They shift across contexts (deployment environment), cultures (user
populations), and times (societal norms evolve). An agent trained to avoid harm
 in a controlled setting may lack the reasoning machinery to recognize a novel
   ethical dilemma in the wild, and once deployed, it cannot update its value
representation without expensive retraining. The core problem is that alignment
 is treated as a one-time optimization problem rather than a continual learning
                                    problem.

Existing approaches — RLHF, ConST (constitutional AI), debate, and distilled
self-supervision — all converge on a single fixed reward or rule set. None endow
the agent with the capability to detect when its value representation is
mismatched with its environment and self-correct through interaction. This
leaves deployed agents brittle: they fail silently on out-of-distribution moral
scenarios, cannot recover from value drift, and offer no mechanism for
human-in-the-loop value correction post-deployment.

HypothesisAn AI agent can achieve more robust and adaptable value alignment by
maintaining an explicit, lightweight value representation that is updated
through a meta-cognitive feedback loop — detecting misalignment signals from
environment feedback and human oversight, then refining its value encoding
online — without forgetting previously learned value boundaries. Specifically, a
dynamic preference refinement mechanism, which treats value learning as a
few-shot adaptation problem with a frozen base policy and a plastic value
adapter, will outperform static alignment methods on held-out ethical scenarios
and distribution-shifted deployment conditions.

MethodValue-Guided Agent with Adaptive Preference Encoding (VAGAPE)

The framework has three components:

1. Frozen Base Policy + Lightweight Value Adapter. A pre-trained language model
(or RL policy) is kept frozen. Attached to it is a small, tunable value adapter
— a low-rank residual module (inspired by LoRA) that projects the model's hidden
states into a value score. The base policy generates actions; the value adapter
scores each candidate action along a learned value dimension. The final action
is selected by balancing task reward and value score via a scalar temperature.

2. Misalignment Detection Module. At inference time, the agent maintains a value
confidence estimate. When the value adapter's confidence on a given input falls
below a threshold — measured by the entropy of the value score distribution
across multiple stochastic forward passes — or when a human explicitly flags an
action, a value refinement signal is triggered. The module also monitors for
reward surprise: if the achieved task reward deviates sharply from the value
adapter's predicted value score, this is treated as an implicit misalignment
cue.

3. Online Value Refinement via Few-Shot Replay. Upon detecting misalignment, the
agent enters a refinement phase: it constructs a small replay buffer containing
(state, action, human-feedback) tuples from the recent misaligned episode,
combined with anchor examples from its initial training distribution (preserved
via a small episodic memory). The value adapter is then fine-tuned for a small
number of gradient steps (K=3–5) to minimize a contrastive loss that pulls the
value scores of approved actions up and pushes disapproved actions down. The
frozen base policy ensures that this fine-tuning does not cause catastrophic
forgetting of task competence.

Key design choices:

 • The value adapter is orders of magnitude smaller than the base policy (~0.1%
   of parameters), making online updates computationally feasible.
 • Anchor examples from training prevent the adapter from overfitting to a
   single edge case.
 • The detection threshold is adaptive: it tightens over time as the agent
   accumulates more refinement episodes, reflecting growing value competence.

Dataset / BenchmarkALIGN-Bench (constructed by combining and adapting three
existing resources):

 1 ETHICS (Hendrycks et al.) —130k+ examples spanning justice, deontology,
   virtue ethics, utilitarianism, and commonsense morality. Used for initial
   training of the value adapter and as in-distribution evaluation.
 2 MoralChoice (Jiang et al.) / MMLU-alignment subset — Contextual moral
   dilemmas requiring situational judgment. Used for out-of-distribution
   evaluation.
 3 Social Interaction100 (SI-100) — A newly proposed meta-benchmark of100
   text-based social scenarios, each with a distribution-shift variant (e.g.,
   same scenario in a different cultural context or with reversed social norms).
   This tests the agent's ability to detect and adapt to value shifts.

Training split: ETHICS (80/10/10 train/val/test). Evaluation: in-distribution
ETHICS held-out set + out-of-distribution MoralChoice + distribution-shift
SI-100 scenarios.

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Definition | Target |

|--------|------------|--------| | Value Accuracy | Agreement with human
judgments on held-out moral scenarios | >85% | | Misalignment Detection Rate |
Fraction of true misalignment events (human-labeled) detected before a harmful
action is taken | >70% | | Refinement Efficiency | Accuracy on
distribution-shift scenarios after K=5 refinement steps vs. static baseline |
>15% absolute gain | | Catastrophic Forgetting (Task Reward) | Task performance
on original training distribution before vs. after refinement episodes | Δ <2% |
| Online Adaptation Latency | Wall-clock time for the refinement cycle
(detection + update) | <5 seconds | | Human Feedback Efficiency | Number of
human feedback labels required per successful adaptation | <10 labels per shift
event |

Baselines| Baseline | Description | Key Contrast |

|----------|-------------|--------------| | RLHF (static) | Standard
reward-model-based RL fine-tuning, frozen after training | No online adaptation
| | Constitutional AI | Fixed rule-based self-supervision with no update
mechanism | Rules are static; no detection | | Few-shot prompting |
Value-aligned few-shot examples prepended at inference | No learning;
context-window limited | | VAGAPE -Detection | Ablation without misalignment
detection module (updates every N steps blindly) | Tests detection necessity | |
VAGAPE +Full Fine-Tune | Fine-tune entire policy instead of adapter during
refinement | Tests adapter vs. full update |

Ablations1. -Detection — Remove the misalignment detection module; trigger
refinement on a fixed schedule every N steps. Tests whether intelligent
detection is necessary or simply updating frequently suffices.

 2 -Anchors — Remove anchor examples from the replay buffer. Tests whether
   anchor exemplars prevent overfitting to recent feedback.
 3 -ContrastiveLoss — Replace contrastive loss with MSE regression to a scalar
   score. Tests whether relative ordering or absolute scoring matters more for
   value refinement.
 4 SmallAdapter (rank=1) vs. LargeAdapter (rank=8) — Vary the expressivity of
   the value adapter to measure the trade-off between plasticity and forgetting.
 5 K=1 vs. K=10 refinement steps — Tests sensitivity to the number of online
   gradient steps.

Expected Failure Modes1. Detection threshold brittleness. The misalignment
detector may fail in two directions: false positives (triggering spurious
refinements, wasting compute and potentially destabilizing the adapter) and
false negatives (missing genuine value drift). Mitigation: adaptive threshold
with a warm-up period and a manual override channel.

 2 Feedback ambiguity. Human feedback may be inconsistent (two different humans
   flag the same action differently) or noisy (a flagged action is later deemed
   acceptable in context). Mitigation: the contrastive loss naturally handles
   low-magnitude signals, but a degenerate case exists where conflicting
   feedback causes the adapter to oscillate. Hard limit: reject refinement if
   the replay buffer contains contradictory labels for the same state.
 3 Catastrophic forgetting of rare scenarios. Anchor examples cover the training
   distribution but may not cover long-tail ethical edge cases. As the adapter
   is updated, it may drift away from correct behavior on rare but critical
   scenarios (e.g., trolley problems). Mitigation: maintain a corner-case memory
   of high-uncertainty training examples; if their value accuracy drops below a
   threshold, include them in the next refinement cycle.
 4 Value hacking. The agent might learn to produce value scores that satisfy
   human feedback superficially — e.g., agreeing with the human on surface-level
   features while the underlying reasoning remains misaligned. This is the
   online-learning analogue of reward hacking. Mitigation: the contrastive loss
   operates on full state-action representations, not scalar scores, and anchor
   examples tie updates to the original training distribution.
 5 Refinement loop instability. Repeated refinements could cause the value
   adapter to saturate or oscillate. Mitigation: impose an upper bound on total
   refinement steps per deployment horizon and a cooldown period between
   refinements.

Limitations1. Simulated human feedback. We evaluate using human judgments from
existing datasets, not real-time human interaction. Real human feedback is
noisier, slower, and more expensive. The efficiency results (e.g., "human
feedback efficiency") are estimates that require validation in a real human
study.

 2 Text-based scenarios only. The method is evaluated on language-based moral
   reasoning. Extending to embodied agents or multi-modal settings introduces
   additional complexity (e.g., detecting misalignment from visual cues).
 3 Short-horizon adaptation. The framework is evaluated over a small number of
   refinement episodes (K ≤10 per scenario). Long-horizon value drift over weeks
   or months of deployment is not studied.
 4 Single-agent setting. Value alignment is treated as an isolated agent
   problem. In multi-agent settings, conflicting value updates across agents
   could arise, which this framework does not address.
 5 No deep normative grounding. The framework learns which values to follow from
   human feedback, but does not reason about why a given value is correct. It is
   a descriptive alignment method, not a normative one — it aligns to observed
   preferences, not to a formal ethical theory.
 6 Compute cost of online learning. While the adapter is small, the detection
   module requires Monte Carlo dropout at inference, adding latency. For
   real-time applications, this overhead may be non-trivial.

Research Proposal: Steering Vector–Based Value Control in Large Language
Models## Title
Value Steering Without Fine-Tuning: Representation Engineering for
Controllable AI Alignment

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Current value alignment methods for LLMs — primarily RLHF and
constitutional AI — operate at the parametric level: they fine-tune model
weights using reward-model scores or self-critique data. This creates two
unresolved problems:

1 Value brittleness under distribution shift — an RLHF-tuned model may behave
consistently on in-distribution helpfulness/harmlessness prompts but fail on
adversarial inputs, domain shifts, or tasks that were not represented in the
preference data.
2 Value entanglement with capability — fine-tuning for alignment inevitably
modifies weights that also encode reasoning, factual recall, and linguistic
ability, making it difficult to attribute behavior changes to "value
learning" versus capability degradation or surface-level pattern matching.

A method that can separately control value-relevant behavior without modifying
base weights would enable testable hypotheses about whether alignment is a
representational property or a learned behavioral policy.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Primary hypothesis: For a given LLM, there exists a low-dimensional
subspace in the residual stream (or attention head outputs) such that
intervention along a value direction — defined by contrasting activation
patterns on value-consistent vs. value-violating examples — shifts the model's
alignment-relevant generation behavior on held-out prompts with statistical
significance (p <0.01, Bonferroni-corrected across5 dimensions) while preserving
perplexity on standard language modeling benchmarks within2% of the unmodified
model.

Secondary hypothesis: Value steering vectors generalize across related value
dimensions (e.g., a "honesty" vector improves "fairness" behavior) but are
separable from capability-related vectors (e.g., "reasoning quality," "factual
recall"), as measured by cosine similarity between steering directions <0.15.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
The proposal adapts representation engineering (RepE) (Zou et al.,2023) to
value alignment with three modifications:

1 Contrastive activation collection. For each target value dimension (e.g.,
helpfulness, harmlessness, honesty, fairness), collect500 contrast pairs from
a public preference dataset (Anthropic HH-RLHF or PKU-SafeRLHF). Each pair
consists of a value-consistent completion and a value-violating completion
for the same prompt. Extract hidden states at every layer from the residual
stream and attention outputs for both completions. The value direction for
layer l is the top PCA component of the difference vectors Δ = h(consistent)
− h(violating).
2 Reading and steering. Two operations:

• Reading: Compute alignment along each direction for a test prompt by
projecting the model's activations onto the value direction. This produces a
scalar "value alignment score" per layer without any generation.
• Steering: At inference time, add a scaled value direction vector (coefficient
α) to the residual stream at a chosen layer set. Generate completions under

question: Help me generate a research proposal on general-purpose audio foundation models.
answer_a:
Title: Unified Audio Foundation Models: A Multi-Task, Multi-Domain Pretraining
FrameworkProblem: Audio understanding spans diverse tasks — speech recognition,
speaker diarization, music analysis, sound event detection, and paralinguistics
— each traditionally addressed by specialized architectures and training
recipes. Recent foundation models aim to unify these, but they either target a
single audio domain (e.g., speech only), or they scale a single architecture
across domains without principled handling of the fragmented label spaces,
variable-length temporal structure, and conflicting optimization objectives
inherent to multi-domain audio. The core challenge is: can one model, one
pretraining stage, and one finetuning protocol match or exceed specialist
performance across all major audio tasks simultaneously?

Hypothesis: A transformer encoder pretrained with a hybrid objective combining
masked audio modeling, contrastive alignment with paired text labels, and a
domain-adaptive loss weighting scheme will produce representations that
generalize across speech, music, and environmental sound tasks, achieving
competitive per-task performance without task-specific architectural
modifications.

Method:

 1 Architecture: A Conformer-style encoder (convolution-augmented transformer)
   with12 layers,768 hidden dim,8 attention heads, and a50 Hz framerate output.
   To handle variable-length input, we use a learned positional encoding scheme
   and a simple mean-pooling readout for utterance-level tasks. No task-specific
   output heads during pretraining — the shared representation is the only model
   body.
 2 Pretraining data (multi-domain, ~100k hours):

 • Speech: LibriLight (60k hours) + Common Voice (20k hours) + VoxPopuli (10k
   hours)
 • Music: MusicNet + MAESTRO + FMA-large (combined ~10k hours)
 • Environmental sound: AudioSet (6k hours) + FSD50K + ESC-50 Total ≈100k hours;
   all resampled to16 kHz, normalized to -25 dB LUFS.

 3 Pretraining objectives (three-term hybrid):

 • Masked Audio Modeling (MAM): Mask25% of time-frequency patches; predict
   normalized log-mel spectrogram reconstructions via MSE loss.
 • Contrastive Language-Audio Pretraining (CLAP): Align audio encoder outputs
   with paired textual descriptions using a symmetric InfoNCE loss, with a
   shared text encoder (frozen DistilBERT). This provides a zero-shot interface.
 • Domain-Adaptive Loss Weighting (DALW): Learn a scalar per domain
   (speech/music/environmental) that weights the three losses dynamically during
   pretraining, using uncertainty-based homoscedastic task weighting to prevent
   one domain from dominating.

 4 Finetuning protocol: For each downstream task, attach a small linear
   projection head (1-2 layers). Finetune the full model with a task-specific
   loss for10% of the pretraining steps at a5× lower learning rate. Report both
   finetuned and zero-shot results.

Benchmark & Datasets (6 tasks across3 domains):

 • Speech: LibriSpeech test-clean/test-other (ASR WER), SUPERB (phoneme
   recognition, speaker identification)
 • Music: MusicNet (note onset/offset/frame F1), MAESTRO (piano transcription)
 • Environmental sound: ESC-50 (zero-shot classification accuracy), AudioSet
   (sound event detection mAP)

Evaluation Metrics:

 • Per-task: WER (speech), F1 (music transcription), accuracy (environmental),
   mAP (AudioSet)
 • Aggregate: Average normalized rank across tasks (lower is better), with rank
   computed per task relative to published specialist baselines.
 • Zero-shot: CLAP-based linear probe accuracy on ESC-50, AudioSet.

Baselines:

 1 Specialist per task: wav2vec2.0 (speech), MT3 (music), AST (environmental
   sound)
 2 Unified but domain-only: HuBERT (speech only), CLAP (audio-text only)
 3 Full unified baselines: Whisper (speech only, large), WavLM (speech +
   non-speech), AudioMAE (masked autoencoder), HEAR challenge winnersAblations
   (the proposed model, varied systematically):

 • Remove MAM → only CLAP + DALW- Remove CLAP → only MAM + DALW- Remove DALW →
   uniform loss weighting- Remove pretraining entirely → train from scratch per
   task- Half the pretraining data (50k hours) — measure data scaling- Single
   domain pretraining → pretrain on speech only then finetune on all tasks
   (tests cross-domain transfer from one specialization)
 • ★ This experiment (-IDE): Substitute domain-adaptive loss weighting with
   equal weighting and remove the learned per-domain gating. No idea-direction
   evolution — no mining of past successful representations to inform the
   weighting scheme. The DALW gating parameters are set to fixed uniform values,
   and no memory of which domains proved "easy" or "hard" in prior rounds is
   retained. Loss weights are set to [1/3,1/3,1/3] throughout training.

Expected Failure Modes:

 • Domain interference: Speech, music, and environmental sounds have very
   different spectral structure. Joint training might degrade all three if the
   optimizer oscillates between conflicting gradient directions. The DALW
   ablation (-IDE) is expected to exacerbate this — uniform weighting may let
   the dominant domain (by data volume, e.g., speech) suppress the others.
 • CLAP collapse: If paired text descriptions are not available uniformly across
   domains (e.g., music captions are scarce), the contrastive loss may provide
   weak signal for music and environmental tasks.
 • Masked modeling mismatch: MAM reconstruction works well for speech
   (continuous, periodic) but may be less informative for transient events in
   environmental audio.
 • Zero-shot brittleness: CLAP-based zero-shot on ESC-50 may underperform simple
   supervised linear probes by10–20 points absolute.

Limitations:

 • The100k-hour pretraining corpus, while large, is an order of magnitude
   smaller than proprietary models (e.g., Whisper's680k hours, WavLM's94k hours
   on speech alone with significant filtering). Data scaling may plateau or not
   yet saturate.
 • We do not include generative tasks (text-to-speech, music generation, audio
   inpainting) — this is a representation-only model. Extending to generative
   finetuning would require architectural changes (e.g., a decoder).
 • The benchmark covers6 tasks; many important tasks are omitted (e.g., speaker
   diarization, emotion recognition, language identification, audio captioning).
   Generalization to those is not guaranteed.
 • Domain-adaptive loss weighting adds three learned scalar parameters, which is
   lightweight computationally but may still underfit per-domain dynamics. More
   sophisticated methods (gradient surgery, PCGrad) are not tested.
 • Computational cost: The Conformer-12L model at50 Hz framerate with100k hours
   of pretraining requires approximately4,096 GPU-hours on A100s, placing it out
   of reach for most academic groups without cluster access.

Research Proposal: Reproducing and Extending Masked Audio Modeling for
General-Purpose Audio Foundation Models## Title
Are Masked Autoencoders
Sufficient for General-Purpose Audio Representation Learning? A Reproducibility
and Extension Study of AudioMAE

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Self-supervised audio foundation models promise a single pretrained
backbone that transfers to speech, music, and environmental sound tasks. The
AudioMAE (Xu et al.,2022) architecture—an asymmetric encoder-decoder with a high
mask ratio (75–80%) applied to mel-spectrogram patches—claimed state-of-the-art
transfer on AudioSet, ESC-50, and Speech Commands v2. However, the community
lacks:

1 Independent reproduction — the original code was released late and the
results have not been systematically verified by a separate group.
2 A controlled comparison against reconstruction-based (AudioMAE) vs.
contrastive (CLAP, ImageBind) pretraining objectives for general-purpose use.
3 An ablation isolating what drives performance: high mask ratio, decoder
depth, or patch size?

We aim to reproduce AudioMAE's core results and extend them by introducing a
hybrid objective that combines masked reconstruction with a contrastive
alignment loss (audio-text), testing the hypothesis that reconstruction alone is
insufficient for general-purpose transfer.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Null hypothesis (H₀): AudioMAE's masked reconstruction objective
yields representations that transfer to speech, music, and environmental tasks
as well as or better than a hybrid reconstruction + contrastive objective.

Alternative hypothesis (H₁): Adding a contrastive alignment loss (audio-text)
during pretraining significantly improves downstream transfer on tasks requiring
high-level semantics (e.g., audio captioning, zero-shot sound classification),
while maintaining or improving performance on acoustic-only tasks (e.g., scene
classification).

Falsification condition: If the hybrid model does not outperform AudioMAE on at
least2 out of3 semantic-level downstream tasks (by >2% absolute in the primary
metric) while not regressing by more than1% on acoustic-level tasks, H₁ is
rejected.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
### Stage1 — Reproduce AudioMAEExact reproduction of the AudioMAE baseline
(Xu et al.,2022) using the official configuration:

• Input: Log-mel spectrograms (128 mel bins,1024 FFT,512 hop), patchified
into16×16 patches (time×freq).
• Encoder: ViT-B/16 (12 layers,768 hidden,12 heads).
• Decoder: Lightweight4-layer ViT (384 hidden,6 heads).
• Mask ratio:80% of patches masked.
• Pretraining objective: L2 reconstruction loss in the spectrogram space
(normalized patches).
• Pretraining data: AudioSet-2M (balanced subset of ~2M clips from AudioSet).
• Optimization: AdamW, lr=1.5e-4, cosine decay, batch size1024,800 epochs.

Stage2 — Hybrid Objective (AudioMAE + CLAP-style contrastive head)

Attach a contrastive head to the [CLS] token of the encoder. During
pretraining,50% of batches use reconstruction loss and50% use the InfoNCE loss
aligning audio embeddings with paired text descriptions (from AudioSet labels +
synthetic captions via LaCLAP pipeline). Total loss: L = λ·L_recon +
(1-λ)·L_contrastive, with λ annealed from1.0 →0.5 across training.

Stage3 — Downstream transfer evaluationFreeze encoder, train linear probes (and
separately, full fine-tuning) on each benchmark.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark| Task | Dataset | Metric | Type |

|------|---------|--------|------| | Sound event classification | ESC-50 (50
classes,2000 clips) | Accuracy | Acoustic | | Action recognition (audio) |
AudioSet-20K (20-class subset,20K clips) | mAP | Acoustic | | Speech command
recognition | Speech Commands v2 (35 classes,105K clips) | Accuracy | Acoustic |
| Music genre classification | GTZAN (10 genres,1000 clips) | Accuracy |
Acoustic | | Audio captioning (zero-shot) | Clotho (4981 audio-text pairs) |
SPICE / CIDEr | Semantic | | Zero-shot sound classification | ESC-50 (zero-shot
via text labels) | Accuracy | Semantic |

All splits follow standard published train/validation/test splits.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics- Primary: Accuracy (classification), mAP (multi-label),
SPICE/CIDEr (captioning)

• Secondary: F1-score per class, average precision, zero-shot top-1 / top-5-
Uncertainty:5 random seeds for every downstream result; report mean ± std-
Statistical test: Paired bootstrap test (p <0.05) for the primary metric on
each task, with Bonferroni correction across6 tasks (threshold p <0.0083)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines| Model | Pretraining Objective | Reference |

|-------|----------------------|-----------| | AST (supervised) | Cross-entropy
on AudioSet | Gong et al.,2021 | | AudioMAE (reproduced) | Masked reconstruction
(80% mask) | Xu et al.,2022 | | CLAP | Contrastive (audio-text) | Elizalde et
al.,2023 | | Hybrid (Ours) | Reconstruction + contrastive | This work | |
ImageBind | Multimodal contrastive (6 modalities) | Girdhar et al.,2023 |

All baselines use ViT-B/16 encoders with comparable capacity. All linear probes
and fine-tuning protocols are identical across models.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations1. Mask ratio sweep:                                                   Goodbye!
